The body in charge of Britain's electricity network has given assurances that the lights will stay on this winter after concerns were raised by some of its engineers.
The National Energy System Operator (NESO) said the country's electricity system was prepared and "resilient to the challenges it may face" during the colder months.
However, its winter outlook report comes after an independent investigation found engineers had "high levels of stress and concern" about their ability to ensure adequate supply due to differences between renewable and gas-fired power generation.
NESO said supplies were expected to remain secure throughout the winter, though warned there could be "tight days".
It added that such days would result in it deploying notices to power producers that additional electricity generation may be needed. It said such an announcement was not a warning of power cuts and was routine.
"While we never take resilience for granted, households and businesses can be confident that Great Britain's electricity system remains secure, reliable and among the most resilient in the world," said Deborah Petterson, director of whole energy system resilience at NESO.
In a separate report, National Gas, a private company that owns and runs the country's gas network, and is separate from NESO, said it expected to have sufficient supply to meet demand this winter, but forecast gas for power generation to increase at peak demand due to the "intermittent" nature of renewables.
Supply under scrutiny
The release of the two reports comes as Britain's energy generation and security falls under increasing scrutiny, given the wars in the Middle East and eastern Europe have pushed prices up and sparked supply fears.
The country's electricity is generated from a wide range of sources, including renewables such as solar and wind, as well as more traditional gas-fired and nuclear power stations.
Wind power was the largest generator of electricity in Britain last year, accounting for almost 30% of all power, marginally above gas.
However, there appear to be challenges in the transition to renewables in ensuring supply keeps up with demand, according to findings from an investigation into practices at NESO, which was commissioned following allegations over operational decision making and record keeping at the grid operator.
'High levels of stress'
Law firm Eversheds Sutherland, which carried out the independent investigation, said there were "high levels of stress and concern" within NESO's Electricity National Control Centre over the "current state of the energy industry generally" and the longer-term ability to keep it balanced.
It said this was, according to evidence gathered from staff, due to the fact that traditional methods of electricity generation such as gas were "easier to manage", compared to renewables, which were "less flexible", and were making the job of ensuring supply meets demand "more difficult".
The probe also found there to be a "significant disconnect" between those working in the control room and NESO's leadership.
Multiple witnesses expressed the view that those in senior leadership and executive positions "do not fully appreciate or understand either the way in which the control room works, or the reality of the pressures faced by those on the frontline who are responsible for 'keeping the lights on'", Eversheds' report said.
The investigation was prompted after Conservative shadow energy secretary Clare Coutinho said in July she had been contacted by a whistle-blower alleging that NESO had been "hiding information about how securely our grid is being run".
One of the claims was that control room staff were encouraged to conceal or alter records to avoid leaving a paper trail linked to efforts to stabilise the grid during a period of extreme heat in June.
This was done in order for NESO, which is owned by the government, to avoid public scrutiny or reputational damage, according to the allegation.
Eversheds said its investigation did not substantiate any of the allegations from whistle-blowers but did identify "cultural, governance and control issues" that it said were "significant findings in their own right".
Fintan Slye, chief executive of NESO, said the investigation identified "areas where we could improve how colleagues can raise concerns and how we respond to them".
"I want all colleagues at NESO to feel heard. We will act on the recommendations, working closely with our trade unions, and be open with colleagues about the progress we make," he added.

40039b3b5985.text: A small group of Rep. Brandon Gill's fellow House Freedom Caucus members are privately questioning whether he still belongs in the hardline group, Axios has learned. Why it matters: The 32-year-old Texas freshman's rapid rise through House Republican ranks has transformed him into one of the party's most prominent young stars — and earned him a growing list of critics. Driving the news: Multiple House Republicans told Axios that Gill is the future of their party, but several Freedom Caucus members told Axios that his engagement with the group has faded as his national profile has grown. The lawmakers spoke on condition of anonymity to offer candid assessments of a colleague. "He's not really in the Freedom Caucus. He's just using it for conservative bonafides," one HFC member told Axios. The Freedom Caucus is "livid" at Gill, another member told Axios. The intrigue : Four sources familiar with the conversations said members have privately discussed kicking Gill out, though the conversations have been informal and the issue has not been raised at a HFC meeting. It's unclear if there would be enough support within the group to boot Gill if there ever was a formal vote. The other side: "Congressman Gill is laser-focused on getting out the vote and ensuring Republicans hold the majority this November," a spokesperson for Gill told Axios in a statement. State of play: Gill has become a favorite in President Trump's orbit, has won praise from GOP leadership and has launched an ambitious bid to head one of the House's most powerful committees. Asked about the criticism from Gill's colleagues, Majority Whip Tom Emmer (R-Minn.) flatly told Axios in an interview earlier this month that Gill "needs to be out front. I don't care where it is," adding, "Brandon is the future of our party, and his communication skills are phenomenal." But his ascent has fueled resentment, with colleagues accusing him of burning bridges and treating fellow Republicans as stepping stones to greater power and influence. Zoom in: Members say Gill benefited from introductions to HFC donors but hasn't adequately financially supported fellow members in difficult races. "For those of us who have been in meetings, who have been in the tough votes over the last two years, he's been M.I.A.," one HFC member said, adding that he's "totally looking for the ladder climbing." Gill, who is in a R+11 district, raised $4.7 million in the third quarter, a massive haul for a freshman member. Gill's office pointed out that he's given to over a dozen HFC members' campaigns. What they're saying: Freedom Caucus Chair Andy Harris (R-Md.) accused the media of "ginning up stories about Republicans based on anonymous sources," insisting the group is "united and laser-focused" on advancing Trump's agenda. One HFC member defended Gill, telling Axios: "I'm glad that young talented patriots like Brandon are not only coming into politics but that they are climbing quickly...Of course I would like to see him stay in HFC." "I'm not frustrated with Brandon at all," Rep. Mark Harris (R-N.C.), also a freshman member of the caucus, told Axios. "He comes to meetings. I don't know why they feel like he doesn't." "HFC is its own worst enemy sometimes," one GOP member told Axios. "They've managed to kick out, alienate some of their members that help them fundraise." The Freedom Caucus has kicked out members before. In 2023, the group voted to oust former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene (R-Ga.) over a fight with Rep. Lauren Boebert (R-Colo.), and in 2024, the group ousted former Rep. Ken Buck (R-Colo.) for "nonattendance." Friction point: Gill's bid to become the top Republican on the powerful Oversight Committee is also creating friction beyond the Freedom Caucus. Republicans Axios spoke with questioned whether Gill's success at generating viral hearing moments makes him qualified to lead the committee, while others have raised concerns about his history of publicly attacking fellow Republicans like Rep. Maria Salazar (R-Fla.) over her immigration bill . "He's kind of skipping a few steps here, and he doesn't necessarily have the credentials to do it," one House Republican told Axios. Gill has also sought to build influence within the broader conference, contributing $1.1 million to the National Republican Congressional Committee in September. Behind the scenes: A House Republican said Gill stopped returning texts and began treating colleagues differently as his national profile grew, echoing complaints from Gill's Freedom Caucus colleagues. The lawmaker told Axios that there was a sentiment among some Republicans that Gill's fame had gone to his head. Gill, who is president of his freshman class, is a frequent guest on Fox News, including during coveted primetime hours. The big picture: The Freedom Caucus is on the cusp of an identity crisis — at least 10 of HFC's more than two dozen members will not return next term, including some of its most prominent voices . Gill has been viewed by some in the caucus as someone who could fill that void and emerge as a leading voice for the next generation. But the group could gain influence at the highest levels of leadership: Founding member Jim Jordan (R-Ohio) is being floated as a potential minority leader if Republicans lose the House. That could reshape the group's relationship with GOP leadership, which the hard-line caucus has made a habit of challenging . The bottom line: "He's already kind of left the Freedom Caucus," an HFC member told Axios. "The only question is whether you formalize it or you don't."

0c7477f6796d.text: With the midterm elections less than two weeks away, a new legal battle is raising questions about the federal government's role in policing who is eligible to vote. A federal judge in California has blocked a Department of Homeland Security effort to identify noncitizens on voter rolls. White House correspondent Liz Landers reports. Geoff Bennett: With a proper welcome to the "News Hour" now, we should say we had a technical issue at the start of tonight's broadcast. So thank you for bearing with us. Now, with the midterm elections less than two weeks away, a new legal battle is raising questions about the federal government's role in policing who is eligible to vote. A federal judge in California has blocked a Department of Homeland Security effort to identify noncitizens on voter rolls. I spoke earlier about it with our White House correspondent, Liz Landers. So, Liz, this federal judge issued this ruling with now less than two weeks before Election Day. So there's some clear urgency here. Liz Landers: Yes, the Department of Homeland Security has been engaged in this operation since August, according to this lawsuit. And this federal judge in California ruled yesterday that they must restrict their field operations to look for voter fraud and noncitizens on voter rolls. DHS cannot do stops in field interviews unless they think someone is a noncitizen. This applies to nine different states, California, Connecticut, Georgia, Missouri, Nevada, New York, Pennsylvania, Washington, and Wisconsin. There are hundreds of DHS agents who are assigned across all states to look for voter fraud. This has been dubbed the Unlawful Voter Initiative. And the judge here is concerned that the lists created by DHS had errors and did have citizens' names on them. It is already illegal to vote if you are a noncitizen and participate in a federal election here. It's also extremely rare for this to happen. The judge is allowing this to go into effect tomorrow, so that the government has time to appeal. Geoff Bennett: And there's a separate lawsuit the DOJ has brought in California related to mail ballots? Bring us up to speed. Liz Landers: Yes, the Department of Justice is suing the California secretary of state and also the top election official in Los Angeles County to halt them and prevent them from counting 20,000 mail ballots there. DOJ has alleged that there are 20,000 noncitizens on the voter rolls there. The L.A. County registrar's office told me today that they have not stopped the ballot processing there. This is still playing out in a court of law. This is a hearing. The next hearing on this is going to be next Tuesday. And the attorney general, Todd Blanche, was asked about the department's intentions behind the lawsuit earlier today. Todd Blanche, U.S. Attorney General: We're not trying to create chaos. It continues to baffle me why anybody, if presented with evidence that there are tens of thousands, 20,000 ineligible voters that are receiving ballots, that there isn't some motivation, anything to do something about that. Liz Landers: In response to these actions from the Trump administration and others, there's now been a group of Democratic organizations that have sued the Trump administration, alleging voter intimidation. And this lawsuit says that there are -- that the Trump administration is using unfounded voter fraud claims to influence how the elections are conducted. Geoff, I want to be clear here that there are very few, but there are examples of noncitizens voting in elections. New Jersey uncovered a few months ago a software glitch -- this happened years ago -- that allowed noncitizens to register and vote in that state. It was a mistake. There were 6,600 people that registered to vote; 340 of those actually vote. Geoff Bennett: When the DOJ alleges that some 20,000 noncitizens are on the voter rolls in California, where is that number coming from? Liz Landers: So the Department of Justice and the Department of Homeland Security are compiling lists based on state data that they're getting, but it's not complete data sets. And that's why you are seeing states like California, like the secretary of state and the Los Angeles County registrar, saying, we don't know if this is an accurate list. And, in fact, some of those lists that they have been giving back to states saying, hey, we think that all these people are noncitizens, as it turns out, especially in Nevada -- this was a recent example -- there were many people on that list, in fact, all of them in Nevada, who were U.S. citizens. Geoff Bennett: Now, beyond all this, you have also reported today that the Justice Department is preparing a large-scale election monitoring effort? What did they announce? Liz Landers: Yes, a senior Department of Justice official briefed reporters on this and said that they're going to send more than 1,000 election monitors across all 50 states in the country. The agency regularly monitors elections, but this year is a big spike in that number. A DHS -- a DOJ official, I should say, told us that the 2022 midterms had 388 people serving as monitors. So this year would be more than double that. These efforts are guided by federal statutes like the Voting Rights Act. And the DOJ official was very clear that their monitors must follow state and local guidance. This is supposed to be a passive act. These election monitors are supposed to observe and take notes. And monitoring these elections is supposed to be a way to ensure that voting rights laws are being followed, Geoff. Geoff Bennett: And how are state and local officials responding to all of this? Liz Landers: Secretaries of state have started to receive these letters from the Department of Justice about this election monitor program. The Kansas Republican secretary of state, Scott Schwab, he said he got notified earlier this week by DOJ. He's going to allow the election monitors to come to Kansas. When I asked him about this larger program, he kind of

40c84d231ced.text: By — Associated Press Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/iran-says-7-oil-tankers-damaged-in-strait-of-hormuz-and-other-middle-east-news Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Iran says 7 oil tankers damaged in Strait of Hormuz, and other Middle East news World Oct 22, 2026 6:48 PM EDT Iran's state television reported on Thursday that seven oil tankers were either struck by attacks or hit naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz overnight, possibly the largest single-day number of vessels damaged in the waterway since the Iran war started on Feb. 28. Here is the latest news from the Middle East. 7 oil tankers reported damaged in Strait of Hormuz Iran's state television reported that seven oil tankers either caught fire or were damaged by mines overnight Wednesday into Thursday after being targeted or striking naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz. If verified, it would be the largest single-day number of vessels damaged in the waterway since the start of the Iran war on Feb. 28 when the United States and Israel launched joint strikes against Iran. READ MORE: Kansas Sen. Roger Marshall in debate blames Ukraine war, not Iran war, for high diesel prices Quoting a statement by the Revolutionary Guard's navy, the Iranian report said four of the tankers were transferring oil when they were targeted and caught fire. Three more were damaged and immobilized after hitting naval mines. The report didn't provide details about possible casualties or the tankers' flags. Beauty giant L'Oreal says the rise of weight loss drugs has affected beauty and skin care sales, as it designs products to specifically target some side effects of rapid weight loss.
The company's head Nicolas Hieronimus said the beauty market was proving resilient in a challenging global context, and that the use of GLP-1s was "a very important phenomenon for us".
He told an investor call that the rise in their use was "having an impact on beauty consumption and skin care consumption in particular".
L'Oreal, which owns other popular brands including Maybelline and La Roche-Posay, announced on Thursday that sales in the three months to September rose by 7.7%, above analyst expectations.
The use of GLP-1s has boomed in popularity in recent years, after drugs developed to treat diabetes such as Ozempic, Wegovy and Mounjaro were found to also lead to significant weight loss because they supress the appetite.
While it is not caused by GLP-1 drugs directly, rapid weight loss can, for some people, come with a side effect of loose skin - including around the face.
Hieronimus said L'Oreal's brands SkinCeuticals and Kiehl's have products "that have been designed to work alongside and complement GLP-1 and its side effects on skin sagging" and other effects related to rapid weight loss.
L'Oreal has also moved further into the clinical aesthetic space, increasing its stake in dermatology firm Galderma to 20% last December.
Both companies have been testing products on GLP-1 users worried about loose skin in separate clinical trials, according to Reuters.
Galderma owns popular aesthetic products including Sculptra, an injectable aimed at stimulating collagen production, and Restylane, which is an injectable dermal filler.
Last year the aesthetic firm released a report into the rise of GLP-1 use and related concerns about changes in facial appearance.
Its own survey of weight loss medication users found the vast majority had noticed changes to their facial appearance after using those drugs.

Scotland is braced for a wet and windy weekend as two named storms hit in two days.
Storm Austen is the first to sweep across the country, with the Met Office issuing a a yellow warning for rain, external in central and eastern areas from 06:00 on Friday until midnight.
Forecasters say some places could experience 60-80 mm of rain, with a risk of flooding and travel disruption.
Storm Boelo will follow hard on its heels on Saturday, with another yellow weather warning issued, this time for high winds, for the whole of mainland Scotland, the Western Isles and Orkney.
The wind warning will come into force from 18:00 on Saturday and last until 21:00 on Sunday.
The wind speeds are expected build on Saturday afternoon, reaching a peak overnight.
Gusts of 50-65mph are forecast widely and could reach 80mph in exposed locations.
The storm will also bring wet and windy weather across the whole of the UK on Saturday with poor travelling conditions expected due to surface water and spray on faster roads and motorways.
Network Rail Scotland said that trains on Friday will be slowed down to keep people safe in the areas expected to see the heaviest rain.
Speed restrictions will be in place on parts of the West Coast Main Line and East Coast Main Line, as well as routes across southern and eastern Scotland.
It said some journeys would take longer as a result, but that the restrictions meant trains could continue running through areas where the weather is at its worst.
Safety priority
Speed restrictions for trains are also expected in some areas as the second storm moves across the country over the weekend.
Craig Gorman, head of operational weather strategy at Network Rail Scotland, said: "We can't control the weather, but we can make sure we're as ready as possible for whatever it brings.
"We know any disruption from these storms will be frustrating, particularly as it's the weekend, but we'll do everything we can to keep people moving wherever it's safe to do so."
Mark Ilderton, ScotRail service delivery director, said: "Safety is always our top priority and with weather warnings in place as Storm Austen and Storm Boelo bring heavy rain and strong winds to parts of Scotland this weekend, there is an increased risk of flooding and disruption on the railway."
He advised customers to check services before they travel.
Power cuts are possible, which could also affect mobile phone coverage and other services.
There is a small risk of damage to buildings, including roof tiles being blown off, while flying debris could pose a danger to the public.

A United Nations fund to help developing nations pay the costs imposed by climate change voted Thursday to allocate money for Nepal as the country recovers from devastating flooding in August.
It was a historic step for the fund—the first time it has allocated money to a vulnerable country in an immediate response to climate impacts. But that also highlighted the severe limitations it faces.
It was 2022 when nations agreed to create the Fund for responding to Loss and Damage. The aim was for wealthy nations to contribute money that would flow to developing countries to cover irreversible economic losses caused by climate change. The fund has yet to disburse any money.
The disaster in Nepal, where flooding unleashed by a landslide and glacial collapse killed some 1,500 people, with more than 5,000 still missing, was exactly what the fund was meant to address. Several members of its board recognized this during a live-streamed virtual meeting Thursday that was called specifically to consider a request for support from Nepal.
“Loss and damage are no longer a future concern,” said Tomás Soley Pérez, representing Costa Rica. “They are a present reality for many vulnerable countries. Today it is Nepal. Tomorrow it will be any one of our countries.”
Yet while the outcome was widely praised by government representatives and civil society groups, many said it underscored the fund’s weakness and inability to meet its mandate.
The decision by the board, composed of 26 representatives from governments around the globe, did not actually provide the money, $20 million, but merely allocated it—Nepal must now formally apply and have its request approved. Assuming that final step is taken, which could come at the next board meeting in December, the amount distributed would represent less than 1 percent of the initial economic loss and damages from the flooding, which the Nepali government said is at least $2.69 billion. Another $4.71 billion is needed for initial recovery and reconstruction, the government said.
Harjeet Singh, global convenor of the Fill the Fund campaign and founding director of the Satat Sampada Climate Foundation in India, said the vote came only after civil society groups and developing nations launched a relentless campaign pressing the board to take immediate action. Even with this success, he said, Nepal is unlikely to receive any money until next year at the earliest.
Ali Tauqeer Sheikh, representing Pakistan on the fund’s board, called during the meeting for his colleagues to move faster, and criticized the lack of a schedule for the money to flow.
Despite the shortcomings, many people who have supported the fund praised the board’s decision. Raju Pandit Chhetri, lead climate finance negotiator for the least-developed countries at the U.N. Framework Convention on Climate Change, said in a statement: “The Loss and Damage Fund Board’s approval of $20 million for Nepal’s flood response shows that when countries come together, they can reach swift, effective consensus to address the urgent needs of vulnerable countries.”
As of March, 27 countries had pledged $822 million to the fund. The largest amount has come from the United Arab Emirates, which pledged $100 million. Actual contributions were only $630 million, and some of that has yet to be transferred in. The United States contributed $17.5 million in 2024, before the Trump administration withdrew from the Paris climate agreement.
“We don’t have sufficient money, that’s the heart of the problem,” Singh said. He added that wealthy countries have been delaying the disbursement of money and “will continue to delay it because the moment that fund is empty, there’s pressure to fill it again.”

While many developing nations called for this more rapid response to Nepal to serve as a model for the fund to take swift action, representatives of some wealthy countries, including Germany and Japan, said the vote should not set a precedent for future emergency funding outside the board’s standard process.
So far, 119 countries have sent 176 requests to the fund, seeking a total $2.8 billion in support. The board is expected to consider its first funding decisions beyond the emergency money for Nepal at its next meeting in December, with up to $350 million available.
How the board will choose among the requests, with only a fraction of the needed money to spend, Singh said, is “the billion-dollar question.”
Toward the end of Thursday’s meeting, the board heard from Maheshwar Dhakal, a representative of Nepal, who thanked his peers for their support and stressed the severity of what people in his country were experiencing.
“In some of the hardest-hit communities, entire settlements have been wiped out, leaving no survivors to report who has perished or who has survived,” Dhakal said. He added that the vote represented a powerful example of solidarity and hope, saying, “behind these numbers are human lives.”

Trump made the comments after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said connectivity to the military-grade Starshield network, which is provided by Musk's satellite-based Starlink system, had yet to be fully restored.
Musk previously denied he was behind the slowdown, which affects Ukraine's ability to use drones to attack Russia and protect itself from attacks.
Trump refused to be drawn on a report that he had called Musk to ask him to lift restrictions to the service, but when asked about it he said: "Bottom line, he put it back."
The Trump administration previously denied instructing Musk's company to restrict access.
The connectivity restrictions came as Trump put pressure on Zelensky to stop attacking Russian oil refineries, which he has argued have caused prices to rise.
Faced with midterm elections next month, Trump has waived some sanctions on Russia and agreed a deal to import Russian diesel for the US market - a move which has been criticised by Ukraine and its European allies.
Ukraine relies on Starlink - owned by Musk's SpaceX company - for a range of battle communications and early warning systems during Russian missile attacks.
Earlier on Thursday, Zelensky said the speed of the system used by Ukraine's military had still not been restored fully.
Speaking at a press conference, he said the speed "has not been restored to 400 [km/h; 250mph] yet", adding: "We are working on it."
He continued: "I am waiting to hear from US Secretary of State [Marco] Rubio. He promised to get back to me with information within 48 hours or so."
The Ukrainian president made the comments shortly before the Wall Street Journal, external reported that Trump called Musk and asked him to lift restrictions on Ukraine's use of Starlink.
The US outlet reported that Trump told Musk he was frustrated the Starlink system's speeds were still capped at around 160km/h, according to officials.
The speed limit made Ukraine's offensive drones and interceptors powerless against Russian attacks.
The journal reported that the system was working more normally on Thursday, shortly after their conversation.
BBC News has not confirmed the Wall Street Journal's report. It has also contacted the White House and SpaceX to ask for an explanation.
Ukraine first reported an interruption to US intelligence sharing on 14 October.
Musk said last week that the US government ultimately controls access to Starshield, the military-grade version of Starlink which Ukraine uses for some of its operation. He said the system was designed for the Pentagon, suggesting it may therefore be behind the restrictions.
The White House has repeatedly said it did not order access to be restricted.

The Prince of Wales has made a surprise appearance on the Graham Norton Show, as part of a special edition to mark the Earthshot Prize.
During the episode, which airs on Friday, he joined Cate Blanchett, Robert Irwin and Hannah Waddingham, who are all involved with the prize.
As Norton spoke about the initiative with the trio he surprised the audience by then inviting the prince out to join them on the sofa.
They discussed the need to pair optimism and urgency when tackling climate change. The prize was founded by William to "celebrate and scale the solutions that will repair our planet".
The guests also chatted about William's long-time support for Aston Villa, and his love of Christopher Nolan films.
William set up the Earthshot Prize in 2020, drawing inspiration from US President John F Kennedy's Moonshot project, which challenged scientists to get astronauts to the Moon and back safely.
There are five Earthshots, or goals, for which an award is given: Protect and Restore Nature, Clean Our Air, Revive Our Oceans, Build a Waste-Free World and Fix Our Climate. Each winner receives Â£1m.
The future king has committed himself to the prize until 2030. This year's winners will be announced at a ceremony in Mumbai in November.
Last year, the ceremony for the prizes drew famous faces such as former Formula 1 driver Sebastian Vettel and then-UK prime minister Keir Starmer. Pop stars Kylie Minogue and Shawn Mendes performed at the ceremony in Rio de Janeiro.
The 2025 winners included Lagos Fashion Week, for "transforming one of the world's most wasteful industries" by requiring designers to demonstrate their commitment to sustainability.
At last year's ceremony, William said the winners were "proof that progress is possible".
The Graham Norton Show is on BBC One at 22.40 Friday.

Federal prosecutors arrested a prominent Virginia lawmaker on Thursday over allegations she oversaw a criminal marijuana enterprise.
Democratic state Senator L Louise Lucas and six other people, including her family members, have been charged in relation to a sweeping racketeering case that allegedly involves fraud, drug violations, and bribery.
Lucas, 82, claimed the prosecution was politically motivated in a statement on X.
"I will not be intimidated," she wrote. "I will not be bullied. And I will not back down."
While she has not entered a formal plea, Lucas' attorney, Anthony Capozzolo, told the BBC she would plead not guilty.
Capozollo said in a statement they were "surprised and disheartened" to learn of the indictment, and that Lucas "denies these charges in their entirety."
Lucas and her co-conspirators are charged with obtaining and illegally distributing large amounts of illegal marijuana. The government has also accused her of using her political influence to benefit herself and her family.
Lucas was herself charged with five counts, including racketeering conspiracy, conspiracy to distribute marijuana, conspiracy to launder money, conspiracy to commit honest services fraud, and maintaining a drug involved premises.
Other alleged participants were charged with a firearm charge and wire fraud.
Lucas is not running for re-election. But her daughter Lisa Lucas-Burke, who is also charged in the indictment, is running for the city council of Portsmouth, Virginia.
"I grew up under Jim Crow," Lucas wrote on X in response to the charges, referencing an era of legal segregation in the US. "I've seen what happens when people in power try to silence those who stand up to them. I spent my entire life fighting back, and I'm not stopping now."
At a press conference on Thursday, US Attorney General Todd Blanche accused Lucas of overseeing a criminal "enterprise", arranging for the "acquisition and distribution of marijuana," and using her power as a lawmaker to influence legislation that would benefit herself and her family.
Lucas has served in the Virginia State Senate since 1992, and assumed the powerful role of Senate president pro tempore in 2000. She has publicly spoken about her cannabis dispensary and her support for legalised usage, as well as her opposition to President Donald Trump and Republican lawmakers.
"I'm a 78 year grandma who legalized pot and now has her own cannabis store. And I'm the last thing standing between The GOP and total control of Virginia. That's worth an RT!" she wrote on X in 2022.
While small amounts of cannabis are legal in Virginia for personal or medical use, major restrictions remain in place regarding its sale and consumption.
Lucas has backed legislation to legalise recreational marijuana.
She is an owner of The Cannabis Outlet in Portsmouth, Virginia, which opened in 2021 after the state decriminalised simple marijuana possession and legalised personal possession of certain small amounts of marijuana, according to WAVY News., external
The Virginia Mercury reported in 2022, external that products sold in her shop may have contained substances and dosages that conflicted with state law at the time.
The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) raided Lucas' office and a cannabis business in May as part of a long-running inquiry, the Washington Post reported at the time.
It is unusual for the justice department to announce major actions involving lawmakers, candidates, or other electorally sensitive matters in the weeks before an election. Early voting is already under way in the US midterm elections, which are held on 3 November.
However, the justice department has announced a series of inquiries against lawmakers and election officials in recent days, including conducting a raid on the home of Democratic Congresswoman Ilhan Omar as the government investigates her immigration status.
Referring to Lucas' case, Virginia Governor Abigail Spanberger, a Democrat, wrote on X: "The timing of this indictment undermines the US Department of Justice's previously longstanding policy of not taking legal actions â to include indictments or significant investigative steps â close to an election."
She added: "And sadly, this timing further erodes the trust the American people deserve to have in the Department of Justice."

A Florida police officer has been accused of stealing the identity of a man he found dead during a welfare check call and then moving into his home, authorities say.
Brian Louis Sguros, 35, a police officer in Lauderhill, Florida, was arrested this week by the Broward County Sheriff's Office.
Investigators allege he impersonated the deceased man, Dennis West, moved into the house he found West dead in, and then renovated the two-story south Florida home. Police say he lived there for years undetected.
Sguros has not commented on the charges. It's unclear whether he has legal representation yet. He has been placed on administrative leave from the Lauderhill Police Department.
In 2022, police were called to check on a 71-year-old resident of Lauderhill, Florida, Dennis West.
Officer Brian Louis Sguros was called in as back-up for the welfare check. When he found West dead of natural causes, he allegedly "created a complex scheme to take control of the individual's home," the Broward County Sheriff's Office said in a news release.
Investigators say Sguros told the medical examiner's office he was West's friend, though authorities found no indication the two knew each other, according to the news release. Court documents detail that the officer appeared in body cam footage during the welfare check and did not appear to have a prior relationship with the man.
He also allegedly told the county medical examiner that West had no living relatives, which authorities say say was also untrue, the release states.
Sguros then had West's body cremated, according to the BBC's news partner CBS.
According to a joint investigation by the sheriff's office and the Broward County Property Appraiser's Office, Sguros took possession of the home in August 2022 and moved in.
Authorities say in 2025, he allegedly filed paperwork with the property appraiser's office stating that his possession dated to August 2022.
Sguros said he took possession of the home because it was hazardous, and he wanted to prevent people from squatting, according to court documents.
He paid utility accounts which were in the deceased man's name. He also applied for a permit to replace exterior doors and windows, at the cost of $8,000 (Â£5970), according to court documents.
Sguros claimed he has increased the property's value, spending more than $214,000 (Â£159,717) on the home, according to the sheriff's office.
Sguros faces charges of official misconduct, criminal use of a deceased person's identification, criminal use of personal identification information, offense against a computer user, and unlawful use of a two-way communication device.
He was released from jail on a $25,000 bond.
Local law enforcement were made aware of the situation when West's heirs tried to sell the property, according a police affidavit.
Once Sguros eventually returned the keys to the property's rightful owners, he allegedly demanded reimbursement for improvements he had made to the property, court documents state.
The Lauderhill Police Department told BBC News that Sguros has been relieved of his duty and was placed on administrative leave with pay.

SpaceXâs $40 billion debt raise is being finalized at sharply higher interest rates than when the rocket company last tapped bondholders, a sign of growing jitters in the AI world.
The lowest-rated portion is expected to carry interest rates of about 8.3%, according to people familiar with the deal, which is being led by Apollo and Goldman Sachs. President Donald Trump purchased $5 million in SpaceX bonds in August.
Goldman and Apollo declined to comment. Pricing could change by the time the debt is finalized, which is expected sometime next week.
Existing bonds at SpaceX, which is currently considering merging with Tesla, have weakened in recent days as strong earnings were overshadowed by massive spending plans and concerns about the companyâs debt load, plus broader AI fears fueled by CoreWeaveâs debt selloff. Are yearlong deployments the Navy’s new normal?
That's what officials are telling sailors' families in Japan, where two destroyers are slated for 12- and 14-month cruises.
When the U.S. Navy destroyer John Finn left home in January, sailors expected to be home in March. Now, after extensions on top of extensions, their families have been told to expect them next March—after a 14-month deployment.
The Mustin, another Arleigh Burke-class destroyer, switched homeports this year, leaving San Diego in February and arriving in Yokosuka, Japan, in March. As the sailors stepped off the ship, they were told they needed to be ready to deploy “tomorrow.”
The Mustin actually left Japan in April for a deployment that was supposed to end in August. Now its crew has been told they will return in April 2027, the spouse of one of the sailors told Defense One.
These marathon deployments—a month or more longer than the carrier Abraham Lincoln’s record-breaking 322 days—may be the new normal for U.S. warships. Last week, a Navy official told families at Yokosuka that all ship deployments and patrols, stateside and overseas, will be 10 to 12 months long for the foreseeable future.
Asked about that statement, a Navy spokesperson told Defense One, “It is U.S. Navy policy not to discuss future operations or movements due to operations security.”
But last month, Chief of Naval Operations Adm. Daryl Caudle said that sailors and their families should expect “longer deployments” until “I can grow the Navy we need.” The service’s battle force currently consists of about 290 warships, down from 295 two years ago but up from about 275 a decade ago.
In recent decades, the Navy has generally kept deployments to six or seven months, although that is not a set-in-stone policy, said Katherine Kuzminski, vice president of studies at the Center for a New American Security. But, she said, “that commitment is being violated now.”
“Certainly, depending on operational needs and demands, I think service members and their families are fully on board with providing—with the requirements that are put on them in ongoing operations,” Kuzminski said. “A potential way that the Navy can mitigate this is actually to just commit to the longer term upfront and be clear with service members and their families.”
After initial reports of the Lincoln’s woes emerged, some veterans of other services and other conflicts were quick to post online about their own longer deployments. But the issue, Kuzminski said, is not so much the length of the deployment, but the “dissonance between what was said at the beginning and what is happening in actuality.”
That dissonance is particularly pronounced for the John Finn, one of several “forward deployed” guided-missile destroyers based at Yokosuka. While other Navy ships tend to deploy for about six months and then return home for a year, forward-deployed ships typically leave for two or three months at a time, then return to port for two to three months of maintenance before heading back out to sea. Those deployments are designed to keep the ships ready for combat in the region, deter aggression from China, and “maintain a free and open Indo-Pacific.”
Last year, the John Finn left home in June for a “normal” deployment in the region and returned in early November. But much of the following two months were spent in hasty preparations to return to sea.
“We really only saw him a collective 20 days,” the spouse of a sailor on the ship told Defense One.
In early January, the ship left again, for what was expected to be a deployment of perhaps 45 to 60 days. It headed to the Indian Ocean and was involved in the boarding of a Venezuelan oil tanker before being directed to the Arabian Sea, shortly before Operation Epic Fury began.
The ship was part of the initial attack on Iran, the spouse said, and they’re “still there.”
Earlier this month, the sailors were told they would likely not be home until March 2027.
“There’s cars that were left on base that have been stickered to be towed and then to be junked. So there’s sailors that are going to come back and have no cars,” the spouse said. “They left in the winter months, and there’s some sailors that live off base and are single sailors and will have abandoned their entire house, their apartment, for over a year. And when they left in the winter months, when they left everything on heat mode, and then the summer came.” Sailors know “that they’re going to come home and all their stuff will be trashed.”
For families, it’s more than a year without a parent—without any of the planning for a long deployment.
“It’s been absolutely gut-wrenching to my kids,” the spouse said, and there is “next to no mental health support” available on base. The deployment length is “absolutely unheard-of for a destroyer,” she said.
The Finn’s story is extreme—but not unique among Yokosuka-based destroyers.
Photos posted on the Pentagon’s DVIDS media site show the Rafael Peralta in the Philippine Sea in November, in the South China Sea in December, and back in the Philippine Sea on Jan. 8. Then, instead of returning home, it headed for the Middle East in April, where it remains today. Families have been told not to expect the ship home until April 2027.
The Higgins, which lost power and propulsion for a few hours in the Indo-Pacific in April, continued its deployment after repairs and is currently operating in the Indian Ocean. The Milius left Japan in February and has been in the Middle East since March.
The Mustin left its old homeport of San Diego in February and arrived in Japan in March. Sailors are usually given 30 days to help their families move and settle in for a homeport shift, particularly when the move is to a foreign country, and the majority of the families had waited until the ship arrived to make the move. But “the moment they pulled in, my husband stepped off the ship, and he goes, ‘We have to be prepared to leave tomorrow,” a Mustin spouse told Defense One.

Kennedy Jr. and a chief advocate for the Make America Healthy Again movement, resigned from his position with the Trump administration Thursday. In a statement, Means did not say why he was leaving. His departure comes as leading voices in the MAHA movement have expressed discontent with what they say is the Trump administration's lack of progress on a variety of issues, including food security and regulating the weed killer glyphosate. WATCH: Some MAHA backers grow frustrated with Trump's health policies Means said he "leaves with tremendous respect" for President Donald Trump and Kennedy. "The past two years have seen historic policy and cultural change to confront the chronic disease crisis and healthcare incentives that profit from us being sick," Means said. "This movement is in the first inning and just getting started." Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Means was hired as a White House adviser early in the second Trump administration. He used his perch at the Health and Human Services Department to attack the nation's leading physician groups, federal agencies and government scientists, claiming they only protect their own interests. READ MORE: RFK Jr. aide attacks U.S. health system as corrupt while running company that promotes alternatives White House spokeswoman Allison Schuster said the Trump administration is "grateful" for Means' time and "he has done a fantastic job for the MAHA movement." A representative from Health and Human Services did not respond to a request for comment. Health activist Kelly Ryerson, a leader of American Regeneration who is also known as Glyphosate Girl on social media, said she is "impressed that he completed over two years at HHS fighting the food battle, despite all of the obstacles presented by corporate interests." "At the heart of MAHA is a shared belief that the nation's health must not be sacrificed to corporate profit, and that a preventable slide into chronic disease is a threat to America itself," she said. Means is the brother of wellness influencer, author and entrepreneur Dr. Casey Means, who failed to be confirmed as surgeon general earlier this year after doubts were raised over her vaccine stance. Means, along with his sister, came to prominence within the MAHA movement by arguing that ultraprocessed foods, additives and pesticides could be blamed for many of the chronic health conditions facing Americans. Means brought those arguments into the Trump administration and frequently clashed with senior White House officials who worried about alienating the powerful food industry. At the same time, Means' emphasis on food was a source of frustration for other figures within the MAHA movement who wanted to see Kennedy focus on "medical freedom" issues. For many, that meant rolling back federal recommendations and approvals for vaccines. Despite Means' efforts, the administration's progress on food reforms has been slow going. Kennedy had promised the release of a first-ever government definition of ultraprocessed food in April. Instead, FDA's acting commissioner, Kyle Diamantas, told a conference that month that defining the class "is really hard." In August, Kennedy staffers again suggested a major announcement on the issue was imminent. Instead, the announcement focused on a proposal bringing greater scrutiny to food additives. It made only passing mention of ultraprocessed foods. Zen Honeycutt, founder of Moms Across America, said Means will be missed by her organization, which operates local and national campaigns warning against pollution, water use and electricity costs associated with data center construction. Honeycutt said Means "brought an energy and fearlessness to the Hill, fighting for our children to have healthy food in schools and for America's health." Military buyers want to move quickly, which can mean companies need to add new tech to vehicles after they’re built. Now, Oshkosh Defense is building a dedicated center to test those modifications.
“We call it the Vehicle Integration Center. It allows us to prove out and test conformance in the real world. So that's work that we'll be doing in ‘27,” Logan Jones, Oshkosh Defense’s chief growth officer, told Defense One.
“The question of ‘does it work?’ is still left way too late in the process,” Jones said. “We want to shorten that from like a year and a half to weeks.”
While the focus is on their own offerings, Jones said the integration center could help other combat vehicle makers test their products.
“The primes are going to be interested,” he said. “The signal in the market that we've seen is we would be taking risk out of their program—and that's what they want. They want speed, and they want low risk, so they can predict when it'll be available.”
The aim, at least in part, is to make the process easier on engineers. For example: Let's say you're an engineer doing the counter-UAS solution. You said ‘I'm going to bolt it on.’ You need to know where the mounting locations are,” Jones said, noting that information is usually in an interface control document, or ICD. “We don't make that easy today…But in the future, it should be a turnkey system” where the ICDs are easy to access.
Oshkosh is cleaning up ICDs and aims to start work at the center early next year.

How the Dutch are rethinking weapons buying. The U.S. isn’t the only nation with procurement woes. The Netherlands has spent recent years trying to revamp its acquisition system, and there’s a push to incentivize manufacturers to stay ready, Derk Boswijk, the minister for arms procurement and personnel, told reporters.

a3483587713f.text: By — Rebecca Boone, Associated Press Rebecca Boone, Associated Press By — Kim Chandler, Associated Press Kim Chandler, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/iv-team-warned-christa-pikes-vein-might-have-blown-during-failed-execution-court-filing-says Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter IV team warned Christa Pike's vein might have 'blown' during failed execution, court filing says Nation Oct 22, 2026 8:35 PM EDT Tennessee execution team members failed multiple times to establish working IV lines in Christa Pike's arms before her attempted execution and warned that some of her veins may have ruptured, or "blown," before she was injected with the lethal drug, her attorney wrote in a court document filed Thursday. The IV team went through about 10 needles and tried several IV sites on both arms, attorney Randy Spivey wrote in the document, which provides the most detailed account of the execution attempt so far. They even struggled to push saline through the last IV site they established, Spivey wrote. READ MORE: Emergency help for Christa Pike was delayed by confusion after failed execution, 911 calls reveal Pike, 50, was hospitalized after surviving two doses of pentobarbital as the state tried to execute her on Sept. 30 for the 1995 stabbing death of classmate Colleen Slemmer. She was 18 when she tortured and killed Slemmer with her boyfriend, becoming one of the youngest women to be sentenced to death. State protocol calls for a second dose of pentobarbital if the first doesn't result in death, but it doesn't spell out what to do if a person survives the second injection. After being taken to a hospital, Pike was on a ventilator for several days. At one point, her attorneys did not expect her to survive. She ultimately regained consciousness and returned to prison after being discharged. The failed execution has brought renewed scrutiny to how Tennessee carries out death sentences. The court document was part of a separate legal proceeding in which people on the state's death row are challenging Tennessee's lethal injection procedures. "Our predictions about the likelihood of botched executions have come true — and will continue to come true — without substantial change," Kit Thomas, an attorney representing people on death row in the case, said. Nearly an hour of IV attempts The execution team began trying to place the two IVs required by Tennessee's execution protocols at 6:34 p.m., Spivey wrote, and when they struggled Pike helped, advising them to look in her upper arm for a viable vein. They managed to set an IV in Pike's right arm within about 6 minutes, but it took them nearly an hour to complete the same process in her left arm. Pike was "wincing and grimacing" as the IV team members moved the needles around inside her left arm, Spivey wrote, and the team members repeatedly expressed doubts after inserting the needles. One team member said a vein "might be blowing" at 6:57 p.m. while examining an IV in Pike's left arm, but two others said they couldn't tell, Spivey wrote. "One of them said something like, 'it's either blood or blown, I need to know,'" Spivey wrote. The team tried again with a different spot in her left arm, and the needle appeared to be severely bent when they pulled it out, the attorney said. "I think it's blown," the attorney recalled one of the IV team members saying at 7:07 p.m. After more attempts, the team decided at 7:13 p.m. that they had successfully placed an IV in Pike's left arm, and they taped her hands down and hooked her up to a heart monitor. Pike complained of burning arm pain A series of phone calls were made to the execution chamber starting about five minutes later. Spivey said it appeared the execution team members responsible for pushing the pentobarbital into the lines — a process that happens in an adjoining room — were asking the IV team for repeated checks of Pike's left arm. It's not clear exactly when the pentobarbital was pushed into the IV lines, but at 7:34 p.m., Pike said her arm was hurting. "I feel like my arm is about to bust. It burns," she said, according to her attorney. She continued to talk to her spiritual adviser for the next 10 minutes before she began making an "agitated snoring sound," Spivey wrote. Over the next 30 minutes Pike strained, flinched, moved her head and seemed to struggle to breathe, Spivey said, and when he asked to use a phone he was led on a circuitous, seven-minute route through the facility instead of being allowed to use the phone in the execution witness room. Spivey called fellow attorneys at 8:22 p.m. and asked them to stop the execution because a third dose of pentobarbital isn't authorized under the state's protocol. He then went back to the witness room and told the deputy attorney general that Pike needed immediate medical care. Spivey was told an ambulance was on the way at 8:50 p.m., and 20 minutes later he was told that medical staff were providing life-saving measures, he wrote. An ambulance was seen arriving at the hospital at 9:14 p.m. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. Qatar looks to bolster its military power with new hub, partnerships
The Kingdom has spent decades cultivating its reputation as a place where enemies can sit down and talk. Apparently, even that requires an air-defense system.
DOHA, Qatar–Wedged between Saudi Arabia and Iran, Qatar has long used artful diplomacy to keep regional conflicts at arm's length: it provides shelter for Hamas leaders, maintains ties with Israel, and hosts the region's largest U.S. military base. But the Israeli strike on this capital city in September 2025 and subsequent Iranian attacks have Qatari leaders racing to secure allies and boost the peninsular nation’s domestic defense industry.
"It's the first time that a mediator has been attacked. This never happened," Sheikh Saoud bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, Qatar's deputy prime minister and minister of state for defense affairs, said Monday at the Global Security Forum in Doha.
Al Thani said Qatar is exploring new defense partnerships with the United Kingdom and other Western and regional partners. The government is also looking to spin up a domestic weapons-production hub. The country's priorities include air defense, counter-drone capabilities, cybersecurity and electronic warfare, areas identified in a defense review conducted in 2025.
A visit to the Milipol Qatar security exhibition, held alongside the Global Security Forum, suggested a banking trade show as much as a military expo, a reminder that Qatar lacks the large defense-manufacturing base of some regional neighbors.
Qatari officials believe the country can participate more directly in weapons design and manufacturing, rather than simply serving as a buyer. Maj. Gen. Mohammed Abdul Latif Al Mannai, a Qatari defense official, said a proposed partnership with Britain could incorporate operational requirements, intelligence and assessments of emerging threats into weapons development. Gen. Sir Roly Walker, chief of the General Staff of the British Army, said the countries were considering a much broader partnership—not just between operators, but their acquisition corps and suppliers.
"We have high-level political ambition for a 50-year strategic partnership to gear ourselves up for the future," Walker said.
"We need to position ourselves almost as a design partner to allow the ingenious engineers and creative entrepreneurs to develop the solutions to our problems."
Qatar is also looking to increase investment in defense companies, rather than simply purchasing their products. Mohammed bin Badr Al Sada, group CEO of Barzan Holdings, said British companies were already involved in discussions about the proposed hub.
"We work very closely with UK industries," Al Sada said. "Actually some of them, they are already in town as we speak. And we hope that we can see this hub active very soon."
Qatar's growing interest in defense production also reflects concerns about the limits of American security guarantees. Iran's June 2025 missile attack on Al Udeid Air Base showed that the presence of U.S. troops on Qatari soil did not, by itself, prevent an attack. And Washington has signaled its intention to play a less interventionist role in regional security.
Tom Barrack, U.S. ambassador to Turkey and special presidential envoy for Syria and Iraq, acknowledged that shift in an onstage interview Tuesday, while emphasizing that Washington was not abandoning its regional partners.
"We're not leaving. But what everybody's doing is saying, 'Okay, I can't rely on America to solve all my problems anymore,”
Defense One is a media partner of the Global Security Forum.

Ilhan Omar says she will move out of her Washington, DC, home after federal search Politics Oct 22, 2026 8:25 PM EDT U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar will move out of her Washington, D.C., home that federal agents searched last week, she said Wednesday, noting that attention brought on by the raid has made her feel unsafe there. WATCH: Rep. Omar accuses Trump of political intimidation after agents search her home Federal authorities are investigating potential fraud in her family's immigration paperwork and have issued grand jury subpoenas to some of her relatives, a person briefed on the investigation told The Associated Press on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss an ongoing investigation. Omar, who was born in Somalia and is a naturalized U.S. citizen, said Wednesday in her first interview since the search that she is "confident in the fact that I didn't do anything wrong." The progressive Minnesota Democrat has been a frequent critic and target of President Donald Trump, who has on multiple occasions pushed for the prosecution of his perceived political enemies. In the interview with MS NOW, Omar said she was rattled by the search weeks out from the Nov. 3 midterms, which will decide control of the House and Senate. She is running for reelection in a deep blue district centered in Minneapolis and is expected to retain her seat. Please check your inbox to confirm. Omar recalled waking around 6 a.m. to Homeland Security investigators banging on her door with a warrant. They searched for four or five hours and seized 17 items, including phones, notebooks, a Somali language children's book and a vintage camera that her husband had received as a gift, she said. The Justice Department has shared few details about the case other than saying it was a criminal investigation. Omar came with her family to the U.S. at age 12, after they obtained asylum. She became a U.S. citizen five years later, in 2000. "It would be a huge undertaking to, I suppose, indict a 12-year-old for so cleverly conspiring to defraud immigration services to come to the United States. I'm sure there are a lot of smart 12-year-olds, but that seems like a leap," she said in the interview. The search drew sharp condemnation from congressional Democrats, who also questioned the timing. The Justice Department has historically avoided overt investigative actions involving candidates in the immediate run-up to an election. Omar said the agents were "intrusive but polite," logging the items they took and putting back everything else in its place. An amber weather warning has come into force in parts of the UK as Storm Austen brings a swathe of powerful winds and heavy rain on Friday.
South West England is forecast to be worst hit by the storm which the Met Office warns could bring travel disruption, power cuts and a possible danger to life.
Wind gusts of 60-70mph, with 80mph in exposed locations, are forecast across Cornwall and parts of Devon, where the Met Office warning is in force until 10:00 BST.
Wind gust of 45-60mph are forecast more widely across most of England and Wales, where two less severe yellow warnings will be in force throughout Friday. A separate yellow warning will also cover part of Scotland, including Glasgow and Edinburgh, from 06:00 BST.
Winds of this strength will blow some trees over, bringing a significant risk of transport disruption and there may also be some power cuts.
Winds of this strength will blow some trees over while buildings could also potentially be damaged, leading to a risk of flying debris at the height of the storm.
A number of schools are closed in the impacted areas with many others opening later than usual to avoid the strongest winds.
Train cancellations and speed restrictions are possible because of the increased danger of branches and trees blocking railways.
A number of ferry sailings have also been cancelled, including crossings between Pembrokeshire and Ireland.
Yellow wind warnings cover most of England and Wales with gusts of wind on Friday forecast to reach 45-60mph, with 70mph gusts likely in some places.
As strong as these winds are, the most damaging winds will run to the south of the low pressure centre.
That puts north-west France firmly in the firing line and parts of Brittany could see gusts close to 90mph.
The Channel Islands are also expecting severe gales with gusts up to 80mph.
All schools in Jersey have been told to close on Friday because of the high winds predicted to be caused by Storm Austen.
Heavy rain in Scotland may cause some localised flooding with a Met Office yellow warning for 20-40mm of rain forecast with up to 80mm accumulating in a few areas through Friday.
Storm Boelo to bring travel disruption over the weekend
Closely following Storm Austen will be Storm Boelo, named by the Met Office on Thursday and set to bring another round of stormy weather to the UK over the weekend.
Boelo will bring wet and windy weather across the whole of the UK on Saturday with poor travelling conditions expected due to surface water and spray on faster roads and motorways.
The Met Office has issued yellow wind warnings for Scotland, Northern Ireland and northern England, valid on Saturday and lasting most of Sunday.
Gusts are forecast to reach 50-65mph widely and could reach 80mph in exposed locations.
There could be some localised disruption with strong winds funnelling through the Central Lowlands for a time.
Transport disruption is expected and there may be some power cuts. Following recent spells of wet weather, there is an additional risk of some localised flooding.
Is it unusual to see two storms so close together?
It is not unusual to get storms one after another - in fact they quite often arrive in clusters.
A strong jet stream is needed to rapidly develop powerful wind storms. The process involved in creating such storms involves shifting warmer air northwards and cooler air southwards across vast areas of the Atlantic.
These temperature contrasts can provide a fertile environment for new low pressure systems to develop and if these subsequently get steered beneath a developmental area of a powerful jet stream, they can rapidly develop to create a new named storm with damaging winds.
When do we see the most named storms?
Although named storms can affect the UK at any time of the year, analysis shows they are much less common in spring and early summer.
May is the only month with no named storms in the 11 years that storms have been named in the UK.
The chances of seeing a storm increases from late summer and throughout autumn with the peak of the season arriving in our winter months.
This increase in storminess is why the storm-naming season begins in September each year.
In about half of the years since 2015, the first storm arrived after 1 November.

"Being the ambassador to Russia was probably the hardest assignment of my career," Lynne Tracy, who represented the US in Moscow from 2023 and 2025, tells the BBC.
US, UK and European diplomats once played a crucial role in Russia, defusing tensions even at the worst moments of the Cold War.
But now, deemed "unfriendly" by President Vladimir Putin's government, Western ambassadors are under constant surveillance, isolated and increasingly cut off from the country they were sent to understand, as the war in Ukraine grinds on through its fifth year.
The BBC has spoken to five diplomats who have served in Russia since it launched its full-scale invasion.
They compare current pressure levels to the Cold War era - when Western embassies were monitored through physical surveillance, listening devices hidden inside gifts, and "spy dust" - a near invisible chemical agent used to track officials.
Hundreds of Russian diplomats were expelled from countries in Europe and the US after the war began in 2022. Moscow responded in kind, declaring hundreds of Western diplomats persona non grata and leaving many embassies short-staffed.
Tracy's 30-year career took her to countries like Pakistan, where she survived an armed attack in 2008. But she says that even under constant physical threat, her posting in Peshawar was, in a sense, easier than Russia.
"There, I still felt that there were things within my control. What made Moscow more difficult were the high levels of uncertainty."
The constant pressure from Russian counterintelligence was the primary source of such uncertainty, she recalls.
Russian diplomats in the West also complain of such unfair treatment. But according to the diplomats who spoke to the BBC, the scope and tactics of Moscow's intelligence services are far greater.
"Expect listening devices, expect cameras in every single room of your house," a former European diplomat says of the warning he received before leaving for Moscow.
Another ex-ambassador says they were forced to dismiss two Russian employees after Moscow's domestic security service, the FSB, tried to recruit them, demanding that they report on everything going on at the diplomatic mission.
The pair told the embassy instead, who let them go - "otherwise, they could have faced some sort of criminal prosecution".
Meanwhile, Russians who would ordinarily build relationships with diplomatic staff - such as those working in academia and culture - are also being intimidated into avoiding contact with Western officials.
One former ambassador says his guests were once "tailed" by FSB agents right up to the doors of the embassy.
Just this June, guests invited to the British ambassador's residence in Moscow for the King's birthday celebrations said they had been harassed by pro-Kremlin activists and state-media journalists, and then questioned by the police.
One of the guests says he has since declined several invitations to events at Western embassies out of fear.
Not everyone can deal with the pressure.
One former ambassador says "constant paranoia" has driven a number of officials to quit their jobs. Even after leaving Russia himself, he adds, he was looking over his shoulder for months.
'Generals prove what they can do in war. The same is true for diplomats'
In the immediate aftermath of the invasion, there were discussions across Europe about whether to recall ambassadors or stop working in Russia altogether, says former French ambassador Pierre LÃ©vy.
He remembers calling Paris immediately to say pulling their envoys would be a mistake, feeling that the worse relations became, the more important they would be.
The invasion quickly transformed their work, says another ex-European ambassador; the co-operation required for their usual efforts on bilateral relations, trade and joint projects was now impossible.
And for those who stayed in Russia, the war left them with a host of new priorities beyond supporting their own citizens and companies.
Firstly, countries viewed as unfriendly by Moscow still wanted at least some channel of communication with Russian officials to get an accurate picture of what was happening inside the country.
But they also had to protect their staff and keep their embassies functioning.
After Russia's ban on hiring foreign nationals in 2021, the US embassy's facilities team was left significantly understaffed. Ðven a minor plumbing issue like a leaking pipe could turn into a major problem, draining the time of diplomatic workers.
One diplomat recalls discussing staffing shortages with a Russian official, who advised him not to get too upset. "He said, 'at least you still have the chef'."
Financial sanctions imposed by Western governments to support Ukraine created different day-to-day difficulties. After Russian banks were cut off from the Swift payment network, and Mastercard and Visa suspended operations in Russia, many embassies struggled with basic operating expenses.
A former ambassador recalls simply running out of cash and being unable to pay his staff - until another diplomat, who was selling his car after being expelled, brought the rubles to the embassy in a suitcase.
"It's completely insane," the diplomat laughs. "But you had to look at it with a sense of humour."
Russian officials make little secret of their attitude towards Western diplomats. They have openly accused those from "unfriendly countries" of engaging in "espionage".
Moscow has been particularly critical of those who show an interest in expressions of dissent against the Kremlin and, according to Russian journalist Alexei Venediktov, has effectively banned most Russian officials from speaking to Western embassies.
This has only worsened relations with the West, says Venediktov, who recalls telling Russian officials: "You are being misunderstood precisely because of your own actions - because ambassadors cannot do their jobs."
Today, Moscow has little to no contact with many Western governments, says one ex-European ambassad

A BBC investigation has found evidence that Sudanese paramilitary fighters systematically destroyed el-Fasher's healthcare system during their long siege and subsequent takeover of the city in Darfur a year ago.
UN human rights chief Volker TÃ¼rk called the findings "deeply disturbing", saying multiple attacks by the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) on civilian infrastructure, including health facilities, were serious violations of international humanitarian law and may amount to war crimes.
The RSF has rejected the BBC's findings.
The paramilitary group's health minister described the allegations as propaganda and a deliberate attempt by the national army and its allies to smear the RSF's reputation.
Using sources who were on the ground in el-Fasher, the BBC has found details of at least 43 separate attacks on hospitals and healthcare sites from May 2024 to October 2025 - some hit multiple times.
Under international law it is illegal to attack health facilities or their staff during conflict.
The investigation also reveals the toll on medical workers in the western city. In the period from April 2023 to October 2025, the BBC's data shows 120 were injured, 55 killed and 10 forcibly "disappeared" or abducted.
"The RSF [were] trying to evacuate the hospitals, to put them out of service because the health system is the cornerstone of any city or any state," says Dr Muhamed Suliman, a surgeon who was based in el-Fasher during the siege and spoke to the BBC.
"The RSF started hitting these areas so citizens have no longer any way to stay there. It was intense. It was deliberate. It was planned."
The investigation comes a year after the fall of el-Fasher, one of the most brutal chapters of the civil war which erupted in April 2023 between the RSF and Sudan's military.
Both sides have been accused of attacks on health facilities.
In March 2026, the World Health Organization (WHO) condemned the bombing of al-Daein hospital in RSF-held eastern Darfur, which killed dozens and forced the site to close. Sudan's military is believed to have carried out the drone strikes, although it has denied responsibility.
But events in el-Fasher represent "one of the clearest and most severe examples of the wider impact of the conflict on health care in Sudan," the WHO said in response to a BBC query.
UN investigators have reported that the fighting in el-Fasher bore the "hallmarks of genocide", where historical ethnic animosities have seen Arab militias - now the backbone of RSF forces - target non-Arab groups such as those that populate the city.
The BBC's investigation reveals for the first time a detailed chronology of attacks on healthcare during the long siege of the city.
Some medical facilities in el-Fasher closed down within weeks of the country's civil war starting in April 2023.
Crucially this included one of the main hospitals - the Teaching Hospital - located in a conflict zone in the middle of the city.
Its operations were moved to el-Fasher's South Hospital. There medical services continued, although increasingly hindered by power cuts and dwindling supplies.
The situation changed dramatically a year later, when the RSF mounted its siege of el-Fasher.
In late May and early June of 2024, the South Hospital was shelled several times as paramilitary fighters pushed forward from their positions in the east of the city.
The first bombing came as a shock, says Dr Suliman.
The area around the hospital that was hit was "very crowded because it was the only working hospital in the city providing surgical services", he says.
On that day medical staff operated on 16 injured patients, he added.
The attacks culminated in an RSF raid on 8 June. Hospital staff were taken by surprise - many of them escaped over the back wall as the RSF fighters entered the building, says Dr Mustafa Ahmed, a pharmaceutical specialist.
But the director general of the hospital, surgeon Izzeldin Ahmed Dawaud Asow, encountered a group of the paramilitaries outside his office.
They did not know he was a doctor, he said, but denounced him with ethnic slurs.
"There are no citizens here. You are Falangi," they said, using a derogatory term implying that non-Arab Sudanese are foreigners.
Dr Asow says he was beaten with rifle butts and lost consciousness at one point. Ultimately, he saved himself by pretending to be dead.
"They put their hand on my chest, and I stopped breathing. And they said: 'Leave him, leave him. The rubbish has died. Leave him.' They left me."
That same day the RSF was driven out by the Sudanese military and its allies and Dr Asow returned to find the bodies of several patients and the surgical equipment in his operating room thoroughly destroyed, he said.
The hospital closed and later fell into RSF hands when the army retreated.
Dr Alaa Eldin Nugud, a prominent Sudanese surgeon who has joined the RSF-backed civilian government as health minister, insisted the South Hospital was being used as a military base.
According to international law, hospitals can lose their protection if they are used by a party to the conflict to commit an "act harmful to the enemy".
In an interview with the BBC, Dr Nugud declared that missile launchers were set up on the grounds and shared a video showing remains of weapons filmed more than a year after the hospital closed, which he said supported his claim.
He also showed us what he called maps of landmines planted around the Teaching Hospital, which is located next to Sudanese military headquarters.
Doctors told us the hospital was not incorporated into the base and said they visited it to pick up medical equipment during the war.
The BBC has found no independent evidence of Dr Nugud's allegations. And the government of the Darfur region categorically rejected the charges.
After the South Hospital shut, its staff and remaining equipment were moved to the Saudi Maternity Hospital in the west of the city, where the army had its main bases.
