fd3c09720844.text: That wince you just made while researching travel options? Get used to it. Why it matters: Soaring jet fuel prices are accelerating changes across the airline industry, seen in higher fares, premium-heavy cabins and fewer flight options for travelers. Airfares rose 22% year over year in September, marking a 10th straight monthly increase in the government's airfare price index , which hit an all-time high. State of play: All the major airlines are feeling the pain: American Airlines reported Thursday that its fuel bill jumped nearly 70% in the third quarter from a year ago, adding $1.9 billion in costs and undercutting its revenue growth. Southwest and United Airlines both slashed their profit forecasts this week on higher fuel costs. And Delta Air Lines expects its fuel bill this year to come in $6 billion above last year's. The impact: To protect their bottom lines, airlines are raising fares and turning to more premium seats to squeeze more revenue out of their flights. At Southwest, the average passenger fare rose 26.9% to $231.69 in the third quarter, compared with a year earlier — and that doesn't include fees. Delta's premium seating revenue jumped 18% in the third quarter, even though the number of premium seats rose only 6%. What they're saying: The airlines have few options to make up for extra fuel costs other than fare increases, said Scott Keyes, founder of flight-deal service Going.com. "None of them are hedging fuel the way they used to, in large part because they had a pretty terrible experience with it," Keyes said in an interview. The big picture: Airline executives, however, see these changes — many of which were already underway — as a necessary new normal. This year's fuel spike has only "accelerated" change, Delta CEO Ed Bastian said on the company's earnings call on Oct. 9. "Regardless of the next move in fuel prices, the forces reshaping the U.S. airline industry will continue with many carriers struggling to earn their cost of capital well before the run-up in fuel," he said. United CEO Scott Kirby told investors Wednesday that the industry's underlying costs — including airport fees, maintenance and engines — have increased so much in recent years that airlines must fundamentally change their economics. Zoom in: Executives echoed Bastian's comments on pricing from earlier in the month, suggesting this week that the higher fares and other changes to protect profitability are likely to remain in place even after jet fuel prices ease. "I'm pretty confident that we're not going to take steps backwards in pricing," Kirby said. "I think we're demonstrating this year that it's different this time." American CEO Robert Isom said the fuel price spike "has just been a catalyst to allow us to realize that there is value," referring to the strong demand from customers willing to pay higher fares. And airlines are becoming increasingly reluctant to operate flights that don't make money — potentially leaving travelers with fewer options. United's Kirby predicted that trend will continue across the industry. "One golden rule — don't fly places that lose money," he said on the company's earnings call. "There's going to be less loss-making flying," he predicted. Zoom out: The fallout from higher fuel prices — triggered largely by the war in Iran, which has throttled supplies — started with the shutdown of Spirit Airlines earlier this year. While Spirit's troubles were many, the fuel price spike was widely seen as the last straw for the budget carrier. And its exit means it's now easier for airlines to get away with charging more to cover their extra fuel costs, Keyes said. "Spirit's demise is another factor in why you're seeing airfare go up so precipitously because they and other budget airlines act as something of an anchor for airfare in general," Keyes said. The bottom line: Fuel prices may eventually come back down. Don't count on airfares following.

The Ebola outbreak that began in DR Congo is becoming a continental crisis after authorities initially underestimated its spread, the head of Africaâs public health agency told Semafor as new cases were reported as far afield as Nigeria.
More than 4,600 people have died in the outbreak of the Bundibugyo strain which was first detected in DR Congo in May, though health experts believe it had been circulating undetected for weeks. It has now spread further across Africa than any previous Ebola outbreak, with cases in the continentâs central, eastern and western regions. Nigeria, Africaâs most populous country, confirmed its first case of the Bundibugyo strain, for which there is no proven vaccine, despite being absent from the agencyâs initial list of 15 countries at risk, he said. Kenya has reported nine cases while Uganda, which recorded 20 cases, was declared free of Ebola in August.
âWe could see every region of Africa affected, and that is beginning to happen,â Jean Kaseya, director-general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, said in an exclusive interview. He said the outbreak had initially been viewed as less dangerous and easier to contain, with little expectation that it would spread to other African regions, which had proved to be wrong.
Ebola is changing how African governments organize their response, Kaseya said, with Nigeriaâs case prompting stronger solidarity across the continent. Health, finance and transport ministers will meet next week with regional organizations invited, to discuss national and cross-border measures.
Kaseya said he expects a response plan dividing responsibilities among regional organizations and other partners to be ready by then, ahead of a summit of African leaders where he hopes to secure funding commitments.
As Ebola spreads across Africa, Kaseya warned against closing borders to contain it. âWe do not recommend border closures,â he said, arguing that the measure had already proved ineffective. âPeople will start using informal, unofficial routes, and they will still cross.â
Know More
The patient diagnosed in Nigeria, a woman who had traveled from Uganda, went roughly 10 days undiagnosed. âThe patient was in one private facility, then another, without being tested,â Kaseya said. That delay posed a greater risk of further spread than in Kenya, he said. Kenya isolated its first patient soon after arrival.
The Nigerian government has pledged funding for the response, Kaseya said, without specifying an amount. Africa CDC has sent a team to support Nigeriaâs response, where Kaseya said aid partners must report their funding and activities to the government.
Nigeriaâs health minister, Muhammad Ali Pate, said authorities had found no evidence that the virus had spread into communities. âThis is a contained single case, and we are diligently working to ensure that it remains so,â he told reporters at a press conference late on Thursday.
Step Back
The spread of the Bundibugyo strain comes against the backdrop of deep cuts to Western aid budgets, which has prompted health experts to argue that a lack of resources reduced the presence of health workers on the ground, slowing the response to the outbreak.
Jullien Harneis, the UNâs senior Ebola coordinator, said the outbreakâs expanding reach required more teams, coordination and logistical support. âIts geographic spread is a real management challenge,â he told Semafor.
Africa CDC warned last week that aid organizations had not reported more than $700 million in donor funding to Congolese authorities. It backed government sanctions, including withdrawing permission to operate, against organizations that continued to refuse to account for their funds.
âWe have now traced $450 million,â Kaseya told Semafor. âWe will never again manage an outbreak in Africa the way we managed it in DR Congo,â he said, referring to the funding dispute.
This latest Ebola outbreak is the second deadliest in history after the 2014-16 epidemic which killed more than 11,300 people, mostly in West Africa. There is no known vaccine for this species of the virus, known as Bundibugyo, but Ervebo, effective against another species, is being tested. The Ervebo vaccine has been administered to 9,000 frontline workers.

Five Israelis have been wounded and two suspected Palestinian attackers killed by Israeli security forces following a shooting in the occupied West Bank, Israeli officials say.
Unverified footage shared on social media shows an intense gun battle between soldiers and the gunmen, at a military checkpoint at the entrance to the city of Hebron.
The attack comes at a time of high tensions in the West Bank, with extremist Jewish settlers targeting Palestinians during the annual olive harvest, and Israel's general election taking place in four days time.
The Israeli military said it had found a large quantity of ammunition in the attackers' vehicle. The military said they believe the gunmen had intended to carry out a much larger attack on the nearby Route 35, but unexpectedly ran into the checkpoint - so instead decided to open fire there.
Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who has built his election campaign on promising security, said he had instructed the military to prepare for a full lockdown of the West Bank, beginning later on Friday. The West Bank was already expected to be placed under lockdown for the election on Monday and Tuesday, according to Israeli media.
Netanyahu added that his Likud party would cancel campaign events for the morning.

d7da5b62a5a7.text: America's largest banks are working to prevent AI worst-case scenarios. But they're also preparing for the "day after" a catastrophe, Axios has learned. Why it matters: America's financial institutions have joined the largest AI companies in scenario-planning for disaster, a prudent but worrisome signal about the extent of the risk that major corporations see on the horizon. State of play: Banks are experiencing unvetted AI agent activity , primarily driven by customers providing login credentials to agents, which in some cases appear to have taken actions independent of user prompts, Axios reported Wednesday. The activity is distinct from the rogue behavior involved in a summer attack on a startup called Hugging Face , where an AI agent swarm hacked a platform in an episode that kicked off an industry security crisis. Instead, banks fear the ripple effects and risks that extend from users allowing agents to log in to their accounts and take action, especially since agents could take steps users haven't sanctioned. Concerns about frontier AI systems, not AI agents, have led banks to invest in prevention and to plan for the worst. Zoom in: The Axios report came amid growing concerns about a burgeoning cybersecurity crisis. Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff posted "code red" on X, quoting an Anthropic security employee who said "as bad as things have gotten in the past 4 days, they are going to get a lot worse before they get better." The Anthropic employee was referring to security researchers finding major vulnerabilities in a programming language used to run millions of websites, marking one of the most consequential cybersecurity discoveries yet made with AI . The Axios report on banks, which referred to agentic AI, not frontier AI systems, sparked calls for regulation from across the political spectrum, including Sen. Bernie Sanders, Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis and Sen. Mark Warner. Former White House AI czar David Sacks said banks should support user-directed agents that allow users to "grant, limit, and revoke access," with read-only as an "interim step." Sacks said conflating "user-authorized agentic behavior and cyberattacks is irresponsible." Flashback: The major banks were part of early testing of Anthropic's Mythos, the most cyber capable models from the AI lab. That was part of an effort from AI labs and major banks to use this technology to better understand and prepare for cyberattacks or other risks. Since then, banks have worked on plans not just to avoid AI related issues, but also how to protect accounts, reassure customers and keep operations running in case a large-scale attack hits. Reality check: This is not just standard, it's required for critical industries that have to answer to the government, shareholders and customers. Scenario planning is a requirement for critical infrastructure providers, including in the financial sector. Avoiding it would be malpractice. The highest-risk scenarios involve fear: Speaking in Chicago earlier this month, JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon warned about the potential for cyberattacks or the possibility AI agents could take steps of which users do not approve. "You're assuming they're going to act properly on your behalf and they may not," Dimon said. The only answer is vigilance, he said, warning that stopping AI wouldn't be possible. "You can't stop it. You just have to, like, manage the hell out of it." One economist last month floated the possibility of a bank run driven by agents moving the household cash of their users into higher-yield accounts. Between the lines: Banks want customers to know they have not seen any rogue agent activity or evidence of a hack affecting customer funds or accounts. Banks strongly advise users not to provide their passwords to agents, especially since services exist or are being developed that can allow customers read-only access. The startup Plaid is one such platform that can pull balances and transaction history, among other functions. "Under no circumstance should customers share passwords with any person or thing. Period," a JPMorgan spokesperson told Axios. "There exist secure open banking platforms that don't involve handing over the keys to your account. Customers are the first line of defense in protecting their accounts." JPMorgan has taken steps to block agent access , along with other banks, although it is exploring secure ways to allow customers to connect with the services they choose. The intrigue: AI companies are anticipating a political backlash. Banks are preparing for potential operational disruptions. The extent of federal planning for a crisis spanning both remains unclear. The bottom line: The pace of AI advances has Wall Street and Silicon Valley preparing for worst-case scenarios while Washington is working to mitigate cyber risks and counting on voluntary safety pledges.

It was just before dawn in the Rio Grande Valley in Texas, and the congregation were arriving for the Friday service at the tiny La Lomita Catholic Chapel.
The whitewashed building, which has been here since the days of the American Civil War, rises from the surrounding scrub and sits about 200 yards from the Rio Grande river itself.
As cars pulled up to the chapel, the sound of Father Roy Snipes' barking dogs signalled his arrival. He has been the priest here for almost half a century - and is known locally as the Cowboy Priest.
"I'm not sure why I picked that up, but it's nice," he said of the nickname.
In truth, it is pretty obvious why. Snipes wears a Stetson in place of the more traditional priest's hat. And moments later, the chapel was filled by the sound of a Roy Rogers song - the singer and actor known as the King of the Cowboys.
During the first Trump administration, Snipes resisted plans to seize the chapel's land to build the president's border wall. Eight years on, at the early Friday service, he focused his short sermon on the actions of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).
"There's no good excuse to detain, incarcerate and deport poor, good folks who are our neighbours," Snipes told the congregation of about 30, mainly Hispanic worshippers.
According to government figures obtained by the Deportation Data Project, Texas accounted for roughly one-third of all ICE arrests nationwide in July 2026 - a larger share than any other state.
"They said we're gonna seek out, capture, detain and deport the worst of the worst," Father Snipes said in his sermon. "Well, we're here on the border and the cartel is the worst-of-the-worst. So we thought, well, that's a good thing.
"But it turned out, you can hear almost every day, some poor guy going to work and they stop him and detain him and start a big fight."
After the service, two members of the congregation stopped to chat. "We're educators, and we have a lot of students that are having to go back because their parents are getting deported," one said.
"The cruelty that we're seeing - I think that's turning the tide, at least I hope so," their friend added.
Turning the tide politically is what Democrats are hoping they can do in Texas in the midterm elections on 3 November. But that will not be easy.
This stretch of the Rio Grande was once one of the busiest crossing points on the US-Mexico border. Under former President Joe Biden, hundreds of thousands of migrants came through here, with more than two and a half million apprehensions recorded in a single year.
President Trump promised to stop these illegal crossings during his 2024 election campaign, and in large parts he has delivered.
Border crossings are now at their lowest level in decades. And it was that promise which in part drove Trump's astonishingly high level of support in the state, taking around 55% of Hispanic votes in Texas alone - a record for a Republican presidential candidate.
Javier Villalobos is the Republican Mayor of McAllen, one of the biggest cities in the Rio Grande Valley. He expects Republicans will find it tough this time around, but credits the Trump administration with stemming the border problem.
"I remember I put out a videoâ¦ thanking the administration for immediately securing the border. That was great," he said. "And I think generally most people are okay with the deportation of criminals, violent people, or people that really are not productive at all."
But if you start deporting people that are productive and law-abiding, that is where the problem is, he added.
Recent polls suggest much of Trump's support among Hispanic voters has ebbed away since 2024. Surveys taken since late summer indicate a majority of Texan Hispanic voters disapprove of the president. They also suggest Hispanic voters are favouring Democrats over Republicans by a significant margin.
"When I voted for President Trump, I voted for him because we saw an influx of immigration during the Biden administration," said Mario Guerrero, a young Mexican-American businessman who leads the South Texas Builders Association. It needed to be fixed, he said.
"We thought that we were in the right by voting for Trump, and that he was going to do what was best in order to fix the crisis on the border.
"And I think to myself, we were really not told the extreme that they were willing to go to make a point," he added, before referencing recent shootings involving ICE agents in US cities.
Guerrero is a reminder that, for many who live and work close to the US-Mexico border, security and immigration enforcement are two distinct issues.
A voter here may be supportive of securing the border and stopping illegal crossings, but oppose the actions of ICE and how the administration is enforcing its crackdown on undocumented migration.
Guerrero voted for Trump three times in a row - but is planning to vote Democrat in November, in part due to his unease with that crackdown.
"There's a man that I know thatâ¦ last year, had 35 workers that were working for him every day," he said. "Right now, he just told me two days ago that he would be lucky if he would get four to six guys to show up to work."
Even though Guerrero plans to vote Democrat, he describes himself as neither Democrat nor Republican. And that, according to Mike Madrid, a leading Republican consultant and expert on Hispanic voters, is key to understanding the largest ethnic demographic voting group in the country.
"Latinos are more likely than any other racial or ethnic group to identify as independents rather than Republicans or Democrats," he said.
It was in part the belief that Hispanic voters were shifting permanently towards the Republican Party that led Trump to press states such as Texas to redraw their congressional maps early, before the once-a-decade census.
The strategy was intended to capitalise on what Republicans saw as a realignment in Hispanic voting behaviour, particularly in border districts that had been Democ

219b6f627028.text: The quickest and most affordable response to historically high diesel prices is also the simplest: Use less of it. Why it matters: Diesel is so entrenched in farming, trucking and other industries that even soaring prices aren't enough — at least not yet — to prompt a wholesale shift to alternatives from electric semi trucks to manure-powered tractors. Catch up fast: Diesel prices have climbed to record highs since the U.S. war with Iran began in March, rising faster than gasoline amid global oil supply disruptions . Diesel averaged $6.31 a gallon Thursday, up 74% from a year ago, according to AAA . Regular gasoline averaged $4.27, up 39%. The big picture: Gasoline gets the attention, but diesel is the workhorse of the American economy. It powers grocery trucks, tractors, freight trains, construction equipment, hospital backup generators and even school buses . Driving the news: The price spike is hitting farmers during the fall harvest. "Farmers buy diesel by the truckload, so we're talking about hundreds of thousands of dollars in diesel, and when it goes up the way it has spiked, that's the difference between profit and loss in a year," said Curt Blades, senior vice president at the Association of Equipment Manufacturers, a trade group representing tractor makers and other heavy-equipment manufacturers. The financial pain varies: Trucking companies can often pass higher fuel costs to customers through surcharges. Farmers, who have little control over crop prices, generally can't. The economic pressure has become political ahead of the midterm elections. President Trump announced $8 billion in one-time aid for farmers at a campaign rally in Kansas on Monday, where Republicans face a competitive Senate race. "It's a bit too soon to tell the impact," Blades said of the aid package, though he welcomed support during harvest. State of play: Trucking and agricultural equipment experts say the most immediate savings come from using existing diesel engines more efficiently. Truckers can slow down and reduce idling. Farmers are increasingly using GPS-guided tractors to avoid covering the same ground twice, a practice known as precision agriculture. Biodiesel and renewable diesel can reduce petroleum dependence without replacing existing engines, but government blending requirements — rather than high diesel prices alone — are driving growth, according to Clean Fuels Alliance America, an industry trade group. Zoom in: Batteries that power truck drivers' sleeping quarters without idling the engine are gaining traction. Nevada-based Dragonfly Energy sells systems that recharge through the truck's diesel-powered engine while driving, then power air conditioning and other appliances while parked. The company projected a 160% increase in third-quarter trucking revenue, a bright spot amid otherwise sluggish financial performance. Texas-based Stevens Transport says 400 of its trucks use Dragonfly's batteries, cutting diesel consumption by about 4% compared with trucks using smaller diesel engines to power their sleeping quarters. The approach illustrates a fundamental tension in energy transitions: Does technology incrementally change an industry or revolutionize it? "We haven't even mastered leaving the truck off when it's not moving, let alone moving it with electricity," said Wade Seaburg, Dragonfly's chief commercial officer. "Let's master the little things first, and that's been a well-received message." "Think evolutionary rather than revolutionary," said Mike Roeth, executive director of the North American Council for Freight Efficiency, a nonprofit researching fuel-saving trucking technologies. Zoom out: The same logic applies across diesel-dependent industries. Expensive equipment lasts for years, and switching fuels often requires new infrastructure and vehicles. "The fact diesel fuel prices are higher matters in the calculations, but it doesn't make the challenges of these alternatives any easier," Roeth said. Yes, but: More dramatic changes are still percolating, particularly in electric trucking . Forum Mobility, which builds shared charging depots and leases electric trucks, says electric trucks have a roughly 40% fueling cost advantage over diesel in California, where diesel prices have topped $8 a gallon. The company has commitments from 25 carriers for 330 Tesla Semis and is building four additional charging depots in California. Meanwhile, on the farm, equipment maker New Holland has spent more than a decade bringing methane-powered tractors to market, including ones that can run on fuel made from livestock manure, after abandoning an expensive hydrogen tractor project. "The increase in diesel prices has generated a little more interest," said Sean Dorosz, a product marketing manager at New Holland. But "I don't think it's going to be the one thing that makes them write a check to buy a methane tractor." Access to manure-derived fuel and state incentives also shape the economics. The bottom line: High diesel prices are strengthening the case for alternatives. Making them practical is a much slower process.

The Congressional Budget Office estimated 100,000 more immigrants will be uninsured by 2034 because of Medicaid eligibility changes under President Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act that take effect Oct. 1. A KFF Health News survey of nine states found many more are at imminent risk of losing health coverage.
Refugees. Sex-trafficking victims. People fleeing war. They’re among the hundreds of thousands of immigrants living in the country legally who no longer qualify for Medicaid. The change, in effect since Oct. 1, is part of the 2025 Republican tax law, which cuts Medicaid spending by an estimated $900 billion through 2034.
KFF Health News rural health reporter Andrew Jones joined WAMU’s Health Hub on Oct. 21 to explain which Medicaid enrollees are affected in the Washington, D.C., region and what other cuts to health services for immigrants are next.

BAKERSFIELD, Calif. — Ulises Hernandez has had health coverage through Medicaid for as long as he can remember. But he had never waited as long for care as he did in September after a dental crown slipped down his throat during a procedure. He spent eight hours in an emergency room waiting for care and more than two days without food.
Sitting in his wheelchair to protest looming federal Medicaid cuts outside Republican U.S. Rep. David Valadao’s Bakersfield office, Hernandez described his wait as a foreshadowing of what’s ahead.
“I couldn’t eat, I couldn’t drink, I couldn’t do anything, and I was in pain,” said Hernandez, who had been discharged from the hospital a few days before. “I’m livid.”
Hernandez, 41, said Valadao “should be ashamed of himself” for voting for the Republicans’ One Big Beautiful Bill Act. The law is expected to reduce Medicaid spending by more than $900 billion through 2034, with provisions such as stricter Medicaid eligibility rules and reducing federal money to states.
Hernandez plans to vote for challenger Randy Villegas in hopes that this Central Valley toss-up district, where roughly 6 in 10 of constituents are enrolled in Medicaid, can help give Democrats control of Congress.
Villegas, a political science professor, has embraced the progressive rallying cry for “Medicare for All” and called out Valadao for a vote “that is going to rip away healthcare from Valley families,” since many working-age adults may not satisfy new work requirements and twice-a-year eligibility checks that, by political design, start after the midterm elections.
Valadao defends his vote on the GOP bill. During a televised Oct. 6 debate, he said “there are no actual cuts” to Medicaid.
An estimated 60,000 more residents of his district could be without coverage by 2034 due to the tax and spending bill and the expiration of enhanced premium tax credits for Affordable Care Act insurance plans, according to the left-leaning Center for American Progress think tank.
Researchers estimate that those new rules will push more than 2 million Californians statewide off their coverage and that the state stands to lose about $30 billion a year, more than any other state.
Fertile Ground, High Unemployment
Bakersfield is an oil town, and it wears that identity proudly. Pump jacks nod in the distance. Streets run wide. The Kern River’s bed lies dry, its water siphoned to feed the agricultural fields. Sitting partially in the southernmost portion of the contested congressional district, this city produces much from the land, but unemployment is high.
Democrats have outnumbered Republicans in voter registrations by double-digit percentage points in Valadao’s district since he was first elected to the U.S. House in 2012, yet he has won six of his seven congressional elections. He has survived by focusing on local issues such as water infrastructure and distancing himself from the Trump administration, said Jeffrey Cummins, a political science professor at California State University-Fresno. Valadao is the last Republican House incumbent who voted to impeach Trump after the Jan. 6, 2021, riot at the U.S. Capitol who is running for reelection to Congress.
“This is an area where, even when we see the registration advantage for Democrats, that they are moderate Democrats who tend to be concerned with agricultural issues, and Valadao in the past has successfully appeased those voters,” Cummins said.
But California’s congressional map was redrawn last year as part of a national mid-decade redistricting fight, and Valadao’s Central Valley seat is considered more favorable for Democrats than before. Cummins said a different mix of voters, coupled with anger toward incumbents, could flip the seat.
“Valadao knows that he’s on notice,” Cummins said.
Nationwide, healthcare costs remain a top affordability concern for voters, and they trust Democrats over Republicans by a 2-to-1 margin on the issue, according to a September KFF poll. Valadao lost in 2018, when Democrats targeted his votes to repeal the ACA, as well as his alliance with Trump. On Nov. 3, he faces Villegas, a populist backed by Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) who favors a single-payer universal healthcare system.
“The system that we have now, we pay twice as much as other countries across the world, despite the fact that we have worse healthcare outcomes,” Villegas said during the debate.
No Mention of Healthcare
Valadao participated in a $1,000-a-ticket fundraiser on Sept. 30. He was joined by House Speaker Mike Johnson, who is campaigning across 22 states in six weeks as Republicans try to hold the chamber. Afterward, press were allowed at an invitation-only reelection event in Bakersfield, held in an office building just outside of the new district Valadao hopes to represent. Arches of red, white, and blue star-shaped balloons framed the small stage.
Neither lawmaker mentioned Medicaid or the rising cost of healthcare when they spoke to the audience. After brief speeches, Valadao repeatedly refused to answer KFF Health News’ questions about his vote for the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and its impact on his constituents’ Medicaid coverage, saying, “I think you are distorting the truth.”
Of the half dozen attendees KFF Health News approached among roughly 50 in the room, none lived in Valadao’s district.
They came anyway. Retired nurse Charlotte Brandt lives in the neighboring Republican-held district but follows Valadao’s votes closely. She called him “a hero for the Central Valley,” citing his work on water, oil, and agriculture, which she said sustain Kern County as the “breadbasket of the world.”
Her daughter, Allison Brandt Oliver, who also lives in Republican Vince Fong’s district, said she favored the stricter Medicaid eligibility rules Republicans put into place, saying her concern is whether spending is going to U.S. citizens who contribute to the economy.

Shopping for an ACA Plan This Year? Here’s What You Need To Know
Consumers who buy Affordable Care Act health insurance are going to see changes both big and small as open enrollment for 2027 coverage kicks off. These include premium increases, possible additional identity checks, potential delays in working with a broker, and new limits on which immigrants can get subsidies.
Shoppers need to plan accordingly.
Open enrollment starts Nov. 1 in most states. Idaho, Connecticut, and Massachusetts start earlier, and some states are already allowing “window shopping” to check premium rates.
A continued decline in overall enrollment is expected, mainly because of the expiration of enhanced subsidies at the end of 2025. Policy experts say the end of those subsidies led millions to drop or lose coverage through the first few months of this year.
But the Trump administration sees victory in the falling enrollment, crediting its various efforts to reduce fraud, including the August cancellation of policies covering 760,000 enrollees suspected to be improperly signed up. A small number of those enrollees have regained coverage.
Have Your ID Ready
One of the biggest changes will be increased scrutiny of both consumers and agents via requirements aimed at thwarting fraud or improper enrollments. For consumers, it could slow the enrollment process.
The new rules, outlined in a Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services FAQ, affect only consumers using agents or brokers to help them enroll through the federal marketplace, which serves 29 states. They do not apply to state-based exchanges, which have their own rules and have in most cases been more successful at preventing fraudulent sign-ups.
For starters, all consumers using an agent in the federal marketplace will need to get a one-time confirmation code or link to authorize a specific agent to enroll them or make changes on their behalf. It will be sent to consumers by text message, email, or an automated phone call from one of the private enrollment platforms used by their agent. Returning consumers who have incorrect or outdated contact information will first need to call the federal marketplace themselves or submit an application online to update it.
Additionally, consumers and policyholders deemed “high-risk” must verify their own identity before authorizing an agent. CMS defines as “high-risk” first-time applicants or those with existing coverage whose applications involve a change of state, as well as consumers working with a new or different agent or with a monthly premium payment of $30 or less.
Joshua Brooker, who oversees an insurance agency in Pennsylvania, said CMS appears to have selected people in those groups for greater scrutiny because “someone who is moving to a new state or switching brokers — that could be a broker trying to impersonate a consumer.”
The $30-a-month cutoff may be tied to concerns that plans with no or low monthly premiums are easier for bad agents to target for unauthorized enrollments because the policyholder may never get a bill. Some rogue agents even pay the low monthly amount themselves and still make a profit from the commission, Brooker said.
The broad nature of the new rules, though, has Brooker concerned “that up to 1 in 5 consumers is going to have to do extra identity proofing” and may just give up and not get insured.
Consumers designated high-risk must prove their identity through a CMS-approved third party such as credit company Experian, which generally asks questions only the consumer should be able to answer. People who fail this test may be asked to call Experian’s help desk or submit their applications themselves by creating a healthcare.gov account, which requires them to upload identification such as a driver’s license, a passport, immigration papers, or another form of ID.
“Some people may have trouble not because they’re not real, but because they don’t have a credit file, or have moved, or have changed names,” said Stacey Pogue, a senior research fellow at the Center on Health Insurance Reforms at Georgetown University.
She said the changes might “be an appropriate response by CMS that targets fraudulent enrollments but might also create extra hurdles.”
There May Be Fewer Brokers
CMS in September issued a rule that places a moratorium on brokers new to offering ACA coverage. Agents not registered with the federal marketplace in 2026 will not be allowed to assist with enrollments for 2027 until February at the earliest, past the end of open enrollment season.
CMS said it took this step because a disproportionate number of “significant compliance concerns” in 2026 came from newly registered agents or brokers. Additionally, the agency has kicked out “hundreds of non-compliant agents and brokers” this year.
Jason Fine, who runs a brokerage in Florida, said he agrees with the concept behind these changes. He has reported multiple times to CMS, for instance, that rogue agents have switched his clients’ coverage without authorization, wanting the agency to take action against them. But he said the updated rules also raise concerns.
“Everything they are doing in the long term makes sense,” he said. However, in the short term, “I don’t know if they care about the chaos it will cause.”
That’s because the moratorium will make it much harder for small brokers to help clients this year. His agency and others often pare their staffing after open enrollment but hire again toward the end of the year. He was planning to add up to 10 agents to his core staff of about five but has been told by recruiters that he’s unlikely to be able to find anyone who was registered for 2026 and is still available.
He suggested that the move unintentionally benefits larger call centers, some of which were doing much of the marketing that regulators feared led to unauthorized switching. Call centers often maintain larger staffs.
“They can afford to keep a staff of 25 or 40 people all year long,” Fine said.

A new report suggests dozens of “forever chemicals” linked with cancer and other human health problems are prevalent in Florida waterways, reflecting widespread contamination of the toxic chemicals in streams, rivers and lakes across the country.
Roughly 96 percent of 23 Florida waterways tested between 2022 and 2024 contained 43 different kinds of PFAS, according to the report published this month by the Environment America Research & Policy Center, the U.S. PIRG Education Fund and Frontier Group.
PFAS are manufactured chemicals used since the 1940s in products such as nonstick cookware, waterproof fabrics, long-lasting cosmetics and firefighting foam. The chemicals do not break down easily in the environment and can accumulate in humans and animals. The problem is a growing concern as climate change increases the amount of rain dumped by hurricanes and other storms, causing more runoff that can wash the chemicals into waterways.
PFAS have been linked with several kinds of cancer, including prostate, kidney and testicular cancers. They are also associated with high cholesterol and obesity, developmental problems such as low birth weight and fertility problems. The chemicals are found across the globe, in regions as remote as Grand Canyon National Park and the Tibetan mountains.
“PFAS chemicals are very persistent. They stay in the environment for a very long time,” said John Rumpler, clean water director and senior attorney at the Environment America Research & Policy Center. “We know that PFAS chemicals can pose threats to health and wildlife at very, very small amounts. So when you find PFAS in the water, even if it’s a few parts per trillion, it’s definitely a serious problem.”
Nationwide, 83 percent of 1,602 waterways tested were contaminated with PFAS, according to the report. Researchers detected as many as 114 different kinds of PFAS at the sites, including the Mississippi River and Lake Ontario. The report drew on PFAS monitoring data from surface waters between 2022 and 2024, collected primarily by the Environmental Protection Agency and also the Waterkeeper Alliance and state environmental agencies in Maine and Massachusetts.
The highest PFAS concentration was found in a retention pond at the Brunswick Executive Airport in Brunswick, Maine, where there was an accidental release in 2024 of aqueous film-forming foam. Other sites with high PFAS concentrations included Holloman Lake, near Holloman Air Force Base in New Mexico; Sargent Creek, adjacent to a fire training facility in Minnesota, and waterways near Milwaukee Mitchell International Airport in Wisconsin.
In Florida, the contaminated waterways spanned from Miami to the Panhandle. Among them was the Hillsborough River, which provides drinking water for Tampa. In central Florida, 36 PFAS compounds were detected at all six monitoring sites in Tiger Lake. The lake, some 70 miles south of Orlando, is used for recreational activities such as kayaking and fishing. This is troubling, as the toxic chemicals can accumulate in freshwater fish, exposing people who eat them.
PFAS accumulation in fish is of particular concern in underserved communities, where people rely on fish they catch as part of their diets, said Christian Wells, professor of anthropology and director of the Center for Brownfields Research and Redevelopment at the University of South Florida.
“In a lot of low-income and rural kind of communities, people use fishing not just for recreation but for subsistence, and they are starting to consume fish that have very high levels of PFAS,” he said. “Not only is that bad for your health, but it’s also very difficult to identify in the environment. It’s difficult to regulate. I suspect the problem is a lot worse than people think.”

The report recommends phasing out PFAS, barring industrial facilities from discharging the toxic chemicals into waterways and ending the use of PFAS-laden sewage sludge on farmland. “There are numerous waterways where there is no data at all,” Rumpler said. “That doesn’t mean no PFAS was found. It just means there is no data that we had available to ascertain whether PFAS was present or not. There could be PFAS across other waterways.”

If you listen to the candidates running for the U.S. Senate seat in Alaska, some of the biggest issues in the race revolve around the state’s fisheries, its oil and gas development and soaring prices for fuel and other staples.
Left largely unsaid, however, is that climate change is playing a role in at least two of these issues. Warming waters are affecting the state’s fish, including declining salmon runs. Concerns for climate change are a chief cause of opposition to expanded oil and gas development in the Alaskan Arctic, where rapid warming is melting permafrost, damaging infrastructure and altering animal migrations that many Alaska Natives rely on for subsistence.
Yet the candidates have hardly mentioned climate change. And that might be one of the few ways the race is similar to others around the country.
But first, what’s different. Take fish.
Mary Peltola, the Democrat who represented Alaska in the U.S. House of Representatives from 2022 until January 2025, has adopted a slogan of “Fish, family, freedom.”
“Potentially that was strange to have fish as one of your top three words for folks in D.C.,” said Chantal de Alcuaz, co-executive director of The Alaska Center, an environmental advocacy group, “but it’s not strange at all for Alaskans.”
Despite stretching across an area nearly one-fifth the size of the contiguous 48 states, Alaska has fewer than 740,000 people. And many of those people consider fishing, and fish, central to their lives. For Alaska Natives, salmon are not only food—cultures revolve around the harvest and processing of the fish. Across the state, many non-Indigenous Alaskans fill their freezers each year with fish they catch, too. In recent years that’s all been getting harder.
Runs of some salmon species have declined sharply. State and federal authorities have issued repeated closures of subsistence and sport fishing along the Yukon and Kuskokwim rivers, which cut across the state.
During a debate last month, Peltola and her main opponent, Sen. Dan Sullivan, the Republican incumbent, agreed that climate change is one of numerous factors affecting Alaska’s fisheries, including salmon runs. Scientists say the causes of the decline in some salmon species are complex and multifaceted, but include warming waters.
Yet the candidates have focused their attention on trawling, a commercial fishing practice that targets other species but is allowed to kill a certain number of salmon and other fish as bycatch. Peltola has proposed banning “factory trawling,” which she characterizes as large, out-of-state boats distinct from smaller, local operations.
At the debate, Peltola said climate change was “not as easy to get our arms around” as trawling. “This is the one place where Congress, Alaskans, has an opportunity to say no,” Peltola said of the fishing practice. “This is a man-made impact.”
Peltola has stressed her history of fishing on the Kuskokwim River with family. Sullivan has worked hard to establish his own credentials on the topic, and has introduced legislation to limit bycatch from trawling.
Alaska’s Senate race is unusual when it comes to oil and gas, too. Unlike the national parties, there is little daylight between the candidates when it comes to drilling.
Alaska relies on oil and gas revenue to fund the state budget, and residents receive an annual dividend from a sovereign wealth fund that was built with petroleum royalties. Many Alaska Native communities in the Arctic North Slope have also generated substantial income from fossil fuels. But production is on a decades-long decline.
The Trump administration has pushed through a series of changes to allow drilling on new lands, including areas some Alaska Natives consider critical to their subsistence hunting of caribou. Recent proposals would strip environmental reviews and opportunities for public comment on drilling in the Western Arctic. Sullivan has said he pressed the administration to take these steps. He also sponsored a bill signed into law last year that repealed protections in the Western Arctic enacted by the Biden administration.
Peltola has stressed that she, too, supports oil and gas. At a September forum of the Alaska Oil and Gas Association, she claimed credit for pressing the Biden administration to approve the Willow project, a large Arctic oil development, and criticized Sullivan for voting in 2021 to confirm Interior Secretary Deb Haaland, who had been critical of oil and gas drilling before taking office.
A Peltola spokesperson declined to answer questions about whether she supports the Trump administration’s moves on oil and gas development, instead issuing a statement saying, “Mary will aggressively advocate for every solution on the table to bring costs down—including increased oil and gas production, as well as restoring tax credits for solar, wind, and hydropower projects that were cut by Dan Sullivan. Alaskans expect their Senator to do both, and as an independent voice for Alaska, Mary will stand up to anyone to deliver.”
Sullivan says he supports an “all of the above” energy policy but voted for the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which repealed renewable energy credits. His office did not respond to requests for comment.
Yet while the candidates’ attention to fish and their similarities on oil and gas might be unusual, their reluctance to discuss climate change is not. Across the country, many Democrats have decided it is safer to discuss energy prices.
“I think some of it is just advertising savvy,” said Amy Lauren Lovecraft, a professor of political science at the University of Alaska Fairbanks. Peltola knows she has support from people who care about the issue, she said, “because Sullivan doesn’t care about climate change. His record is pretty clear.”
Enei Begaye, executive director of Native Movement, an Indigenous advocacy group in Alaska, said many Alaskans care about warming, “led by Alaska Native people who are feeling the impacts, the deadly impacts of climate change right

The Trump administration is steadily ratcheting up pressure on Iran with sanctions, but experts and former officials say the penalties thus far are having a limited effect on the Islamic Republicâs willingness to negotiate.
Nate Swanson, who served as a State Department representative on the second Trump administrationâs Iran negotiating team, said the pressure has failed to change Iranâs strategic calculations.
âThink about everything Iranâs been through in the last eight months. Theyâve endured incredible setbacks to their physical infrastructure, military, and physical livelihood,â Swanson said. âWeâve not seen any kind of capitulation or even willingness to compromise, but a more rigorous hard ine taking form. Theyâre not more willing to negotiate, theyâre actually less flexible. They would rather have more war than compromise. So I donât see it leading to a positive strategic end game for the US at this point.â
Alex Vatanka, a senior fellow at the Middle East Institute, said that the blockade has been more difficult for Iranian authorities to manage than sanctions alone, as it has cut off much of Iranâs trade.
âThe blockade is whatâs different from sanctions. It will have an additional cost and impose a pain on an economy that was already in a very bad place,â Vatanka said. Yet âthere is no sign â as far as I can tell â of an imminent collapse of the Iranian economy.â
A further limitation on the Trump administrationâs strategy on sanctions is Iranâs ability to maintain trade ties with China, a country that has little incentive to enforce US restrictions.
âChina views our sanctions as unilateral and illegal, so they have no interest in abiding by them,â said Philip Luck, director of the Center for Strategic and International Studiesâ economics program. âAs long as Chinaâs not going to concur with our sanctions, Iranâs going to be able to get what it needs, and itâs going to be able to get some amount of revenue from its sales of oil.â
Luck added that Chinese manufacturers can supply many of the industrial goods and components Iran needs to rebuild damaged military components and infrastructure.
The failure of sanctions and the blockade to bring Iran to the negotiating table on Washingtonâs terms is likely why the US is reportedly considering renewed military strikes as another way to force concessions. But experts caution that escalating pressure does not necessarily mean Tehran will back down.
âThe regime will try to bend, but not break,â Tom Warrick, a nonresident senior fellow at the Atlantic Council, said.
âThe problem here is both sides are intent on wanting the other side to be seen to be defeated,â he continued, adding conflicts are harder to resolve when âyour only way out to end the war is the strategic humiliation of your opponent.â Such conflicts, he warned, âtend to go on longer than they otherwise would have.â
The administration insists its strategy of inflicting economic pain is working.
âOperation Economic Outcast is isolating the Iranian regime into desperation,â a Treasury spokesperson told Semafor. âIran has loaded zero oil onto vessels since August 25, the day after Economic D-Day. The value of the rial continues to reach new lows. Inflation is through the roof as the regime scrambles to print more money. Iranâs access to foreign currency is severely diminished. We have seen flights grounded, Iranian bank branches shuttered, and trade halted. The regime is out of options, and the clock is ticking.â
Warrick also cautioned against dismissing sanctions as a tool for diplomacy, pointing to past diplomatic deals with Iran following sanctions, including the 1981 Algiers Accords; an agreement at the end of the Iran-Iraq War in 1988, and one alongside the Obama-era nuclear deal, formally known as the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action.

Could the Tesla-SpaceX merger that Elon Musk floated this week pose antitrust problems?
One former Justice Department official told Semafor that the risks are real.
Antitrust regulators view such âverticalâ mergers as pro-competition, the official said â because they can make supply chains more efficient â but could try to stop the merger if Tesla-SpaceX gets deemed a possible âvertical foreclosure.â
A foreclosure situation arises when a firm uses its position to restrict competitors operating at another level of its supply chain, the official explained; in this case, other driverless or electric car companies could stand to lose out if, in the future, only Tesla cars got access to SpaceX technology like Starlink.
Of course, that depends on the terms of the still-hypothetical deal. It also depends on how much Trump-aligned US antitrust enforcers want to clash with Musk, a major Republican donor.
Even so, should Democrats take back the House next month, Musk would face congressional investigations â and lawmakers would closely scrutinize any attempts to merge his companies.
âIf Elon Musk moves forward with the merger of Tesla and SpaceX, the deal would carry real risks that âantitrust enforcers across the world would scrutinize,â Sen. Cory Booker, D-N.J., told Reuters. âWhen one person controls the infrastructure that governments and militaries depend on, his business decisions become national security decisions, too.â
Reuters reported that Teslaâs work in China could also complicate things, as Starlink technology is used in foreign conflicts and the company has a relationship with the Pentagon.
Any Tesla-SpaceX merger could also get examined by global antitrust enforcers for its impacts on overseas auto, AI, and aerospace industries.

ALLENTOWN, Pa.—In all her 38 years living in South Whitehall Township in the Lehigh Valley, Laurie Gilley had never attended a municipal meeting, much less gotten involved in the politics of her community. But then she learned that a data center was being planned for 400 acres of land across from her home and the local high school.
Now, Gilley, who helped form the South Whitehall Township Civic Alliance to fight the center, is at the vanguard of an informal political movement experts say could impact the midterm congressional elections, especially in tight races like the one in her district, where incumbent U.S. Rep. Ryan Mackenzie, a Republican narrowly elected in 2024, is now facing Democrat Bob Brooks, a retired firefighter.
Gilley said she has been energized by the unified resistance to data centers. “Both sides of the aisle seem to come together on this,” said Gilley, 61, who runs Madeline’s Fairgrounds Marketplace at the popular farmers market here, where the chatter these days in her baked goods and sandwich shop often turns to data centers and politics. “Everywhere I go, we’re talking about it.”
Opposition to data centers—especially in places where they are proposed near residential neighborhoods or close to environmentally sensitive land or water—has been intense in Pennsylvania. Residents worry about property values, rising utility bills, the impact on the water and power supply, the loss of the state’s rural character and environment and even whether artificial intelligence is a good idea at all. And the voices are coming from both parties.
With the looming midterm elections, the question is whether all that talk will translate into votes—and which candidates might benefit.
“It doesn’t take much to tip elections” in Pennsylvania, said Christopher Borick, a political science professor and director of the Lehigh University Opinion Observatory. He said it’s still hard to predict the impact of the opposition that has spread “almost like a wildfire” across Pennsylvania.
But “it is front and center,” he said, in the Mackenzie-Brooks race and three other congressional races that are expected to be decided by thin margins.
Borick said President Donald Trump’s declining approval rating could hurt Republican incumbents in all four of those districts. “That’s a big weight and anchor on Republicans” in tight races, he said, adding that the “straw that breaks the camel’s back” may well be how the data center issue resonates with voters. And there may be far-reaching implications up and down the ballot, he said. “It’s in all the races,” said Borick.
Trump won the state in 2016 and in 2024, and helped two Republicans eke out narrow wins in Pennsylvania in 2024 for their first terms in the U.S. House of Representatives: Mackenzie, who is now facing Brooks in the 7th Congressional District in the Lehigh Valley; and Rep. Rob Bresnahan, who is facing Democrat Paige Cognetti, the mayor of Scranton, in the 8th Congressional District in northeastern Pennsylvania.
Two longtime incumbents also won new terms in 2024—U.S. Rep. Scott Perry, a Republican who is now facing Democrat Janelle Stelson, a former TV anchor, in the 10th Congressional District in the Harrisburg area, and U.S. Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick, a Republican who is facing Democrat Bob Harvie, a county commissioner, in the 1st Congressional District in Bucks County.
All eight candidates essentially agree that developers should pay for infrastructure and power needs and not leave residents with higher utility costs. Harvie is the only candidate so far to say he supports a moratorium. Perry, meanwhile, has adopted Trump’s strong overall support for data centers, saying they are essential to helping the United States stay ahead globally on artificial intelligence.
“The last thing we need are data centers raising our energy costs while big corporations get rich,” Brooks said in a statement to Inside Climate News. “My job is to make sure the people of the Lehigh Valley have the final say over what gets built in their backyard.”
Bresnahan, a Republican, struck a similar note in the 8th District race: “I am not going to allow data centers to be forced on northeastern Pennsylvania without the approval of the people,” he said in a campaign ad, adding that “families know what is best for our communities. We should decide if data centers get built here.”
Ginny Marcille-Kerslake, a senior organizer for the environmental advocacy group Food & Water Watch who is involved in the fight against data centers in Pennsylvania, said she doesn’t know how the issue will play out in the elections, but candidates clearly recognize “that support for these projects makes them vulnerable” in this election.
“I have never seen anything like this in terms of public engagement,” said Kerslake, with opposition coming from “across the political spectrum. We don’t see that these days.”
A Quinnipiac University poll of registered voters in Pennsylvania, published in July, found that 74 percent would oppose a new data center being built in their community. That’s up from 68 percent when the same question was asked of voters in February.
With lots of open space, water and energy resources, Pennsylvania is attractive to data center developers, who are looking for large chunks of land that are near adequate power sources or in places that will allow them to build their own power source, as well as near water, which is needed to cool the massive computer systems housed in these centers.
So far, about 70 data centers have been proposed, are under construction or have some kind of preliminary activity in Pennsylvania, according to the Data Center Proposal Tracker, a citizen-run database that tracks projects across multiple states. They are scattered in and around each of the four competitive districts, with a heavy concentration in the northeastern Pennsylvania region that includes the 8th District.

11ed2dbc6620.text: Democrats in a pair of deep-red states are testing the religious right's dominance by putting their Christian faith at the center of their campaigns — potentially creating a template for the party to compete in similarly forbidding terrain. Why it matters: Upsets by Texas' James Talarico and Kansas' Adam Hamilton would all but ensure that Democrats take the Senate. A recent poll from Pew shows both an opening and an obstacle: White evangelicals still strongly favor Republicans, while many other Christian groups lean Democratic or are more narrowly split. The big picture: Talarico , a Presbyterian seminary student, and Hamilton, a United Methodist pastor, are challenging conservatives' claim to speak for faith. Their bids come after Democrat Raphael Warnock, senior pastor of Ebenezer Baptist Church, was elected to the Senate in 2021. President Trump won both Texas and Kansas by double digits in 2024. Neither state has sent a Democrat to the Senate in the 21st century — the last time Kansas did was in 1932. Both races this year are considered toss-ups . Zoom in: Talarico's "religiosity is a way to soften his liberalism" and potentially win over Christians turned off by his scandal-plagued opponent , says Brandon Rottinghaus, who co-hosts Houston Public Media's "Party Politics." Talarico has also made several visits to Black Baptist churches . Trump made inroads with minority communities in Texas, and Talarico looks to do the same after besting Rep. Jasmine Crockett (D-Texas), who is Black, in a brutal primary. He's harnessed scripture in his pitch against Christian nationalism and for protecting the vulnerable, invoking the biblical campaign slogan, "It's time to start flipping tables." "We're in a populist political moment, and many of the teachings of the social gospel give him an opportunity to link the politics and his faith together," Rottinghaus adds. By the numbers: A September Marist survey of 1,139 Texas registered voters showed Paxton with a 75% to 22% lead over Talarico among white evangelical Christians. In Kansas, the race will hinge less on whether Hamilton can win large numbers of religious Republicans and more on whether he can replicate Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly's coalition, says Alexandra Middlewood, the political science department chair at Wichita State University. Hamilton has presented himself as a bridge-builder, drawing on his experience leading the largest United Methodist church in the nation. His well-known religious background could appeal to less engaged, moderate Christians and center-right voters, Middlewood says. Yes, but: While Kansas has elected blue governors and voted to keep abortion legal in the state, Republicans have a massive registration advantage that's made a Democratic Senate win "near impossible," notes Bob Beatty, Washburn University's political science chair. Establishment Democrats have long been viewed with suspicion, especially in western Kansas, he said. But Hamilton being a pastor "gives him an open doorway to approach those voters in western Kansas that I would argue previous Democrats have not had." Zoom out: Black clergy — including Warnock — have a history of political action. But white clergy are stepping up to run as Democrats in substantial numbers. In Iowa, Sarah Trone Garriott, a Lutheran minister, and Lindsay James, a Presbyterian pastor, are running in tight House races. Pastor Doug Pagitt, executive director of progressive Christian group Vote Common Good, says the religious left's surge is driven by candidates' personal convictions and years-long efforts from groups like his that have trained politicians on how to connect with faith voters. But Trump, who Pagitt says has repeatedly offended Christians , is also a motivator: "There is no single person who could be more helpful to Democrats reaching out to religious people right now than Donald Trump. He is the greatest recruiting tool." Yes, but: Trump has repeatedly defied predictions that the religious right wouldn't vote for him. The other side: Ralph Reed, chair of the conservative Faith and Freedom Coalition, tells Axios he's doubtful the Democrats' effort to lean into religion will attract voters of faith. "Voters will not vote for a candidate who professes to hold to their faith, but doesn't share their values," he says. One GOP opponent labeled clergy running for office as Democrats "PINOs" — Pastors in Name Only. But while Reed says he's confident Republicans will turn out after Trump's battleground blitz, he acknowledges their economic struggles. "Evangelicals and other conservative voters of faith, they live in the real world too," he says. Whether evangelicals are motivated to show up will be a major story of the midterms, says Ryan Burge of the John C. Danforth Center on Religion and Politics. The other will be how Catholics shift: "If the Adam Hamiltons, the James Talaricos of the world can win over people, it's going to be ... marginally attached Catholics," Burge predicts. The bottom line: There's a clear movement on the religious left — but the question remains whether voters will join it. Go deeper: "Shocking" number of white clergy run as Democrats in 2026

Hundreds of flights in the East Asia region were cancelled on Friday as powerful Typhoon Champi roared close to Taiwan's north-east coast.
Schools and offices in Taiwan were shut as Champi neared the island. While it is uncertain if it will make landfall, the storm was forecast to bring 90cm (35in) of rain and strong winds to the north-east until Saturday.
One person died after being swept away by waves, authorities said. The storm also injured 171 people and forced 1,000 others to evacuate.
Champi is the latest in a string of intense typhoons as a Super El NiÃ±o heats up the Pacific Ocean and fuels storms. At its peak earlier this week, it was the planet's strongest storm of the year so far.
On Friday afternoon, Champi was packing wind gusts of 191km/h (119mph) .
After passing Taiwan's north-eastern tip and the Okinawa islands in southern Japan, Champi is expected to hover over the waters off China's eastern coast, before curving farther to the north-east to Japan's main island.
Weather agencies in Taiwan, Hong Kong and Japan forecast that the eye of the storm is expected to pass without making landfall in Taiwan,
However, a forecaster in Taiwan's Central Weather Administration told Reuters that they could not rule this out completely - especially if the storm "stalls, loops or wobbles from side to side" as it approaches.
Rainfall is expected to peak on Saturday morning and continue to batter Taiwan until Saturday evening, the Central Weather Administration said.
Taiwanese authorities have urged people to stay away from coasts and mountains.
Work and classes were suspended in nearly all of Taiwan's 22 counties and cities on Friday - what's colloquially known as a "typhoon holiday" - as Champi approached the island.
Taiwan's $5tn (Â£3.7tn) stock exchange was also closed on Friday because of the severe weather.
Only Kinmen county, an archipelago located to the west of Taiwan's main island, continued work and classes as usual.
In Japan, power cuts were reported in nearly 8,400 households in the southern Okinawa prefecture, according to the local power company.
More than 160 flights have been cancelled across four Japanese airlines.
Champi has also stirred up heavy rains and winds in Batanes, a Philippine island chain below southern Taiwan.
Photos posted on the local government's Facebook page showed waves crashing into seaside villages and roads closed to traffic. There were no immediate reports of casualties.
Typhoon Champi became the strongest storm of the year earlier this week, when it attained a maximum sustained wind speed of 185mph (298km/h) as it moved over the Philippine Sea - the equivalent of a Category 5 hurricane.
While initially categorised as a "super typhoon", Champi weakened on Wednesday as it continued barrelling through the sea.
This is shaping up to be one of the most active typhoon seasons the region has seen in years. Champi is Japan's 30th typhoon of the year - making this the first time since 2013 that the country has seen so many storms.
The recent frequency of storms is due to an unusually strong El NiÃ±o - a naturally occurring phenomenon that hits the Pacific Ocean every few years and can trigger extreme weather events, from droughts to typhoons.

The Signal Interview
âWhen I came to Silicon Valley, we thought we were all making the world a better place,â Brian Chesky recalls, 19 years after he co-founded Airbnb. Now, he tells The CEO Signal, âSilicon Valleyâs in a bubble, and society feels like AI is happening to them, not for them.â
Chesky is an unusual figure in Californiaâs tech heartland. An industrial designer surrounded by mathematicians and engineers, he describes Silicon Valley as a nightclub he somehow snuck into as a 26-year-old when the bouncer wasnât looking.
âI wasnât supposed to be here,â he says. But he has grown close to CEOs like OpenAIâs Sam Altman, and he thinks he can help the AI industryâs leaders understand what people who stay in Airbnbs really think of them.
The aesthetic Chesky honed at the Rhode Island School of Design permeates his San Francisco headquarters, a former Eveready battery factory whose meeting rooms look like Airbnb rentals from around the world. But he implies that other pioneers around him have lost sight of who theyâre designing their products for. Tech executives love talking in lofty terms about âhumanity,â he says, but his fellow founders should be talking about people â like school teachers and mill workers â and listening to them, too.
âI talked to one famous person â I wonât mention who â and I said, âDo you talk to a regular person?â He goes, âYes, such and such.â Iâm like, âWell, thatâs your nanny,ââ Chesky says. âWe should talk to normal people we donât pay, people who are willing to tell us to F off and tell us why they donât like us.â
A $250 million pitch to get on âthe right sideâ of the housing issue
Chesky has had plenty of blunt feedback as Airbnb has grown, with cities from New York to Barcelona blaming his company for making housing less affordable. Despite years of engaging with local politicians, Airbnb has failed to stop some of them from implementing caps or outright bans on short-term rentals.
Asked whether he has any responsibility for the housing affordability crisis, Chesky replies: âI think we have a responsibility. I think thereâs a difference between having responsibility and being the primary cause.â
Listings on Airbnb typically comprise just 0.5% of the housing stock in cities where it operates, he says, and many of those properties are primary or second homes someone is already living in, rather than units that have been removed from the long-term rental market. Bans on short-term rentals havenât reversed housing inflation in cities like New York, he notes.
The bigger issue, Chesky argues, is a shortage of new construction. Last month, Airbnb positioned itself as a partner in solving that problem by announcing a $250 million fund to provide âlast-dollarâ financing for housing projects with funding shortfalls. Itâs a small sum for a company with a $100 billion-plus market capitalization, but he says it should unlock an additional $5 billion of new housing.
âItâs not philanthropy,â he says. Airbnb will make a return â albeit a smaller one than some real estate investors would expect â âbut weâre also going to be on the right side of this issue.â
Even so, he says, concerns about housing affordability are only going to get âmuch worseâ as more people want to move to cities. The two biggest issues in the 2028 US presidential election, he predicts, will be affordability and AI.
Cheskyâs advice for AIâs âPromethean momentâ
Chesky says he does not believe that AI will destroy humanity any time soon, but he thinks society is unprepared for the technological power that has been unleashed in this âPromethean moment.â Technology used to feel like a train that people just had to jump on to âride into the promised land of progress,â he says. âAnd now people feel like theyâre [on] the train tracks, and the train called AI is coming for them.âÂ
Silicon Valley cannot credibly police AI, he believes, warning his peers that if the technology is left unregulated, âbad sh*t is going to happen, and thereâs going to be overcorrection, and then thereâs going to be a hammer coming down.â
Nor does he believe that Washington can regulate AI successfully, because policymakers donât understand the technology well enough. âBridge-buildersâ between Silicon Valley, Washington, and ordinary people are needed â and he is putting himself forward as one of them.
One of his recommendations, he says, is that AI founders should stop talking about impossible-sounding goals like âsaving humanity.â Instead, they should take on one issue at a time, starting with the most immediate problem AI has exacerbated â cybersecurity. In the meantime, Silicon Valley is âlosing people because weâre not talking about people,â he warns. âWe just need to put design principles and humanity into AI.â
A new mission in matchmaking
Even as Chesky critiques Silicon Valleyâs blind spots, he is using them to define a new ambition for Airbnb.
Innovations like e-commerce and online banking mean that people are spending more time on their devices and less time bumping into friends and strangers in shopping malls, banks, and âthe real world,â he observes. Even our on-screen lives are more isolating than they were, he adds, since tech companies have rejected the form of social networking that was filled with updates from our friends for more advertiser-friendly social media. Health officials are investigating whether Ebola patients in Nigeria and Kenya may have crossed paths at Uganda's main airport earlier this month.
Both travelled through Entebbe airport on 3 October and investigators are examining whether they could have been exposed through shared equipment or other contact, the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) said on Thursday.
Dr Wessam Mankoula, the agency's head of emergency preparedness and response, said this was "one of the possible scenarios", but stressed that no link had been established.
Nigeria is battling its first Ebola case in more than a decade, while Kenya has confirmed nine infections, including one death.
The Nigerian patient, a 42-year-old Ugandan-born woman who lives in Abuja, is receiving treatment in isolation and is showing signs of improvement, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).
She is married to a Swiss diplomat based in Nigeria, Switzerland's foreign ministry has confirmed. Her husband, who accompanied her on a trip to Uganda, is also in isolation but has not developed symptoms.
The woman returned to Nigeria on 3 October after spending about two and a half weeks in Uganda, travelling through Ethiopia's capital, Addis Ababa, where she had a two-hour stopover.
She developed symptoms four days after arriving in Abuja and sought treatment at two private health facilities before testing positive for Ebola on 20 October.
Health officials are now trying to establish where she contracted the virus and whether her movements overlapped with those of the Kenyan patient.
The Kenyan man had travelled from the Democratic Republic of Congo through Uganda before arriving in Nairobi on 3 October. He later died, becoming Kenya's first recorded Ebola death ever.
Although both patients passed through Entebbe airport on the same day, health officials have not established whether they met, used the same facilities or had any other contact.
"One of the issues we are currently investigating has been some sort of interaction between the two cases at the airport," Mankoula told journalists on Thursday.
Investigators are also examining whether the two infections could have a common source.
The WHO said it was too early to determine where the patient in Nigeria became infected.
"The source of exposure is still not known. The travel history of the patient is still being pieced together," said Dr Patrick Otim, a WHO emergency response official.
He said investigators had struggled to obtain a complete account of her movements because opportunities to interview her were limited while she remained in hospital.
Nigeria's Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) said it was carrying out genomic sequencing, which could help investigators understand whether the infection is related to other cases.
"The investigation is reconstructing the full travel and exposure history. Genomic sequencing is given a high priority," said Dr Pavel Ursu, the WHO's representative in Nigeria.
Ugandan health officials previously said the woman had travelled to eastern DR Congo for business, where the current Ebola outbreak began.
However, the WHO, Africa CDC and Nigeria's health ministry said they had not received verified information confirming that she had visited the country.
Uganda has maintained that it has no confirmed active Ebola cases and says the woman's travel through the country does not necessarily mean she contracted the virus there.
Meanwhile, Africa CDC said Nigeria had identified additional people who may have been exposed to the woman, beyond the 44 contacts initially reported.
"Most of those contacts, they are from the healthcare workers in different facilities where this case has been receiving treatment. We have also some few family members," Mankoula told journalists on Thursday.
He said Nigerian authorities were working to identify and quarantine those considered at high risk, but declined to give an updated figure before the government released its findings.
"The position of the country [is] to bring those high-risk contact and put them on quarantine," he added.
Dr Ursu said the woman was receiving a high standard of clinical care and that her condition was stable.
In Kenya, the first group of people quarantined after possible exposure to Ebola will begin returning home on Sunday after completing 21 days of monitoring without developing symptoms.
Health Director-General Dr Patrick Amoth said all nine confirmed infections were linked to the first patient, with no evidence of wider community transmission.
"We are not out of the woods," he warned, urging the public to remain vigilant but not panic.
He said the remaining eight patients remained in isolation and were responding well to treatment.
The developments have renewed concerns about the movement of infected people across international borders, particularly between the DR Congo and neighbouring Uganda, where thousands of people cross daily for trade, work and family visits.
Dr Otim warned that the long and porous border between the two countries made it difficult to screen everyone entering or leaving, as many people used unofficial crossing points.
The WHO's regional director for Africa, Dr Mohamed Janabi, called for "regional vigilance" and urged countries to strengthen surveillance, investigate infections and protect frontline health workers.
Ebola is a serious viral disease that spreads through direct contact with the blood or other bodily fluids of an infected person, or with contaminated objects. It does not spread through the air like flu.
The virus can cause fever, severe weakness, vomiting and diarrhoea, and can be fatal. People are not considered infectious before they develop symptoms.
Health authorities say tracing contacts quickly, isolating suspected cases and providing early treatment are crucial to preventing further transmission.
