A magnitude 7.0 earthquake has hit a mountainous region in Tibet, killing at least 16 people and injuring dozens, according to Chinese state media.
The centre of the quake hit BaqÃªn County in the Nagqu region on Thursday night, Xinhua reported, citing the local emergency management bureau.
The county - located in what China calls the Tibet Autonomous Region after annexing it in the 1950s - is 400km (250 miles) north-east of the region's capital, Lhasa.
Authorities have declared the incident an emergency and deployed rescue teams to the affected area, where 65 others have been injured, including 11 people with severe injuries.
The electricity supply has been cut off and 339 homes have collapsed in the affected region, though by Friday morning there were reports of power restored in some areas.
Local media said more than 12,400 people had been relocated following the earthquake.
Rockfall has forced roads in the region to close, making it more difficult for crews to reach impacted high-altitude areas.
The US Geological Survey (USGS) has recorded seven tremors close to the epicentre, all of which are located in the mountainous region. The largest tremor was recorded at 5.2 magnitude at a depth of 10km.
Shallow earthquakes and tremors closer to the Earth's surface are more damaging than deep quakes.
Several survivors of the earthquake have told local media about their harrowing escape.
Nagqu resident Yixi Cuomu told Tibet Daily that she was asleep in her bed when her house started shaking violently. Realising it was an earthquake, she headed outside barefoot, her "legs trembling uncontrollably" as she descended the staircase in her home.
Another eyewitness said the shaking was so violent "that in that moment I felt as if several hundred yaks were running past us".
Residents chose to spend the night outdoors in subzero temperatures, seeking shelter in tents or their cars, as they feared aftershocks could trap them in their homes, according to the news outlet.
Chinese state media reported on Friday morning that more than 400 aftershocks had been registered since the quake occurred.
China's Premier Li Qiang has called for "urgent efforts" to organise rescue operations and medical treatment for the injured, and relocate and resettle affected residents appropriately, according to state media.
Li noted that the earthquake-hit area is at a high altitude, around 4,800m (15,750ft), and prone to aftershocks.
The Ministry of Emergency Management has dispatched a working group to the affected area to guide rescue and disaster relief operations.
Separately, the Chinese government announced it was allocating 50 million yuan (Â£5.6m; $7.5m) for disaster relief efforts in Tibet.
Videos on social media of the moment the quake struck show villagers running into the streets as buildings shake violently in the dark. These have not been independently verified.
The region is prone to devastating seismic activity.
In 2023, a 6.2 magnitude quake killed more than 120 people in the nearby mountainous Gansu province of China.
Tibet and Nepal were also recently devastated by massive floods and landslides less than two months ago, unleashed by a glacier collapse, which killed at least 1,400 people. Hundreds of others are still reported missing.
Despite the region presenting some of the most challenging rescue conditions, rescue teams on the Tibetan plateau are highly experienced and have shown an ability to mobilise quickly.
In January 2025, military personnel, firefighters, police and specialist rescue teams were in the area within hours after a powerful eartquake struck the Shigatse region of Tibet.
The Chinese military also have drones to help survey the area.
Tibet, which has long demanded greater autonomy, is one of the most tightly controlled regions in China.
With foreign media restricted from the region and information heavily censored by authorities, Chinese state media is the main source for updates and details when such disasters happen.

A farmer hit by England's first outbreak of avian flu this season has said the loss of 32,000 egg-laying birds is likely to cost her business more than Â£100,000.
Catherine Armstrong, who has a free-range farm near Belford, Northumberland, told the BBC of the "shock" of her worst fears coming true when she found "a carpet of dead birds" in her barns this week.
The outbreak's source is not yet known but the virus is thought to have been brought onto the site, which has strict biosecurity measures, by wild birds. The farm's remaining poultry were culled.
The Animal and Plant Health Agency (APHA) has put control measures in place to contain the outbreak, external but warned cases were likely to rise.
So far, there has been one other case of highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) in the UK, external, on the Isle of Lewis, Scotland.
Armstrong said her birds, which normally produce 28,500 eggs a day, which are then supplied to a range of UK supermarkets, began to die a week ago.
"At this age of the flock, you would tend to see the odd death but on the Friday my lady who works in the shed messaged me at night to say that 39 had died," she explained.
During the weekend, the virus spread rapidly, with more than 1,000 birds dead by Sunday night.
The APHA was contacted and a vet came out to carry out tests but Armstrong said she knew it would be bird flu: "In my heart of hearts, when you are shovelling dead birds out of a shed, you feel... well, I didn't need the results. I knew what the results would be."
By Tuesday, the virus had been confirmed, with thousands of birds dead. Within two days, all the remaining birds had been culled to control the virus' spread.
"All your worst fears, I suppose, are realised then. It is an emotional roller coaster. I mean, for instance, on the Sunday, I just felt numb. On the Monday, just a bit like 'Why me?'. Angry, cross, upset.
"On the Tuesday, it's a bit matter of fact. It's like, 'Right, we've got to do this. I've got to do that'. And on Wednesday, I was just desperately sad.
"Normally, you'd open up a hen shed door and there'd be 16,000 birds looking at you but to see them all lying dead, just a carpet of dead birds, is quite shocking.
"As a poultry keeper, it's a horrible shock."
'Dreadful disease'
Armstrong praised the APHA staff for their work and the wider industry for its support.
She said despite the high cost of the outbreak - which she estimated would be more than Â£100,000 - she was "not going to sit back and let it beat us".
Gary Ford, of the British Free Range Egg Producers' Association (Bfrepa), said the farm had high standards of biosecurity but "sadly, as was the case here, that does not always prevent infection as free-range hens come into regular contact with wild birds, which spread this dreadful disease".
He added the association would be calling on the government to bring in a regional housing order to protect "those poultry farms close to coastal areas and known flight paths of migratory wild birds".
Meanwhile, farmers are still waiting for the results of a recent government trial of a bird flu vaccine in turkeys.
A spokesman for the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) said that, while the trial concluded in August, results would not be available until the end of the year and vaccination would not be an option for this bird flu season.
Meanwhile, an APHA spokesperson said it expected colder temperatures and the arrival of migratory birds "to see a rise in infection cases, which is why it is so important that bird keepers have robust biosecurity measures in place to limit the spread of this devastating disease".
The UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) said the risk to the general public's health posed by avian influenza remained very low while the Food Standards Agency (FSA) said it posed a very low food safety risk, with properly cooked poultry and poultry products, including eggs, safe to eat.

On Sunday evening, Bollywood actor Tiger Shroff went to play football in Juhu, a leafy, affluent Mumbai neighbourhood where film stars live, fans congregate and celebrity sightings are a part of life. But as the 36-year-old was leaving the ground in his BMW, shots rang out. His driver was wounded, as was a vlogger who had come to film the actor.
Shroff, whose films usually include elaborate action sequences and choreographed escapes, had just survived an actual shooting attempt.
Four days later, the case still dominates headlines in India, with each new revelation spawning fresh theories, competing claims and a growing list of alleged conspiracies.
Police have detained or arrested 10 suspects, with investigators tracing alleged weapon deliveries through several states and examining payments made to the alleged attackers.
The attempted shooting has also brought the name of Lawrence Bishnoi, one of India's most notorious gangsters, back into the headlines. Soon after the attack, a screenshot of a social media post purportedly made by an alleged associate of the Bishnoi gang circulated online, claiming responsibility. A separate audio recording emerged in which a man identifying himself as Anil Pandit repeated the claim and said Shroff had been targeted over his alleged links to actor Salman Khan, who Bishnoi has been threatening for years.
Mumbai police have not verified the claims or established that the Bishnoi gang was behind the attempted shooting. Investigators are still trying to determine who ordered the attack and why.
The targeting of Shroff follows a series of threats and attacks involving prominent Bollywood figures, including gunfire outside Khan's home in 2024 and filmmaker Rohit Shetty's house earlier this year. Together, the incidents have revived fears about the reach of organised crime into the film industry, stirring memories of a darker era in Mumbai's history.
During the 1990s and early 2000s, the city's underworld exerted formidable influence over the film industry, financing productions, demanding protection money and sometimes using violence to enforce its demands. It took years of police operations, and the gradual arrival of institutional financing, to loosen that grip.
Now, as fresh allegations and theories emerge almost daily, a question that once seemed to belong to Mumbai's past has returned: is the underworld trying to control Bollywood again?
Those who confronted organised crime in Mumbai at its peak say the answer is not as straightforward as the attempt to shoot Shroff might suggest.
D Sivanandhan, who took charge of Mumbai's Crime Branch in 1998, remembers a time when a phone call from Dubai, where some of the most notorious gang leaders were based, could decide the fate of a film - who starred in it, financed it or profited from its distribution.
In an industry dependent on private money, the line between investor and extortionist could be perilously thin. And the threats were real. In 1997, music mogul Gulshan Kumar was shot dead outside a Mumbai temple. Three years later, filmmaker Rakesh Roshan survived an assassination attempt.
Sivanandhan investigated the financing of Chori Chori Chupke Chupke, a Salman Khan film whose producer and his assistant were each sentenced to six years in prison under Maharashtra's organised crime law for underworld links. The film's financier received a one-year sentence for withholding information about those links. Police seized the film's negatives, and its release eventually happened under court supervision.
Gangsters were not always imposing themselves on a reluctant industry. Some filmmakers willingly sought their money, Sivanandhan recalled, in arrangements that could benefit both sides and proved difficult for police to dismantle.
But Sivanandhan is reluctant to see the latest violence as a return of the mafia he once fought. The men he pursued - Dawood Ibrahim, Chhota Shakeel, Arun Gawli and others - belonged to criminal networks rooted in Mumbai, even when their leaders operated from abroad.
"This is not the Mumbai mafia which we know in the last 60 years," he said. "This is something else."
That something else has become inseparable from the name Lawrence Bishnoi. A gangster with roots in northern India who has been in jail for years, Bishnoi has acquired an aura of folkloric menace: a prisoner said to command gunmen across continents, his name invoked in threats and claims of responsibility that spread almost instantaneously online.
Bishnoi has publicly threatened Khan over a 1998 poaching case involving blackbucks, a species of antelope revered by the Bishnoi community. In April 2024, gunmen fired five rounds outside Khan's Mumbai home. Six months later, Baba Siddique, a politician close to Khan and other actors, was murdered. Mumbai police have linked both attacks to the Bishnoi gang, though they have not established any personal involvement by Lawrence Bishnoi in Siddique's killing.
Some allegations against his network are backed by police investigations; others remain untested. But the distinction between what the gang has demonstrably done and what is claimed in its name can become blurred in the public imagination, doing little to diminish Bishnoi's notoriety.
Rakesh Maria, a former Mumbai police commissioner, has cited Bishnoi as an example of a new generation of gangsters who are more technologically adept and internationally connected than their predecessors. "The old underworld was visible and territorial, but the new one is dispersed, fluid, making it harder to pin down," Maria told The Print, external last year. "They no longer need to reside in the city to command it."
The relationship between gangsters and Bollywood has changed in another way, too, in who gets to shape their image.
In the 1990s, Bollywood itself helped turn Mumbai's feared underworld figures into objects of fascination. Films such as Satya (1998) and Company (2002) brought a gritty, visceral realism to their world, whil

US First Lady Melania Trump has "successfully secured" a ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky, the White House has said.
The statement said the truce in the "front-line war city on the brink of disaster" would begin on 29 October, though Ukraine and Russia have so far not commented.
"Oleshky's remaining population is comprised primarily of elderly residents who urgently need medical attention, medicine, food, and clean water," it added.
Oleshky, in the Kherson region, was seized by Russian forces during the first days of Moscow's full-scale invasion in February 2022. Remaining residents have recently resorted to eating garden weeds to survive.
The White House statement said Melania Trump and her representative had worked "directly with Russian and Ukrainian leadership to define the terms of the localised ceasefire".
"Non-military, civilian leaders from both countries will work together to visit Oleshky residents in their homes and determine the level of assistance they require," she is quoted as saying.
"Residents who wish to evacuate will receive coordinated support and transportation to their preferred destination. I anticipate some will want to go to Russia, and some to Ukraine."
Melania Trump added that Oleshky residents "have limited electricity, live amid mined roads, and endure regular military attacks" and that "without my intervention, the possibility to bring humanitarian aid into the city and to evacuate the elderly would be impossible".
The statement did not say how long the ceasefire would be in place for.
Last month, some of the remaining Oleshky residents told the BBC harrowing accounts of how they were surviving in the city that was being constantly shelled and cut off from food and water.
They said that children remaining in wider Oleshky were suffering from malnutrition, a lack of medical services and were "degrading" without access to education.
Many also told the BBC there was only one hospital partially operational, opening a few days a week to perform critical amputations.
The local population was living under a "full blockade" by Russian forces, according to Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha.
Ukraine says it has attempted to deliver supplies to the area but has not had success in recent months.
The Kremlin in September acknowledged that Oleshky was facing "a critical situation" and "problems with supplies of food and medicine", but added that "Russia's military was working to resolve them" and blamed Kyiv.
Oleshky is trapped between the Dnipro River, which separates it from Ukrainian positions, and Russian forces.
The city was home to 24,000 people before Russia's full-scale invasion. Now Ukraine estimates that some 6,000 people remain in the city and its surrounding areas, including 200 children.
While the US first lady is relatively lower profile than some of her predecessors - and only occasionally seen at White House events - she has become involved in addressing humanitarian issues stemming from the Russia-Ukraine war.
In August 2025, Melania Trump penned a letter to Russian President Vladimir Putin, telling him it was "time to protect children and future generations worldwide".
Although she did not mention Ukraine by name, just days later at the White House Ukrainian President Volodomyr Zelensky handed over a letter from his wife Olena, thanking her for her efforts on children.
In a rare public appearance in October the same year, the US first lady said that Putin had answered directly in writing and that her representatives were working with the Russian president's team to repatriate Ukrainian children from Russia and vice versa.
Some 34 children have reportedly been returned since 2025, including five this July.
According to US President Donald Trump, his wife has also privately expressed scepticism about Putin and his desire to achieve peace.
"I'd get home, I'd say, 'First lady, I had the most wonderful talk with Vladimir. I think we're finished'," Trump said in July last year.
"And then I'll turn on the television, or she'll say to me one time, 'Wow, that's strange because they just bombed a nursing home'."

Six people were killed when gunmen opened fire on a funeral in central Jordan, a government spokesperson has said.
Another 28 people were injured in the church in the village of Hmoud, in the Karak governorate on Friday.
The unidentified gunmen are reported to have arrived in a car, entered the church and opened fire before fleeing, in what government spokesperson Dr al-Momani Mohammad described as a "heinous attack".
Jordan's King Abdullah II said the authorities would "confront the terrorist act that targeted Karak with the harshest penalties."
Dozens of people had been inside the church for the funeral when the shooting began, Khaled Burqan, one of the mourners, told Jordan's al-Mamlaka state-run TV.
He said two attackers armed with a rifle and a pistol had been firing at the mourners for several minutes.
CCTV footage, verified by the BBC, appears to shows three gunmen making their way from a road toward the church.
Two of the attackers are seen making their way onto what appears to be a vehicle entrance to the church grounds, before retreating briefly and returning with a third man. All three appear to be armed with handguns.
Separate footage believed to be from the aftermath of the attack appears to show several dead and wounded bodies on the ground amid some chaotic scenes.
No-one has so far claimed responsibility for the attack.
A news briefing by interior ministry officials is expected shortly, and al-Momani has said the country's prime minister will chair a meeting of the Security Council to be attended by all ministers.
In his post on X, King Abdullah II offered his condolences to the families of the victims, writing: "Whoever imagines that the bullets of treachery can divide the ranks of Jordanians will fail in his endeavour before our steadfastness and unity."
Karak has a sizeable Christian community in the majority-Muslim Jordan.
Such violence is rare in Jordan, but deadly attacks have been carried out in the country in the past.

85f692654a79.text: By — Associated Press Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/rescuers-search-for-survivors-after-deadly-earthquake-in-chinas-tibet-region Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Rescuers search for survivors after deadly earthquake in China's Tibet region World Oct 23, 2026 10:25 AM EDT BEIJING (AP) — Rescuers combed through a remote area in the Chinese region of Tibet on Friday after a magnitude 7 earthquake that killed at least 16 people, injuring 54 and collapsing hundreds of homes, according to Chinese state media. The disaster struck Nagqu, a city north of Tibet's capital Lhasa that's some 4,800 meters (5,249 yards) above sea level, on Thursday. At least 339 homes collapsed, and officials told journalists they were concerned about further building collapses from aftershocks, as well as casualties from rockslides. WATCH: Wall of mud and debris floods communities in Nepal and Tibet Search and rescue efforts are complicated by the geography and low temperatures, officials said. As of Friday afternoon, rescuers had done three rounds of searches, going through each household, and each village, said Dunzhu, the acting mayor of Nagqu city, said in a press conference. More than 5,000 people from three local counties were deployed for rescue efforts. Supplies including 2,000 prefabricated housing units, around 3,400 tents and 2,000 folding beds, as well as flashlights and winter clothing arrived in the region. The U.S. Geological Survey said the quake occurred at 10:33 p.m. local time on Thursday, with its epicenter 191 kilometers (119 miles) east-northeast of Nagqu. It put the earthquake's depth at 18 kilometers (11 miles). The U.S. agency recorded at least seven aftershocks with magnitude between 4.3 and 5.2, all of them with a depth of 10 kilometers (6 miles), according to its website. China's official news agency Xinhua said on Friday that communication in some areas hit by the quake was down. Local railway authorities have taken emergency actions to halt trains passing through the region. The earthquake also caused rockfalls that have forced local authorities to close a section of National Highway 317, allowing only emergency, rescue and official support vehicles through as crews worked to clear debris, according to Xinhua. Intermittent snows are expected in the earthquake region over the next three days, Xinhua said. Chinese President Xi Jinping called for all-out efforts in rescue operations and medical relief work, issuing instructions Friday morning. Paris St-Germain's Ligue 1 match against Lyon has been pushed back 24 hours to Monday as the French capital prepares for another weekend of protests.
The fixture at the Parc des Princes in Paris had been scheduled to kick off at 19:45 GMT on Sunday but will instead take place at 20:30 on Monday.
The Ligue de Football Professionnel (LFP) announced the postponement in a statement, external on Friday after French police prohibited the fixture from taking place on its original date.
French authorities are preparing a major security operation for demonstrations planned for Saturday.
Around 550,000 people took part in demonstrations last Saturday to protest rising fuel prices, education standards and the cost of living, which have escalated after weeks of student protests.
Marches took place in several major French cities, including Paris, backed by unions and student groups, and were marred by some incidents of violence, looting and destruction.
The security challenge is further complicated by Sunday's NFL match between the Pittsburgh Steelers and New Orleans Saints at the Stade de France, an event expected to require a significant police deployment.
The game will be played in Saint-Denis, about 10km from Place de la Bastille, where the protests are expected to begin.
The disruptions have already affected France's domestic football schedule with Toulouse's Ligue 1 home game against Troyes moved from Saturday to Sunday at the request of authorities.
Reigning French and European champions PSG are second in the standings after seven matches, while Lyon lead the table on 14 points, ahead of the holders on goal difference.
The match will also now be played on the same day as the Ballon d'Or ceremony in London.
Injured PSG pair Ousmane Dembele, the 2025 winner, and Khvicha Kvaratskhelia are among the contenders for the award.

One person has been killed and five others wounded - three seriously - in a gun attack in a Parisian suburb which authorities are investigating as "terrorism".
Several drive-by shootings took place on Friday - first in Trappes to the south-west of Paris, and then in nearby La VerriÃ¨re. The rampage lasted almost 15 minutes, said Interior Minister Laurent NuÃ±ez. A12-year-old girl is among the wounded.
The suspected attacker has been arrested. The motive remains unclear, but the National Anti-Terrorist Prosecutor's Office (PNAT) said the incident appeared to be "murder in connection with a terrorist enterprise".
NuÃ±ez told reporters in Trappes: "It's clearly a terrorist crime, that's what [the prosecutor] has said."
The Mayor of Trappes, Ali Rabeh, said that "an individual fired shots from his vehicle at several people he encountered" on Friday morning.
The gunman drove through several neighbourhoods in a grey Renault Clio, according to witnesses. Rabeh said he had "fired randomly" with the seeming intent of causing "as many casualties as possible... he wanted to cause carnage", he said.
The mayor said people had been targeted at a petrol station, a medical centre and a playground in Trappes before the attacker had driven on to nearby La VerriÃ¨re.
A police union official said the suspect had been detained in La VerriÃ¨re on the main N10 road that runs through the town.
Asked what the motive for the shootings may have been, the mayor of Trappes said that the victim who had died was of African origin and one of those in a critical condition was of North African descent.
The attack had a "racist, probably Islamophobic overtone", he said.
In its own statement, the anti-terror prosecutor called for caution regarding the identity of the victims.
However, among the alleged offences covered by the investigation, the prosecutor listed "murder in connection with a terrorist enterprise" with the aggravated circumstance of acts committed because of "real or perceived membership of a particular race, ethnicity, nation or religion".
The attacker reportedly travelled down a main road, shooting intermittently out of his car window.
A local police chief told BFMTV that the suspect had used "an older-style semi-automatic weapon" with bursts of fire. Le Parisien reports that the gun dated back to World War Two.
Rabeh said the shooter had hit a health centre, a petrol station and several vehicles during the spree.

The life of a woman who filed a lawsuit alleging she was drugged and raped at a Cornell University fraternity house has been completely upended, her lawyer has said.
Speaking to the BBC ahead of a hearing in the civil case on Friday in New York, her lawyer Thomas Giuffra said: "She feels under fire."
The woman, known anonymously as Jane Doe, is suing her former school and the fraternity over the alleged incident involving several men at the Chi Phi fraternity house in October 2024.
When the case went viral, a series of "I am Jane Doe" solidarity posts appeared, but there was a separate campaign aimed at unmasking her and defending the men, who have all denied any wrongdoing.
The men, who are also being sued by the woman, have not been charged with any crimes.
With initial proceedings now under way in the civil case, Giuffra told the BBC that these last few weeks have been "a very hard time" for his client, who isn't doing a lot beyond "surviving".
Her decision to sue was rooted in a desire for closure and to take power back, he said.
Giufrra visited Jane Doe this week and found that she hadn't been sleeping well â relying on medication to get rest.
Now in trauma therapy, he says she doesn't feel safe in her own home following malicious threats that were directed at her and her family.
After her address was published online without her consent, someone called in a fake emergency that led to police in full tactical gear drawing assault rifles on her father, her friend and her brother at their family home.
"It's just constant fear," he said.
He added that despite this her resolve hadn't been shaken and she remains determined to overhaul the university system at Cornell, and across the country, to protect survivors.
Cornell University, after initially defending its disciplinary measures, acknowledged it fell short in its handling of Jane Doe's case.
After facing intense pressure, the college's president announced that fraternity parties would be suspended until the end of the academic year to allow for a thorough review to determine whether and how they can safely continue.
The school also said it would add sexual assault investigators to its police force.
Giuffra, however, says he is surprised that Cornell has not reached out to him and believes they have been focused solely on "damage control".
He says any agreement with Cornell to resolve the civil lawsuit will need to include "steps to ensure there are no more Jane Does" and if there are, that they are going to be supported.
The BBC contacted Cornell for comment who directed us to the university's previous statements and comments on its internal investigation in 2024.
New York's governor Kathy Hochul appointed a special prosecutor, New York's Attorney General Letitia James, to oversee a reopened investigation into whether criminal charges are warranted.
Giuffra expects it will take a long time to do a proper investigation but is concerned that they will be going after evidence that is now "stale".
"A lot of the communication was on Snapchat, Snapchat goes away," he told the BBC.
"The best time to get evidence is around the time of the crime and that just didn't happen."
However, Giuffra believes he can win the civil case against the university, the men and others, where the burden of proof is lower than a criminal case.
Civil cases require a preponderance of the evidence, that it's more likely than not it happened, while criminal cases require proof beyond a reasonable doubt.
Recent high profile cases have shown the way juries evaluate consent can be unpredictable.
"I wouldn't have taken the case if I didn't think it was a strong case that I could win and get her some closure."

Do you have three days' worth of food and water in your home?
That is what the government has told all of us to have on hand to get through a national emergency, as well as some other basic items.
Its "Be Ready" campaign warns that severe weather and cyber attacks could disrupt essential services, and British households need to make sure they have what they need to get through a rocky few days.
On Friday, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said unexpected events "seem to becoming more common" and everyone should have "those supplies in the house to get you through those moments".
As one expert warns the UK is "light years" behind our neighbours when it comes to preparing for major disruption, we've drilled down into what you need and why.
What is on the 'Be Ready' checklist?
The government recommends having enough supplies in the kitchen to last three days, including bottled water and non-perishable foods.
Wet wipes, a torch and cash are also recommended - you can scroll through below to see the full list.
Disaster planning expert Professor Lucy Easthope said the goal of asking household to prepare is to make it easier for emergency service to cope in the event of a national emergency.
For example, the government says people who need medication should have an extra supply just in case. Prof Easthope says: "If people have got their heart pills for an extra for an extra 48 hours, it stops [response crews] from having to immediately find an emergency pharmacist."
While the latest government campaign only launched on Thursday, some people are well ahead of the game.
Speaking to Radio 5 Live, Bridgette Clamp, who lives in near Penzance in Cornwall, said she has stocked up on "lots of tinned goods" as well as "flour, yeast and everything to bake bread".
"We're rocking and rolling," she says.
One woman, who spoke to 5 Live anonymously, said she bought "loads and loads" of emergency food - but ended up eating it before it was strictly necessary.
Like others, she wondered if the government was "scaremongering", adding: "I don't know but I've certainly bought into it."
Rob, who lives off-grid in north Wales, told the programme he has stocked up on so many supplies he "wouldn't even notice" if a disaster struck.
But he said he still felt there was "a bit of scaremongering" going on and wondered if he would ever need it all.
Why is the government telling people to stockpile now?
Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said the advice - which is similar to guidance issued by the previous government - was not triggered by any "particular piece of intelligence", but rather about improving "national resilience" more generally.
The government's announcement focused on extreme weather events, which are becoming more frequent because of man-made climate change - but Streeting also referred to the threat of "increasingly sophisticated cyber-attacks" on businesses, and supply chain disruption caused by "hostile state actors or terrorists".
Prof Easthope said she has been lobbying the government to launch this sort of campaign for "about 16 years".
She said successive governments have been hesitant of "putting out information that might cause tension" - and speculated that this advice may have been "rushed" out ahead of Storm Austen hitting the UK.
While many of us will already have a stash of tinned food in the cupboards, fewer homes are likely to have a store of bottled water.
Paul from Torquay, Devon, said to Radio 5 Live: "Who on earth carries three day supply of water?"
He added: "I think they've made it our responsibility, rather than their responsibility."
Do other countries have similar emergency advice?
Prof Easthope described the UK as "light years" behind neighbouring countries when it comes to preparedness.
"Countries like Scandinavia, Denmark, Sweden, Norway, they've been good at this for years," she said.
France advises people to store 72-hours' worth of food, while the German government says homes should have enough supplies to last for a 10-day period.
"This is one area where I'm very comfortable saying we are playing massive catch-up," added Easthope.
Awareness campaigns such as "think 72 hours" make a big difference in the US, Australia and "all around Europe", she said.
However, in the UK, she said disaster messaging often gets parodied, or governments are accused of "panic-mongering".
"We have seen the pendulum shift" in recent years, she adds, saying that "we are now seeing people recognise this" as an issue that needs tackling.

The Welsh government has announced plans to ban the use of traditional steel pylons to support electricity lines over which it has control.
Plaid Cymru ministers favour burying cables underground instead.
Plans for a network of pylons in the Towy Valley have faced a fierce local backlash with local Plaid politicians speaking out against the proposals.
The company behind the plans, Green Gen Cymru, said it welcomed the consultation and that it supported using "the right infrastructure in the right place".
Prohibiting the use of large steel lattice pylons for new lines up to 132 kilovolts was a Plaid Cymru manifesto pledge before May's Senedd election.
Launching a consultation on its policy on Friday, the Welsh government said undergrounding electricity circuits could "reduce the visual impact of electricity infrastructure, helping to protect landscapes and local amenity".
It also said that burying cables could make them less vulnerable to severe weather and could reduce the potential impact on birds and other wildlife.
However, the consultation document also acknowledges that undergrounding was "generally considered more expensive to install and maintain and could create construction impacts during installation".
The government's policy would allow for wooden poles or "equivalent, less intrusive infrastructure" to be used to support overhead cables where undergrounding isn't feasible.
Green Gen has plans to build three major power line routes connecting onshore wind farms planned by its sister company Bute Energy with the wider grid network.
It has previously said it would invest nearly Â£1bn by 2030, with proposals affecting parts of Carmarthenshire, Ceredigion, Powys and Shropshire.
But it has faced considerable opposition in certain communities, with groups representing hundreds of landowners taking the company to court in 2025.
In a bid to address concerns, Green Gen recently unveiled a "slim and compact" 22 metre (72ft) pylon, designed "with the Welsh landscape in mind".
The company has consistently said that undergrounding its cables would cost on average 4.5 times more, external than running them overhead.
That would mean an extra cost of Â£500m for the Towy Usk project between Carmarthenshire and Powys, according to Green Gen.
Welsh Energy Minister Adam Price said: "We know the necessary changes in the way energy is generated and used in Wales will require new grid infrastructure, however, we also know that new infrastructure can impact on the communities and the environment that hosts it.
"We want to see infrastructure that is sensitively designed to minimise impacts on the environment and the communities that host them, while offering the maximum benefits for Wales."
Andrew Hardcastle, executive director at Green Gen Cymru, said: "We welcome the Welsh government's consultation and its recognition of the importance of delivering the electricity infrastructure Wales needs in a way that is sensitive to our landscapes, environment and communities.
"Like all grid companies across the UK, we believe there is no one-size-fits-all solution to developing new electricity networks.
"Our approach is to use the right infrastructure in the right place, drawing on a range of technologies including underground cables, wooden poles and our recently announced lower-profile monopoles."
The company said it was "pleased that the consultation recognises the potential role of less visually intrusive overhead infrastructure, including monopoles, and invites evidence on their use".
Reform's Senedd spokesperson for rural affairs, Laura Anne Jones, said: "As part of our energy policy, we will continue to push for new power lines to be placed underground wherever possible, protecting our landscapes and rural communities.
"Reform will always stand up for our countryside and fight against its industrialisation."
The Welsh Conservatives welcomed the policy consultation.
The party's environment spokesperson, Andrew RT Davies said: "We recognise that Wales needs a modern electricity network to support economic growth, but communities should not have to accept eyesores across our beautiful natural landscapes, which must be conserved."
The consultation, external will run until 15 January 2027.

For people with asthma, switching from a gas stove to an electric one might be a breath of fresh air. The combustion that creates the flame of a gas stove or oven releases pollutants, including nitrogen dioxide, which can trigger asthma symptoms. After a research-backed electric stove replacement, people reported more symptom relief than is often achieved with asthma medications.
“We were really surprised at how large the benefit was,” says Ashwini Sehgal, a clinician who studies community health at Case Western Reserve University in Cleveland. With funding from the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency during the Biden administration, Sehgal and colleagues spearheaded a project to install electric stoves in Cleveland households that had at least one person with asthma.
Eighty-five participants who had poorly controlled asthma were given a questionnaire a few months after the switch. They reported symptom improvement that was roughly two to three times as large as what’s typical with medication. Those with the worst symptoms saw the biggest improvement. Participants also reported fewer emergency room or hospital visits and said they missed work or school less often.
One 38-year-old woman told Sehgal’s team that whenever she cooked on her gas stove, she felt like her throat was closing. But the sensation disappeared after she switched to electric. Another participant, a 36-year-old man, found it difficult to walk uphill and play with his kids. With the stove swap, “he described how much better he felt as ‘magical,’ ” Sehgal says.
While heating, steaming or frying on a gas stovetop, nearby NO2 levels can skyrocket, reaching hundreds of parts per billion. That’s much higher than the EPA’s one-hour outdoor air quality standard of 100 parts per billion. NO2 exposure is linked to increased asthma symptoms. For example, research in children has found the pollutant can boost wheezing, coughing and asthma attacks.
The project was initially funded to follow 1,200 households for 12 months. But the Trump administration terminated the EPA’s Community Change Grants early, which drastically reduced the number of study participants. Yet even with this small group, the symptom improvement was significant.
The decision to replace a gas stove “depends on how much you are struggling with your own illness,” says environmental epidemiologist Carrie Breton of WashU Bursky School of Public Health in St. Louis. As a trial run, Sehgal suggests using an electric hot plate and a toaster oven to see if keeping the gas stove off helps improve symptoms.
If a stove swap isn’t in the budget, reducing NO2 exposure is still worthwhile, says pulmonologist Laura Paulin of Dartmouth Health. She recommends using kitchen ventilation, either via an exhaust hood that vents to the outside or an open window. A HEPA filter with a carbon insert can trap NO2 to decrease airborne concentrations. And try to keep children with asthma out of the kitchen when the stove is on, Paulin says. “It is a daunting task to replace a stove, but it doesn’t have to be an all-or-nothing thing.”
For researchers, the next step would be to measure lung function before and after a stove switch, Breton says. It would also be helpful to account for more factors, such as seasonal effects. “Many things can trigger people’s asthma,” Paulin says. Researchers could do a randomized trial in which some people get the electric stove right away while others wait for six months, Sehgal says, to allow time for comparison.
If electric stoves continue to be linked with fewer trips to the emergency room, fewer hospitalizations and better symptom control than medication can provide, “health insurance companies should consider paying for or subsidizing” stove swaps, Sehgal says. “If it truly works this well,” Breton says, “it’s got a bigger bang for your buck.”

Gulf economies as a whole are expected to shrink 4.8% this year, almost matching the COVID-19 shock, with non-oil output receding in four countries. âThis conflict has disrupted energy production, shipping, tourism, trade, and confidence,â Jihad Azour, director of the IMFâs Middle East and Central Asia Department, told reporters in Dubai.

October's full Moon, nicknamed the Hunter's Moon, is set to light up the night sky this weekend.
It will be visible in the UK from Sunday 25 October into the morning of Monday 26 October.
Marking the 11th full Moon of 13 in 2026, it is the final one before a run of four consecutive supermoons, external.
If you want to catch a glimpse, keep an eye on the forecast to see if the weather will allow a clear view.
When is the best time to view the Hunter's Moon?
The Moon will rise in the east at just after 16:00 GMT on Sunday and set towards the west between 07:00 and 08:00 GMT on Monday - times vary across the UK.
The Moon will be officially full at 04:11 GMT on Monday. This is the moment of "syzygy" when the Sun and Moon will be aligned either side of the Earth.
However, the Moon will appear full on both Sunday and Monday nights, giving skygazers two chances to spot it.
During a full Moon, the whole of the Earth-facing side of the Moon is illuminated by the Sun.
You may notice an orange or reddish hue to the Moon when it is low in the sky due to the scattering of short wavelength blue light as it passes through a large depth of the atmosphere.
The longer wavelength red and orange colours are not scattered as readily so pass through to our eyes.
The Moon may also appear larger in the sky near moonrise and moonset - something called the "Moon Illusion".
This is when our brain makes us think the Moon looks bigger because it is viewed alongside objects on the horizon such as buildings and trees.
As well as looking out for the full Moon, there is also a chance to spot some shooting stars, with the Orionid meteor shower just past its peak.
The extra lunar light, however, may obscure some of the meteors, so be patient and leave time for your eyes to adjust.
Why is it called the Hunter's Moon?
Full Moons throughout the year have traditionally been given names that reflect what is going on in nature.
Different cultures use different names for the 12 or 13 full Moons across the lunar calendar, but many of the common ones we use today originate from Native American cultures.
In October, the term Hunter's Moon comes from the time of year hunters would have been most active, preparing for the colder and darker winter months ahead.
The Hunter's Moon is known to sit in the sky for a particularly long time - similar to the preceding Harvest Moon - giving hunters extra light in the skies.
Will the weather be clear enough to see the Moon?
Storm Boelo will continue to bring rain and very strong winds to northern Scotland early on Sunday night, but prospects of seeing the Moon increases as the night wears on.
There will be plenty of blustery showers in west Scotland and north-west England - any gaps between these could give a brief chance to view.
For the rest of the UK prospects are better, especially early in the night with clearer skies, before cloud tends to spread in from the south-west later.
If the weather fails to cooperate where you live, the next chance to see a full Moon will be on 24 November as the Beaver Supermoon.
This will be followed by a Christmas Eve Cold Supermoon on 24 December.
The succession of supermoons will then continue into 2027, with January and February's full Moons both set to be supermoons too.

Mink farming will end in Denmark by August 2029 after the government decided to drop plans to pursue an exemption to an EU-wide ban on the practice.
Denmark was once the largest producer of mink fur in the world, but the industry has declined due to global bans on fur farming, a decline in the fur trade and an earlier outbreak of a Covid strain in the nation's mink population.
The ban is due to come into effect on 7 August next year, and is followed by a two-year transition period to phase out the practice.
Danish Nature Minister Christian Rabjerg Madsen said the government had chosen animal welfare.
"A business should not continue just because it has existed for a long time. It should also make sense for society, for the economy and for the animals," he said.
The Danish government had initially sought an exemption for its mink industry when the EU added the mammal to its list of invasive species in 2025, prohibiting people from keeping them.
However, the current coalition government, elected in June, reversed this decision and decided not to proceed with the application on Friday.
Social Democrat MP Brigitte Vind said it was "a good day for animal welfare".
"It is absolutely the right decision not to apply for a special scheme for mink breeding in Denmark," she said.
The Danish Mink Association, which represents breeders, has been approached for comment.
Denmark is one of the few European countries to still produce mink fur, one of the more common pelts used in making fur garments.
However, its production has slipped behind that of other countries, such as Poland and China, in recent years.
The industry faced a crisis during the coronavirus pandemic, when the government ordered a mass cull of mink after a mutated strain of Covid-19 was found in the animals. Approximately 15 million were killed.
At the time, the country had huge export markets to China and Hong Kong. The government later admitted it had no legal basis for the culling.
There are now approximately 15,000 mink left in Denmark.
No costs have yet been determined for closing Denmark's seven remaining mink farms, but an animal welfare spokesperson for one of the governing coalition parties previously estimated it would be around 14m Danish krone (Â£1.56m), local media report, but the final amount could be higher.
The wearing of fur is a controversial subject within fashion circles, with publications and fashion brands choosing not to use or promote it several years ago.
But it re-entered the spotlight last year, with celebrities and fashionistas wearing both vintage and so-called faux fur.

5fb8a1db7381.text: On a recent evening near a secure U.S. facility, three federal agents saw a flying object they couldn't identify: a large "matte black triangle" that moved as fast as a fighter jet, made no sound and then disappeared, according to FBI and Defense Department reports. Why it matters: The 15-foot flying triangle is classified as a UFO-like "Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena" because the U.S. doesn't have the technology to make such a craft — and neither do its adversaries. The reports of the drone-like aircraft is of growing interest and concern to intelligence and military officials. Driving the news: The two reports about the mysterious triangle were included in a batch of 10 documents released Friday by U.S. officials under President Trump's order this year to disclose UAP records from all government sources as soon as possible. Friday's disclosure marks the seventh release of a tranche of documents under the order. Some of the documents found in the National Archives are from the 1940s. Zoom in: The flying triangle reports are the most intriguing because the incident — from this year — is so recent. The month and day are redacted. The FBI document is labeled an "Unidentified Aerial Object Observation Report" and the Defense Department 's report on it is classified as a "Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena" report. The observers were federal agents, including two with "extensive operational experience" and familiarity with drones. One had a "thermal monocular" for infrared tracking and yet couldn't detect "discrete heat sources associated with propulsion" from an engine on the mysterious craft. The agents reported seeing the drone-like triangle, with a wingspan of about 15 feet, rise vertically for as many as 300 feet above a mountain ridgeline without tilting or swaying. It stopped, hovered for about 20 seconds, and then flew horizontally as fast as a fighter jet for about 1.5 miles in three seconds without making a sound before it vanished. The intrigue: One of the documents released Friday doesn't concern a flying object. It's a declassified 2010 report about the Utah property known as the "Skinwalker Ranch," named after supernatural shapeshifting witches in Navajo culture. "Witnesses have reported unidentified balls of light at close range, daytime sightings of "dog-like" creatures running on two legs, unnatural animalistic howling/screaming, 'little people,' prehistoric-like birds and a maggot which measured about 8 feet long and 2- to 3-feet in diameter," the report said. The report's authors present no final conclusions or hard evidence, such as photographs, of the supernatural. DNA tests from one clump of hair from a suspected "Skinwalker" showed it came from a raccoon. The ranch is now the subject of a Netflix show . Other items in the tranche include: A 1954 report from a Swedish Transair pilot who said he and his crew witnessed flying saucers: "Previously I have been extremely skeptical about all the stories of mysterious objects — called flying saucers — that have been seen at diverse points," the captain said. "Now I don't know exactly what to think; but it did seem to me that we had seen a robot of some kind." A 1957 report from a B-52 pilot over Saudi Arabia who said he witnessed an unidentified aircraft. 1949 and a 1952 UFO reports from California's Catalina Island, site of some of the nation's first "flying saucer" sightings. A 1963 interagency coordination memo and 1960s records concerning how NASA and the Defense Department would handle and publicly discuss the collection of "fragments or suspected fragments of space vehicles of all types." Yes, but: The records released by the administration do not express any conclusions as to whether the government believes the UAPs represent the existence of alien life. They also don't indicate any conclusions as to whether UAPs represent a national security threat to the U.S.

7f22a8f4658e.text:
Matthewâs view
Just four years ago, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman was at the peak of his powers. He was feted by the Chinese president and snubbed the US president, all while sitting atop a gusher of oil wealth that allowed him to pour money into trying to turn his wildest ideas into reality.
Those days seem a long time ago.
This year was always going to be tough for MBS, as Prince Mohammed is widely known. Even before the Iran war, Saudi Arabiaâs budget deficit was widening, signature investment projects were being scaled back, and the sugar rush from the sweeping economic and social reforms was wearing off.
US President Donald Trumpâs war with Iran, which MBS warned against, has made matters worse. MBS now faces crises on multiple fronts: a global energy shock, a regional security emergency, and a deteriorating domestic economic outlook. Together, they form a perfect storm and expose the limits of his ability to shape events in the region.
Looking through the prism of oil, the attacks on shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb boosted prices enough to offset lower export volumes. But the short-term gains mask a longer-term risk. Despite heroic efforts to keep crude moving, the Gulfâs reputation as a reliable energy provider has been damaged. The longer the disruption lasts, the more key energy importers will prepare for life without Saudi oil. Consumers will seek alternative sources of hydrocarbons and accelerate investments in renewables. The result could spur a global scramble to pump more oil as quickly as possible, leaving the kingdom fighting to win back market share when the conflict ends amid a glut and lower prices.
But that is the future, and the war may be showing signs of escalation, making MBSâs vision of Saudi Arabia as the center of a prosperous Middle East â a place for international firms to invest, holidaymakers to visit, and the wealthy to buy homes â a much tougher sell. To be sure, as the recent Kuwait oil pipelines deal showed, attracting global capital into some critical infrastructure will still go ahead. But sustained uncertainty will make the kingdomâs diversification push harder to pull off.
The Houthis in Yemen, whom the kingdom has been battling on and off since 2009, have demonstrated an alarming ability to strike deep inside Saudi Arabia, from airports to the Aramco head office, with no regard for civilian lives. Residents and potential visitors are unnerved. If the war with Iran intensifies again, foreign executives will be reluctant to even visit Saudi Arabia, let alone invest in it.
Lastly, efforts to diversify the domestic economy away from oil and build new industries are losing steam. After allocating about 8% of GDP to NEOM, once contract cancellations are included, the government has admitted a costly defeat. Plans for the 2034 menâs soccer World Cup are being scaled back, as are other giant projects. Yet the security crisis and higher fuel costs are pushing expenditure up faster than oil revenues. Government debt is still low by global standards, but is climbing. Higher defense spending will be vital, but wonât do much for economic diversification.
MBS sits in an uncomfortable position, facing the limits of his power. Efforts to get close to Trump by promising investments into the US and putting money into Trump family business interests havenât translated to leverage in Washington. Despite Riyadhâs $1 trillion US investment pledge, Trump remarked in March that MBS never imagined heâd be âkissing my ass,â a crude display of how roles have been reversed since the prince snubbed Trumpâs predecessor, Joe Biden. China, which brokered a rapprochement between Saudi Arabia and Iran in 2023, is either unwilling or unable to help. And despite huge military spending, Saudi forces have struggled to deter their enemies.
The crown prince revealed a bold ambition to transform the kingdom, and the region, by 2030. The vision has never felt further away.

Nurdles found along the Danish coast are likely to originate from the spill in north-east England, according to the country's environment agency.
Masses of plastic pellets were found along the western coast of Denmark in September.
The Danish Environment Protection Agency has now confirmed tests carried out on the microplastics suggest they originated from the River Tyne spill in July.
It said the nurdles had the same characteristics as the one billion which had been spilled in north-east England and their arrival in Denmark in late September and early October - about 390 miles (630km) away - was consistent with "current patterns and circulation in the North Sea".
Signe Simonsen, the head of startup Race for Oceans Technology, first spotted the nurdles on the island of MandÃ¸ in Denmark on 26 September.
"There were just so many milk white plastic pellets," she said. "So many that I've never seen before in this area."
Simonsen said the discovery of the nurdles had made her "really sad" considering the "pristine" nature of the Wadden Sea.
Simonsen then said she drove along the coast of several nearby islands which are roughly on the same latitude as Newcastle.
She said there were nurdles "all over" where the tide had washed up.
Simonsen said she had collected nurdles from 10 different spots along the Danish coast and Sylt in Germany.
Simonsen, whose firm aims to detect microplastic pollution from drone images, then passed on some of her samples to the Danish Environment Protection Agency.
The agency, which tested the pellets alongside Aarhus University, said another factor which suggested the Danish nurdles were the same as those spilled in the River Tyne was the fact there were no other recorded spills in the area that could explain their presence.
Nurdles from the spill have washed up along the coast of north-east England including Teesside and Durham.
As of September, about 28% of the nurdles are believed to have been recovered.

The News
South Africa has proposed a new fiscal law in an attempt to shield its public finances from future populist governments as the treasuryâs current projections show debt is set to decline for the first time in nearly two decades. Finance Minister Enoch Godongwana framed it as protecting âhard-won gainsâ at a time when his party, the African National Congress, dominant since Nelson Mandela led it to victory in 1994, can no longer assume it will remain in charge after it was forced into building a coalition following the 2024 election.
Under the draft measure released alongside Wednesdayâs budget update, future governments could set their own targets such as debt-to-GDP ratio â a key measure watched by rating agencies â but an independent parliamentary oversight body would check if they were being adhered to. If it was decided that the government had deviated elected officials would have to explain their reasoning. Unlike laws in many other countries, South Africaâs prospective fiscal rules have no prescribed numerical ceiling on debt or spending; rather they would enshrine the principle that governments should keep to their announced plans.
In his statement to parliament, Godongwana said that government debt stabilized at around $366 billion, or 78% of GDP, after rising from around 24% in 2009. He told lawmakers that the budget deficit would start to decline as a proportion of GDP over the next three years. He also announced a last-minute decision to offer a second fuel-price relief package costing $600 million â further help for struggling motorists.
Economists say the numbers are good enough to warrant a credit rating upgrade. Gina Schoeman of Citi says the US bank sees a shift as âprobableâ but more likely to come in the first six months of next year rather than in the next few weeks.
Know More
South Africa first floated the idea of this fiscal anchor in March 2025, when the treasury published a discussion paper that presented two options: The establishment of a numerical target, which is more conventional, or an approach that weds governments to their own announced goals.
Godongwanaâs approach puts him at odds with the IMF, which argued earlier this year that a âfiscal rule, anchored in a prudent debt ceilingâ would bolster South Africaâs credibility. But while the idea is becoming more popular in Africa, there is no guarantee that setting a specific target works. Both Ghana and Kenya have missed fiscal targets with the former hit by pre-election slippages in 2024, and the latter suffering under revenue shortfalls, punishing interest payments, and repeated budget overruns.
Tiisetsoâs view
The treasuryâs effort to lock in the progress in reining in spending rests on an optimistic premise that letting politicians explain themselves will keep them in line. The flaw in the proposed anchor is that South Africaâs fiscal problems have never been short of explanations.
Since the 2009 financial crisis, Africaâs biggest economy went on a spending frenzy, running deficits, racking up debt and offering a rich menu of excuses â ranging from global crises, sluggish growth, state capture and COVID-19. That is not to say these explanations were not valid. But debt rose anyway, from 24% of GDP in 2009 to nearly 80% last year.
The draft law asks future governments to disclose, assess, and explain. Worse still, it requires each administrationâs fiscal plan to be âconsistent with the electoral mandate.â Thatâs disappointing. For one thing, imagine an election campaign fought on populist policies such as raising welfare grants and public sector hiring sprees. An incoming government would simply write those ambitions into its fiscal plan in keeping with the proposed measure. A cascade of ratings downgrades will follow, bond market investors would demand higher risk premiums and the economy would take a hit after spending commitments were already made.
Granted, governments bend or break hard numerical laws when politics demand it, as is the case in Ghana and Kenya. In fact, a 90-country study by the Bureau for Economic Research, a South African think tank, shows half of the countries broke their own debt-ceiling rules. If politicians can toss out hard and visible targets, why would anyone expect them to feel constrained by a law that only asks them to explain?
Room for Disagreement
Godongwana argued that the disadvantage with setting specific targets is that they lack flexibility and require well-defined escape clauses if economic circumstances change and his proposal takes that into account.
âMost importantly, it helps to ensure that developmental priorities and constitutional obligations are pursued at a pace that public finances can sustain,â he told lawmakers.
Michael Grobler, fixed-income strategist at Ashburton Investments, echoed this sentiment, writing in Business Day that âits appeal is flexibility. Shocks are inevitable, and a rigid annual target can force damaging cuts in a downturn or encourage decisions designed only to hit a number.â

Malawi's opposition has demanded an explanation for President Peter Mutharika's prolonged stay in South Africa, as the country struggles with fuel shortages, power cuts and economic difficulties.
The 86-year-old Mutharika left Malawi on 6 October, for what officials described as a private visit. This is his fifth visit this year, with limited information made public on each of these trips.
"Malawi is at a critical moment, and there is a need for decisive action," the opposition Malawi Congress Party (MCP) said.
Information Minister Shadric Namalomba has denied that Mutharika's absence had created a leadership vacuum.
Mutharika returned to power in October last year after defeating then-president Lazarus Chakwera.
He previously governed Malawi between 2014 and 2020.
His latest absence comes amid growing public scrutiny of his frequent visits to South Africa.
On Thursday, MCP campaign director Moses Kunkuyu told journalists in the capital, Lilongwe, that the opposition was not questioning the president's right to travel for personal reasons but wanted Vice-President Jane Ansah to address the nation over the country's mounting challenges.
He said that Malawians deserved to know who was managing the country's affairs.
"The issue is not that the president has traveled," he said. "The issue is that people are suffering and want reassurance that somebody is in charge."
He called on the government to explain how it intended to address persistent fuel shortages, frequent electricity blackouts, shortage of essential medicines in public hospitals and difficulties accessing foreign currency.
The information minister responded by telling local media that "a state president is always in charge at any time, anywhere," insisting that the president remained firmly in control of government affairs.
Asked about the purpose of the visit, the minister said: "A private trip is private."
He accused the opposition of attempting to exploit problems he said had developed under its previous administration.
"That is why Malawians voted us into government, not them. May I request them to seal their mouths as we address the problems they miserably created and failed to solve," he added.
On Thursday, Mutharika delegated the trade minister to lead Malawi's delegation to the Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa (Comesa) summit in Zimbabwe.
Earlier this month, officials dismissed reports on social media that Mutharika had travelled from South Africa to India for medical treatment.
Chief Secretary to the Government Justin Saidi said the president remained in South Africa and urged the public not to spread unverified information.
Mutharika has previously dismissed speculation about his health, describing such claims as "silly and laughable" and insisting that he was well.
Malawi faces a severe shortage of foreign currency, which has disrupted fuel imports and contributed to rising transport costs.
Long queues have formed at petrol stations, while unreliable electricity supplies and shortages of medicines have added to public frustration.

A Â£2m fund has been launched to help businesses switch their vehicles to greener vehicles, Bradford Council has announced.
Reform UK council leader Stephen Place said it would help businesses counter the rising cost of petrol and diesel as well as modernise their fleets.
The funding is part of Bradford Council's Clean Air programme, which will allow businesses to apply for up to Â£16,000 in support.
Announcing the fund at the Scale Up Bradford event on Tuesday, Place said it would help businesses invest in cleaner, more efficient technology to "future proof their operations for years to come".
Earlier this month, Place said he was committed to scrapping Clean Air Zone (CAZ) charges as it had a negative impact on businesses.
He accepted the move would have "quite a lot of legalities surrounding it" but said the council would "work to run it out naturally".
Funded by the Labour government, the Zero Emission Grant Programme will be targeted at small businesses, charities and organisations, according to the Local Democracy Reporting Service.
Businesses will be able to apply for up to Â£16,000 to improve heavy-duty vehicles and Â£4,500 for light-duty vehicles.
Bradford Council said the fund would provide practical support to help businesses remain competitive while adapting to new vehicle technologies.
"We want to help organisations to upgrade their fleets and position themselves for future success," said Place.
"I hope that this will appeal to tradies, they are the people out there every day keeping the nation moving."
Petrol and diesel prices have risen significantly since the US-Israel war with Iran.
Currently the average price of petrol in the UK is 173.2p per litre, while diesel costs 199.9p per litre.
Mark Casci, of West Yorkshire Chamber of Commerce, welcomed the plans and said a lot of businesses were looking to "decarbonise" their vehicles.
"Every large business with a fleet is looking at this issue very carefully, it is very much on their agenda," said Casci.
"It is the right thing to do and what customers want. It is driven by customer demand as well as moral responsibility."

Police in Cyprus have opened an investigation into the financial affairs of Roman Abramovich, following revelations by BBC Panorama that accountancy firm Deloitte helped in falsifying documents to hide his wealth and evade tax.
Serious questions about the integrity of some of Abramovich's professional advisers were raised earlier this month in a joint report from the BBC and the Bureau of Investigative Journalism (TBIJ).
A Cypriot Ministry of Justice official told MPs this week that the report's findings would be looked at as part of a new investigation by the police's Financial Intelligence Unit.
Lawyers for Abramovich have said that he denies evading tax or concealing his fortune. Deloitte Cyprus said it acts "in compliance with applicable laws".
The police investigation was announced at a parliamentary committee meeting in the Cypriot capital, Nicosia, held to discuss the combating and prevention of money laundering.
The Ministry of Justice official told MPs the police would try to determine whether any criminal acts had been committed.
Last week, the report from the BBC and TBIJ detailed how accounts signed off by Deloitte in Cyprus in 2006 meant assets such as superyachts, mansions and private jets worth $672m (Â£508m) vanished from Abramovich's company accounts.
Deloitte, which is the world's largest accountancy firm, also appears to have advised on a scheme to evade a huge tax bill on the oligarch's wealth, through the falsification of documents.
The evidence was contained in leaked files, including thousands of documents about Abramovich's finances and the operations of a network of offshore companies, administered from Cyprus between 1995 and 2022.
The BBC and media partners including TBIJ, the Guardian, Paper Trail Media, the Organised Crime and Corruption Reporting Project, and Cyprus Investigative Reporting Network, have been reporting on the leaked files since 2023 as part of the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists' Cyprus Confidential, external investigation.
A representative from the Cypriot police, Andreas Anastasiades, confirmed to MPs that its Financial Crime Unit had already begun to gather evidence, and said the investigation was expected to last several months.
When asked by the BBC if the investigation would look into Deloitte's work, Andreas Anastasiades said: "We will look at any company or person who may be involved."
He added: "We will see if there has been fraud or if some documents have been manipulated."
Lawyers for Abramovich say that Panorama has provided no evidence that the billionaire knew about, authorised or directed the falsification of any document. They also say it was legitimate for his companies to rely on advice from professionals.
Deloitte Cyprus says it is unable to comment because the documents are more than 20 years old and no longer accessible.
The BBC and TBIJ have previously reported on a tax scheme that allowed Abramovich to dodge millions in tax on the running costs of his yachts.
Following that report, two former company directors have been indicted and are due to stand trial in Cyprus next month over â¬25m in unpaid VAT.
Mr Abramovich's lawyers previously told the BBC that he had "always obtained independent expert professional tax and legal advice" and "acted in accordance" with it.

The western Indian port town of Jamnagar is not a usual stop for foreign leaders, yet it featured prominently in US Secretary of State Marco Rubio's recent visit.
So, why did Rubio visit the town? And, more importantly, why did he skip the Indian capital, Delhi?
The answer to both questions may have less to do with India and more to do with Donald Trump administration's domestic compulsions â or, more precisely, its domestic oil needs.
Rubio arrived in the financial capital Mumbai on Tuesday, where he met Indian Foreign Minister S Jaishankar and some of the country's top business leaders. He officially ended his trip in Jamnagar - in the western state of Gujarat - home to the giant oil refinery owned by one of Asia's richest men, Mukesh Ambani.
It was his second trip to the country this year and experts say what is significant this time is the timing of the visit as well as his choice of destinations.
The Trump administration is under pressure to keep fuel prices in check ahead of November's US midterm elections, while rising tensions in the Middle East threaten global energy supplies.
With little new refining capacity expected in the immediate future in the US, India's ability to process large volumes of crude oil offers Washington a potential way to ease pressure on the fuel markets.
And that puts Reliance's Jamnagar refinery at the centre of the equation.
The visit, however, comes at a tricky moment in India-US relations. Trump has imposed tariffs on Indian goods, there are sanctions against Delhi for buying Russian energy (though currently paused) and there is a trade deal between the two countries that has remained elusive for around 20 months now.
Announcing the visit, the US State Department had earlier said that it would focus on energy cooperation, commercial investment and economic ties.
The official itinerary also did not include Delhi, which raised some questions, especially from Indian opposition politicians. But analysts say the choice was strategic.
"Delhi is where the trust gap is largest. Officials there are unhappy with a number of decisions and policies from Trump's administration," Michael Kugelman, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council, told the BBC.
But former Indian ambassador to the US, Meera Shankar, cautions against reading too much into him skipping the capital.
"This was primarily an energy-focused visit," she says. "And after all, Rubio did meet the foreign minister in Mumbai."
The meeting between the two foreign ministers at the Taj Hotel covered trade, investment, energy security and defence cooperation, according to official statements. India's foreign ministry also said both sides welcomed progress in trade negotiations and reaffirmed their commitment to concluding a deal, which has long been in the works.
But once the diplomatic meetings were over, Rubio headed to Jamnagar, where the crown jewel of the Ambani business empire is located. This came to define the trip.
Shankar says the refinery visit "showed how much importance the US is attaching to getting more refined fuel into the market before the November midterms".
Reliance's Jamnagar complex can process about 1.4 million barrels of crude oil a day, roughly 1.5% of global refining capacity, according to the company website.
It is also a major exporter of diesel and other petroleum products, giving it a crucial role in global fuel markets.
During a tightly controlled visit on Wednesday, with limited media access, Rubio toured the facility and met members of the Ambani family, including Mukesh Ambani.
The company later released a statement, saying, "the visit included wide-ranging discussions on the global energy landscape and opportunities for commercial partnerships across conventional and new energy". It, however, did not specifically address any commitments to buy crude oil or supply refined products.
Just a day earlier, while speaking to the press, Rubio had called India a "refining superpower" and said the US wanted Reliance to process more Venezuelan oil.
"They have the capability to refine heavy crude. They've done so in the past, and I think as more and more Venezuelan oil comes online, that's something they could do," he told reporters.
Rubio added that oil from Venezuela "can certainly provide relief" in the short term and can possibly help ease supply pressures amid tensions in the Middle East.
Reliance was once among the largest buyers of Venezuelan crude before US sanctions disrupted trade. After Venezuelan President NicolÃ¡s Maduro was captured in a US intervention earlier this year and Washington eased sanctions on the country's energy sector, Reliance re-emerged as a major importer.
Experts also say the visit might ease some tensions in the Delhi-Washington relationship over India's purchase of Russian oil.
India became one of the biggest buyers of Russian oil since Moscow invaded Ukraine in 2022.
Between December 2022 and July 2026, it accounted for 37% of Russia's crude oil exports, according to the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA).
And Reliance was among the Indian companies that processed Russian crude.
In August 2025, US President Donald Trump imposed an additional 25% tariff on Indian goods over its Russian oil purchases, taking total tariffs on many Indian goods to 50%. The US, however, withdrew the additional penalty in February 2026 but India's import of Russian oil has continued to be an irritant in Washington-Delhi ties.
India has always said that securing affordable and reliable energy for its 1.4 billion people was its priority.
Then earlier this month, the US itself temporarily lifted sanctions on Russian diesel.
In that context, experts say Rubio's Jamnagar visit is aligned to three goals that the US appears to be pursuing: reducing India's dependence on Russian crude, encouraging greater imports of Venezuelan and American oil, and advancing a trade deal in which energy cooperation could become a key area of agreement.
