Experts are testing out a new method that could see a way to tackle blue-green algae blooms.
The toxic algae is actually cyanobacteria rather than a true algae and can increase dramatically in heat, making people and animals sick when ingested.
Dr Sanjay Nagarajan, from the Institute for Sustainability and Climate Change at the University of Bath, took his child to the Warminster Pleasure Grounds in Wiltshire when he saw the lake there closed because of the bloom.
He and colleagues have since created a machine to help eliminate it from the water which he hopes he can make bigger and loan to councils.
More from Wiltshire
From January to October this year alone there have been more than 168,000 visits to the park in Warminster.
People would usually be able to take boats out onto the lake and an active model boat club is in the area.
However, while it tends to die off in wintry weather, the algae has been causing problems over summers and this year it has been closed to activities for several months, with warning signs up round it.
"Every year it gets worse and worse with climate change," said Kevin Whitehorn, the estates manager for Warminster Town Council.
"Water levels in the lake have gone down which meant the blue-green algae has grown even more than it has done in the previous years," he added.
Nagarajan, a chemical engineer, visited the park with his child and emailed the council saying he wanted to test something.
His colleague, Dr Madhubalaji Chegu Krishnamurthi, has been studying algae for a decade and said "there many good algae as well as bad algae".
"Whenever the bad algae grows more, because of the nutrients in the lakes, it will release the various toxins that are very harmful for humans."
Nagarajan, with colleagues and a PhD student, have put together a machine with a reactor that uses bubbles to get rid of the algae. The type of reactor is not new, but its use like this is.
As with many new inventions, in order to get the water in and out of the reactor, they have had to improvise. This devices uses a generator and equipment usually used for home beer brewing.
A small box at the side does a lot of the work - Nagarajan explained that it is the reactor.
"If you take a small drinks can, fill it up with some water, heat it up and then invert it into an ice bath, it gets crushed. That's exactly what happens inside the reactor and we call it cavitation.
"Whenever we are able to manipulate the conditions to produce these cavitation bubbles, these bubbles will actually be crushed or imploding.
"Once the implosion happens those effects will help in destroying the bloom."
Nagarajan said they have had positive results: "We've seen up to 20% degradation in terms of toxins and we've also seen a lot of the algal cells being destroyed because of the effect of cavitation."
The next stage is to get their results published and apply for funding to create a bigger machine they can loan out to councils.

1e54b71e448f.text: By — Hannah Schoenbaum, Associated Press Hannah Schoenbaum, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/trump-administration-stopped-sharing-evidence-in-good-and-pretti-killings-minnesota-officials-say Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Trump administration stopped sharing evidence in Good and Pretti killings, Minnesota officials say Nation Oct 23, 2026 2:56 PM EDT The federal government has stopped sharing evidence with Minnesota authorities who are investigating the killings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti by federal officers, state officials said in recent court filings. The Trump administration has suggested that state prosecutors don't have jurisdiction to investigate federal officers, while Minnesota officials have said they don't trust the federal government to investigate itself. READ MORE: Renee Good's family sues U.S. government and immigration officials over her killing The state is still seeking the cell phones of the officers involved in both shootings and recordings of key interviews. State prosecutors announced in July that the federal government had begun turning over evidence in the cases, including police body camera video and hard drives containing statements. Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty said at the time that the state expected to receive "all the evidence." But Minnesota investigators said in October court filings that the transfer of evidence stopped soon after the July announcement. Moriarty said the U.S. Attorney's Office for Minnesota told her on Sept. 10 that evidence sharing would be on pause indefinitely "in light of challenges with D.C.," according to the documents. State prosecutors have again asked a judge to order federal agencies to hand over the evidence, arguing they "have identified no legal authority or rational basis justifying their obstruction of state criminal investigations." In a reply filed Tuesday, attorneys for the Justice Department argued it's within their discretion to decline to share information with state authorities. They cited the department's rules for responding to record requests, known as the Touhy regulations, which apply only when formal legal proceedings are underway. The attorneys said there was no active court case when Minnesota made its requests. READ MORE: Minnesota prosecutors obtain long withheld evidence in probe into fatal shootings of Good, Pretti Drew Evans, superintendent of the Minnesota Bureau of Criminal Apprehension, said in a legal declaration that federal authorities still have Good's clothing, the cell phone of the officer who killed her and interview recordings that state authorities have never been able to view. An Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer fatally shot Good, a 37-year-old mother of three, while she was leaving a Minneapolis protest on Jan. 7. Bystander video shows Good in the driver's seat of an SUV, repeatedly honking the horn, when masked immigration officers order her to step out of the vehicle. She starts to pull forward, and an officer standing in front of the car fires at her windshield. The officer, now standing about an arm's length from the open window on the driver's side, fires twice more, according to an analysis of the videos by The Associated Press and others. Federal officials at the time said the officer acted in self-defense. Good's death and that of Pretti, a 37-year-old intensive care nurse who was killed weeks later by a federal officer in Minneapolis, ignited nationwide protests against the Republican president's immigration enforcement efforts. No criminal charges have been filed in connection with the fatal shootings. Evans said the federal government also has not shared a recorded statement from an officer who shot Pretti, the firearms used by the officers, their phones, projectiles and casings, and a gun taken from Pretti before he was shot. The Trump administration wants to block the certification of the Senate election in Alaska if Republican Senator Dan Sullivan loses, arguing that another candidate with the same name may confuse voters.
In a federal lawsuit filed on Thursday, the justice department said the inclusion of another Dan Sullivan on the ballot could lead some to mistakenly cast their votes for the wrong candidate.
Polls suggest the race between Sen Sullivan and Democrat Mary Peltola is tight, with Peltola holding a narrow lead in the final days before the 3 November vote.
The government wants the judge to bar the state from certifying the results if Sen Sullivan loses by a margin less than the other Sullivan.
"I'm the one that said do it," President Donald Trump told reporters when asked for his thoughts on the lawsuit after he landed in Florida for a campaign rally on Friday.
Trump has referred to the second Sullivan's candidacy as a "scam" and said his administration was looking at "powerful legal options" to end it.
Previous efforts to remove that Sullivan, a retired teacher, from the ballot have been rejected by the Alaska Supreme Court.
For the 3 November midterm election, the senator will be listed on the ballot as the Republican incumbent.
Alaska's ranked-choice voting system means that voters could select both Sullivans if they are unsure at the ballot box.
In court documents, the justice department said Alaska "will fail in its obligation to protect the integrity of its elections" if it includes "any electoral results tainted by the inclusion on the ballot of Daniel J Sullivan".
The second Sullivan, who was also a US Forest Service worker, was reportedly once a member of the Alaska Independence Party before registering as a Republican earlier this year.
In the filing, Associate Attorney General Stanley E Woodward Jr asserted that the sole purpose of his candidacy was to benefit Peltola's campaign by reducing the number of votes for the senator.
"Given the substantial likelihood that the inclusion of Dan J. Sullivan will confuse or mislead voters looking to cast a vote for Senator Sullivan and thus distort the will of Alaskan voters, there is a substantial likelihood that a certification of the election will reflect an electoral process that lacked integrity," Woodward argued.
Dan J Sullivan has repeatedly denied those claims, telling the local Petersburg Pilot newspaper earlier this year that he "wouldn't even know who to speak to" in Peltola's campaign.
In a separate interview with Courthouse News, he said that it is his "sincere hope that people know who and what they are voting for but ultimately, choice is good and voters' intent will be as varied as the candidates who are running".
In the event Peltola wins, and the margin of loss suggests possible confusion, the lawsuit calls for certification to be delayed pending an investigation into whether voters were mixed up on the names as well as any "necessary and appropriate" steps to determine what would have happened had the second Sullivan been kept off the ballot.
Neither candidate has so far commented on the lawsuit.
The Senate race in Alaska - which President Trump won by 14 percentage points in 2024 - is among the most closely watched in the upcoming midterm elections.
The president's approval ratings in the state have been badly hit by voter disapproval of rising prices and the war in Iran.

More than 15,000 homes are without power as Storm Austen continues to batter southern England and Wales, with more bad weather expected this weekend.
The first named storm of the season brought gusts of up to 84mph (135km/h) to Jersey, while in southern England the wild weather disrupted travel with fallen trees blocking railway lines and roads.
In Brighton, part of the iconic West Pier - an abandoned structure that first opened in 1866 - collapsed into the sea.
On Saturday, Storm Boelo is forecast to bring more strong winds and heavy rain. The Met Office has put in place an amber warning for wind on Saturday and Sunday to cover parts of Scotland, northern England and Northern Ireland.
Austen made landfall in the south-west overnight and tracked eastwards throughout the day. All schools on Jersey and Guernsey closed for the day and some in Cornwall were closed or started later than normal.
Ahead of the worst of the storm on Thursday afternoon, families were evacuated from a holiday park in Perranporth, Cornwall. Among them was Hannah Dawson-Turk, who told the BBC "the night before last, it sounded like our caravan was going to be ripped apart".
"The storm is very loud outside now, and the waves look huge from our windows," she said from a nearby hotel.
The National Grid said engineers had restored power to more than 60,000 properties since Storm Austen began.
Some ferry services between the UK and France were cancelled, while National Rail advised many routes were travelling at slower speeds.
In Brighton, onlookers filmed as a section of the West Pier fell into the sea as it was pummeled by large waves.
Stephen Royle, who lives opposite, said the waves rolling in were "enormous" and he is "shocked" by how much of the pier ended up in the sea.
The pier closed to the public in 1975 and fell into disrepair, but the ruined structure became a symbol of Brighton for some.
On the Channel Islands, fresh food shortages are expected in the coming days due to a lack of ferry services, according to the boss of the Co-op there.
"It's rare we get this level of disruption to storms backing up so quickly and probably a little bit more heavier than what we've had to deal with in the past," Mark Cox said.
Paul Aked, head of Jersey Met, said there were gusts in Guernsey up to 76mph (122km/h), equivalent to a severe gale, force nine. Residents told BBC Radio Guernsey that they could hear the wind rattling through their homes.
Jersey Airport said flights won't be running "until at least 17:00" while Cornwall Airport Newquay is warning passengers to check with their airline before travel.
Departure boards at Exeter airport were showing multiple cancellations.
Train operators across the country have warned that services are likely to be disrupted over the weekend.
The UK will continue to be battered by strong winds and heavy rain over the weekend as Storm Boelo follows on the heels of Storm Austen.
The Met Office has issued an amber weather warning for wind for much of Scotland, excluding the Northern Isles, as well as the far north of Northern Ireland and England.
Wind gusts of 60-70mph are forecast, with exposed coastal areas potentially seeing speeds of up to 80mph.
The Central Lowlands could also experience disruption as strong winds funnel through the region.
Damage caused by strong winds could lead to further power cuts, while travel disruption is also predicted.
Yellow wind warnings also cover Orkney, the rest of Northern Ireland and northern England.
Gusts of 55-75mph are possible in these areas, with isolated gusts potentially reaching 80mph.
Alongside the strong winds, heavy and persistent rain is forecast across the UK on Saturday.
Spray and surface water could make driving conditions hazardous, while further downpours increase the risk of localised flooding.
The Met Office has advised the public to drive cautiously in strong wind, and to secure loose items outside their homes such as bins and trampolines.
People living or working in coastal areas were advised to take extra care during windy or stormy weather, including staying indoors as much as possible.
The storm came as the government released general advice for households to stock up on tinned food and bottled water in order to be prepared for emergencies.
The government has drawn up recommendations for households to have three days' worth of bottled water and tinned food to deal with a crisis such as a war, an online attack or a natural disaster.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said: "It's not about panic buying... It's about just taking sensible measures to have enough in the house to tide you over should there be a difficult situation."
Last month, the National Audit Office warned Britain's food supply chain is at risk given the growing threat of cyber-attacks and the climate crisis.
It said the Department for Food, the Environment and Rural Affairs had not done enough in recent years to improve supply chain resilience.
Additional reporting by Joshua Askew and James Kelly

Mississippi authorities have released body camera footage showing how a toddler was fatally shot by a police officer responding to a report of shoplifting in a Walmart car park.
Kohen Wiley, aged one, was on his mother's lap in a moving car when officers surrounded the vehicle in the city of Senatobia on 14 June.
The state's attorney general found the policeman was justified in using force, and the officer's lawyer argued in a statement to the BBC that the driver was attempting to kill law enforcement.
The child's family disputes that the shooting was justified. Their lawyer, Ben Crump, has called the police response "excessive from the very start".
Crump said an allegation of shoplifting "does not warrant the death" of a child.
Kohen Wiley was riding in the vehicle with his mother, Vellesiya Wiley, and another woman at the time of the incident.
Senatobia Mayor Greg Graves confirmed to the BBC's US partner CBS that Hunter Foster, the officer who opened fire, had resigned.
The Senatobia Police Department did not immediately respond to the BBC's requests for confirmation.
The footage released by Mississippi authorities on Thursday shows a first-person perspective of the officer who opened fire.
After being told by a staff member that suspected shoplifters were getting away, five law enforcement officers run towards the car with guns drawn.
The vehicle reverses, crashing into a parked car, before pulling forwards.
The officer wearing the body camera raises his gun and aims it at the moving vehicle as he runs closer, shouting: "Stop!"
As the car closely passes the officer, he fires his gun, shattering the passenger-side window.
Four gunshots can be heard, as police command the driver to stop. The car continues to drive off slowly through the car park.
CCTV video from the storefront appears to show that at the moment the policeman opens fire, another officer is standing near the front of the moving vehicle.
"The driver of the vehicle was attempting to kill those 5 officers," Martin Zummach, an attorney representing the officer, said in a statement to the BBC, adding that his client "had no choice but to discharge his weapon".
"We are very sad for the loss of life," Zummach said. "But the outcome of the investigation was not only expected, but it was overdue."
The child's mother, Wiley, has denied she and her friend stole nappies from the store. No charges have been filed against them.
The boy's death has sparked protests and vigils in Mississippi.
At a news conference, relatives demanded accountability.
"After what I've seen today, I'm having a difficult time understanding the word, 'justified,' said LaSandra Williams, Kohen Wiley's grandmother.

7167973faba2.text: The Trump administration sued Alaska on Thursday to delay certification of election results if incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan loses. Why it matters: The race between incumbent Sullivan, Democrat Mary Peltola , and retired teacher Dan Sullivan has been marked by controversy, with Republicans accusing Democrats of trying to confuse voters by planting a candidate with the same name. Alaska's use of ranked-choice voting, which eliminates candidates in rounds if no one gets 50% of the initial vote, complicates matters. "An election result may be impacted by voter confusion if: (1) Senator Sullivan does not win the election; and (2) had all votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan been cast instead for Senator Sullivan and Alaska's rank-choice process played out accordingly, Senator Sullivan would have won the election," the lawsuit , filed in Alaska District Court, states. Zoom in: Because of a previous Alaska Supreme Court decision and Sullivan's name already being on the ballot, the administration contended in the lawsuit that the only means to ensure that the winner of the race is voters' choice "is to ensure that the certification is not impacted" by his candidacy. The lawsuit requests a delay in certification until after an investigation determines "whether votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan were meant to be cast for Senator Sullivan." What they're saying: "Alaska's Division of Elections determined that Mr. Daniel J. Sullivan's candidacy was intended to mislead voters and compromise the fairness of the ballot," a DOJ spokesperson said in a statement. "Therefore, the Justice Department, consistent with the National Voter Registration Act enacted by Congress, is taking the necessary steps to ensure that this frivolous candidacy does not undermine the integrity of Alaska's election or the will of its voters." The White House referred Axios to the DOJ. Catch up quick: The retired teacher Sullivan will appear on the ballot as Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. after the state's Supreme Court ordered the state's Division of Elections to include him in the race in June. Senator Sullivan will appear as "Sullivan, Dan S. (Registered Republican) Incumbent," per the state's sample ballots. Sullivan has argued his candidacy is not a sham, and Peltola's campaign has denied any involvement with his run. The intrigue: The race is among those being closely watched as Democrats appear to be making inroads in red territory . The administration acknowledged the tight race in its lawsuit, saying "there is a realistic chance" that the non-incumbent Sullivan's presence on the ballot could tip the scales for Peltola. Flashback: In the primary, Senator Sullivan collected around 41% of the vote, versus Sullivan's 2.5%. Peltola earned 49.5% Cook Political Report currently rates the race as a toss-up. Reality check: Notre Dame law professor Derek Muller tells AP that the Alaska suit won't survive long, since the statute "simply doesn't let the Department of Justice enjoin certification." Go deeper: Scoop: NRSC pleads for $9M to defend three red seats Editor's note: This story has been updated with a statement from the Department of Justice.

By 2075, the vast majority of the world’s shallow coral reefs could cease to function as both critical habitat for marine life and a lifeline for hundreds of millions of people who rely on them.
According to a new assessment by the International Union for Conservation of Nature, 96 percent of the planet’s 127 major warm-water reefs are now classified as critically endangered, primarily due to heat stress induced by climate change. These ecosystems—which people depend on for food, livelihoods and protection from storms and flooding—include the Great Barrier Reef in Australia, the Mesoamerican Barrier Reef System in the Caribbean and the Coral Triangle in the western Pacific Ocean.
“They are at extremely high risk of collapse in the next 50 years,” said Mishal Gudka, the
For coral reefs, collapse means losing most, if not all, of their living hard corals that build and maintain their defining three-dimensional structure. As vibrant coral communities disappear, so do the fish and other marine life that live amidst them. Eventually, the reef becomes rubble covered in algae. “It’s effectively degraded into a different type of ecosystem,” Gudka said.
This is the first time the International Union for Conservation of Nature has produced a global assessment of coral reefs as part of its Red List of Ecosystems initiative, designed to guide and encourage conservation efforts before irreparable loss occurs. And its findings are “alarming,” said Susanne Pedersen, the International Union for Conservation of Nature’s director of the Centre for Science and Knowledge.
“It must serve as a renewed call to action on climate change and other drivers of biodiversity loss to save the world’s coral reef ecosystems,” she said during a news conference Thursday at the United Nations biodiversity summit known as COP17.
The two-week conference is being held in Yerevan, Armenia, where representatives from nearly 200 countries are taking stock of their progress toward achieving a set of 23 targets outlined in the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework. The landmark international agreement, adopted in 2022, is aimed at halting and reversing biodiversity loss through commitments such as conserving 30 percent of the world’s land, inland waters and marine areas by 2030, restoring degraded ecosystems and reducing pollution.
But several recent reports indicate countries are falling behind on their commitments, especially when it comes to conserving marine ecosystems. More than 90 percent of ecosystem restoration efforts are occurring on land in comparison to just 2 percent in coastal and marine areas, according to a joint report, released Friday, by the Society for Ecological Restoration and the Secretariat of the Convention on Biological Diversity.
Changing the trajectory for coral reefs outlined in the latest Red List assessment is vital. At least a quarter of all marine species, including thousands of species of fish, live and feed on coral reefs.
“The actions we take over the next few years will determine what these ecosystems look like at the end of the century, whether they persist as we have known them, or whether they transform into a different ecosystem, which is worth less to both nature and people,” Gudka said at the press conference in Yerevan.
As global temperatures rise, the intervals between marine heat waves are shrinking, leaving reefs less time to recover in between. Even under a moderate warming scenario, the new global Red List assessment for coral ecosystems projects that within the next 50 years, these events will occur too frequently for most reefs to withstand.
When corals become too hot, they expel the algae living within their tissue that provides them with much of their food and color. The invertebrates then turn white in a process called bleaching. If water temperatures cool down fast enough, corals can recover. But if not, they eventually die. Already, that trend is accelerating and taking a toll.
From January 2023 to September 2025, during the world’s fourth global bleaching event, more than 80 percent of the world’s coral reefs in at least 83 countries and territories were impacted.
In Florida, a record-breaking marine heat wave in 2023 wiped out most colonies of two important reef-building species: staghorn and elkhorn corals. Both have since been deemed functionally extinct there, meaning there are too few left in the wild to reproduce naturally and they can no longer help build or sustain reef ecosystems.
In many places, including the Caribbean, climate change and other local pressures exacerbate one another.
“Rising sea temperatures are adding to the damage caused by overfishing, pollution and poorly planned coastal development, making it harder for reefs to recover after each disturbance,” said Tadzio Bervoets, from Sint Maarten, who was not involved in the assessment. He is a Caribbean coral researcher for the Coral Restoration Consortium and the executive director of a marine conservation organization in Jamaica, the Alligator Head Foundation.

Overfishing—which threatens at least 63 percent of coral reef ecosystems, according to the Red List assessment—also undermines their ability to recover from heat stress. Without herbivorous species like parrot fish that graze on the reef, aggressive algae can smother weakened or recovering corals and take over space on the reef needed for new coral growth.

Viruses may be minuscule, but one could have influenced major differences between human and chimpanzee brains.
Millions of years ago, a virus left DNA behind in an African ape’s genome, and the genetic material stuck around in modern day chimps. Those ghosts of infections past appear to influence genes involved in neuron development, which may help explain how human and chimp brains ended up so different, researchers report October 23 in Science Advances.
Compared with the brains of their chimpanzee kin, human brains are three times larger and more cognitively powerful. Yet “most of their protein-making genes are very similar,” says Johan Jakobsson, a neuroscientist at Lund University in Sweden. In the absence of large differences in the genetic code, Jakobsson and his colleagues decided to look at the parts of the human and chimp genome that control when and where genes are turned on or off.
Changes in gene regulation can come from viruses. Some viruses called retroviruses insert their own DNA into their hosts’ genomes to command host cells to build more viruses. But those parasitic bits of DNA can linger long after an infection. If this happens in reproductive cells, the viral DNA gets passed down with the host’s DNA.
These leftover bits, called endogenous retroviruses, no longer code for the production of infectious viruses, but they can have a big impact on the host’s biology — especially if they make copies of themselves across the genome. And they have. Such viral remnants make up at least 8 percent of the genomes of humans and chimps alike. More generally, these DNA leftovers have been linked with some major evolutionary events, such as the evolution of the mammalian placenta.
Jakobsson and his colleagues focused on a particular viral vestige in chimps. The holdover came from an infection in an ancestral African ape somewhere between 5 million and 7 million years ago. In chimpanzees, the viral DNA had stuck itself into the genome at 158 different locations. However, it is curiously absent in humans. It’s still unknown why.
The researchers wanted to know how that exact pathogen footprint might affect chimpanzees’ brains compared with those of humans. Working with chimpanzee stem cells, they removed the viral DNA using CRISPR, a gene editing technology that allows for precise, targeted cuts in DNA. Once the viral DNA was gone, a nearby gene called LINC00662 — normally silenced in chimpanzees — turned on, making RNA the team could detect. This matches the normal condition in human brain cells, in which LINC00662 is active. The team also used CRISPR to shut off LINC00662 in the human cells, matching the silenced condition seen in chimpanzees.
When LINC00662 was active in chimp or human cells, the researchers noticed activity boosts to other genes that may be important to brain development — such as genes involved in the development and maturation of neurons and in making new neural connections. It’s not yet clear exactly how the viral DNA’s shutdown of this brain gene network affected the biology of chimpanzee brains. However, this genetic difference may have contributed to a divergence in how human and chimpanzee brains evolved, Jakobsson says. “Our findings show one way an ancient viral [DNA] insertion could create a lasting difference in how a gene is regulated in humans and chimpanzees,” Jakobsson says. Other genetic and environmental changes could be involved in the puzzle as well, he says.
Researchers have previously looked to single letter swaps in DNA to help explain how humans and chimp brains drifted apart in their evolution. But the new study highlights that creatures can rack up genome changes in other ways, says Giorgia Modenini, an evolutionary biologist at the University of Padua in Italy who was not involved with this research.
The researchers do a convincing job of showing that these particular viral leftovers influence developmental differences between human and chimp neurons, says Ravinder Kanda, an evolutionary geneticist at Oxford Brookes University in Oxford, England. “They’ve proved that absolutely. How far that goes, I don’t think we can quite say yet.”
It could be that other controls on genes’ activity are also involved or that this particular ancient lever-puller may represent just a sliver of the viral holdovers that have shaped brain development, Kanda says. “I think there are many, many more retroviruses to be discovered, and at the moment we’ve only touched the tip of the iceberg.”

Casino operators and sports betting companies have spent record amounts on campaign donations and on lobbying in Washington thus far this year, hoping it will help win back millions of bettors and gambling dollars that prediction markets have lured away.
Sportsbook operators, including FanDuel and DraftKings, have funneled more than $80 million into state senate and congressional races, via Win for America, a PAC launched in November 2025. The casino industryâs primary lobbying group, the American Gaming Association, has spent a record $2.06 million through September â the biggest lobbying spend by the group since 2013, when online gambling was reinstated after being banned in 2006.
Prediction markets and some of their executives have also been spending on local elections and on lobbying â primarily spending on the campaigns of politicians who oversee and shape their regulatory body, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission.
Kalshi executives, including co-founders Tarek Mansour and Luana Lopes Lara, have contributed more than $1.6 million directly to campaigns and to PACs supporting both political parties â nearly as much as the $1.79 million, including $1.28 million to outside firms, the company has spent on lobbying thus far this year. Polymarket has spent $270,000 via outside lobbying firms this year, and has made a $1 million donation to a Democratic nonprofit, according to a private remittance document seen by Reuters. And a new PAC, Coalition for Prediction Markets, backed by Kalshi, along with prediction market operators Robinhood, Coinbase, Crypto.com, and Underdog have spent an additional $200,000.
âKalshiâs political giving reflects our strong relationships with lawmakers on both sides of the aisle,â John Bivona, Kalshiâs head of federal government relations, said in a statement, adding that their giving reflects the companyâs belief that keeping prediction markets safe âisnât a partisan issue.â
Lobbying efforts are to âsupport the responsible development of federally regulated markets,â a Coalition for Prediction Markets spokesperson said. Polymarket declined to comment, and FanDuel, DraftKings, and Win for America didnât respond to requests for comment.

Prediction market companies are fighting against several state attorneys general, who argue that the sites operate as illegal online gambling operations and should be shut down, limited to non-sports betting or regulated on a state-by-state basis instead of by the federal agency.
Sports betting companies are hoping to retain their footholds in more than 30 states amid new scrutiny of the industry. Some recent studies have highlighted addiction problems, and some organizations have raised alarm bells that the rise in youth gambling is a public health crisis, which has motivated policymakers to propose legislation to regulate sports betting.
Four major sportsbooks â FanDuel, DraftKings, Bet365 and Fanatics â are also donating money to state races via Win for America â a super PAC that disperses money to the states via subsidiary partisan PACs, American Future and American Conservative Fund. Their aim is to fight tax hikes on gaming, and to expand the number of states that allow âiGamingâ products. Sportsbooks are also lobbying against legislation to regulate sports wagering on a federal level, such as the SAFE Bet Act, which would establish a minimum national standard for regulating mobile and sports gambling if it passed.
âItâs spooked a lot of legislators,â Brianne Doura-Schawohl, the director of Campaign for Fairer Gambling, told Semafor about state-level political giving efforts by sports betting companies. âTheyâre worried about their seats and their ability to continue to legislate, and if they pick a fight with [them], I believe so to speak, it could become an issue.â
The casino industryâs spending efforts are aimed at supporting or swaying policymakers to restrict prediction marketsâ operations, which they argue is eating into their businesses illegally.
There are âso-called âprediction marketsâ that state attorneys general across the country have declared to be illegal gambling operations,â the American Gaming Association said in a statement, adding that the gaming industry creates jobs and helps grow the economy. Prediction markets, it says, âare mocking congressional intent on sports betting, thumbing their nose at state and tribal law, allowing teenagers to sports gamble, and robbing the states of revenue.â
The traditional casino operators and the sports betting companies are also lobbying in Washington for tax relief. They want to be able to deduct 100% of their gambling losses from their taxes, a shift currently written in the FAIR BET Act, that recently passed through the Ways and Means Committee. At least six cosponsors of the bill have received political contributions from sportsbooks. Casino operators have also donated to individuals on the Ways and Means Committee.
Eleanor Mueller contributed reporting.

Warhound, a new defense technology company, has launched with $200 million in seed funding from investors including Sequoia Capital to create dogs genetically engineered for military use.

Those charges could lead to years in prison and thwart their efforts to naturalize. The Justice Department said in a statement that six people would be charged with voting as a noncitizen, a misdemeanor. She later admitted to registering to vote while getting her driver's license renewed last year and said she voted once, according to the charging documents. Line, who is from the Philippines, told authorities she thought she was a U.S. citizen because her mother had become naturalized after they moved to the United States more than four decades ago. In June 2013, torrential rain spurred one of the worst flooding events in Canada’s history. Sadie Vipond, who grew up in Calgary along the Bow River, was just a young child at the time when she and her family had to flee their home. “That was pretty scary with the evacuation,” she recalled.
Her family was among thousands forced to evacuate as the city declared a local emergency. The disaster was the costliest Calgary had ever experienced, with $1.7 billion in insurable damage, and many residents—including Vipond—still carry that trauma to this day.
Vipond is now a 20-year-old university student studying environmental science at the University of British Columbia. Next week, she will be sitting inside a courtroom in Vancouver telling her story of how extreme weather and climate change have affected her health and quality of life.
She will not be alone. More than a dozen other young Canadians will also be in court testifying in a historic climate change trial against their federal government. It will be the first time in Canada, and one of the first times anywhere in the world, that a national government faces a full evidentiary trial over the adequacy of its climate policies in a case brought by youth activists.
The trial, which starts Monday, is happening against a backdrop of warnings that the climate crisis is accelerating and that in just a few short years warming will exceed the 1.5 degrees Celsius limit that countries agreed to strive to avoid surpassing. Current climate policies are off track to achieve the Paris Agreement objectives, and some countries like Canada and the United States are doubling down on fossil fuel production while at the same time rolling back measures to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and advance green technologies.
Activists around the world have turned to the courts in recent years in pursuit of accountability. Last year the International Court of Justice delivered a landmark advisory opinion affirming that governments have legal obligations under existing laws to do their utmost to act on climate change in accordance with the best available science.
Now that guidance, and the strategy of pursuing climate accountability through the courts, faces a critical test in a case putting one of the world’s largest greenhouse gas emitters and oil and gas producers on trial.
The case, La Rose v. His Majesty the King, challenges Canada’s climate policies, specifically the Net-Zero Emissions Accountability Act and its 2030 climate plan. The 2021 Net-Zero act establishes a legislative framework for Canada to emit no greenhouse gases by 2050 beyond the amount removed from the atmosphere, requiring the government to set interim emissions reduction targets and develop plans to implement them.
The lawsuit argues that this legislation, as well as Canada’s 2030 reduction plan, enable a “trajectory that is inconsistent with a safe climate system.” Youth plaintiffs say this violates their constitutional rights, namely the rights to life, liberty and security of the person under section 7 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. They seek not only a court declaration that their rights have been violated, but also an order for the government to develop and implement a science-based plan for rapid decarbonization.
The young activists filed their case in 2019, launching it during a Fridays for Future climate rally in Vancouver attended by an estimated 10,000 people, including environmental activist Greta Thunberg. The suit had originally targeted a wide range of government conduct, inspired by a similar youth-led case in the U.S. that ultimately never made it to trial.
After a federal court initially tossed out the Canadian case, an appeals court allowed the plaintiffs to amend their complaint by honing in on a specific action or piece of policy. The revised case was greenlit for trial, which is about to begin nearly seven years to the day since the suit was first filed.
Defendants include Canada’s federal government and attorney general. Government representatives did not respond to a request for comment on the case or the trial.
Plaintiffs are 15 young Canadians, including several indigenous youths. Like Vipond, they have all personally experienced extreme weather and health impacts linked to climate change, from extreme heat and floods to increasingly severe wildfires and toxic wildfire smoke.
“Every summer is now defined by how bad the wildfires are, by the extreme heat, by either drought or extreme precipitation and flooding,” plaintiff Lauren Wright said during a recent webinar. Wright enjoys farming and working outside, but climate change is making that at times uncomfortable and harmful to her health.
“When I’m out in the field, I can’t exactly take days off when the smoke is so bad that my lungs are burning and my eyes are blurring,” she said. “It’s a struggle to work in 30-plus degree [Celsius] temperatures outdoors in the sun without any availability to avoid the harms.”
“Carney Climate Carnage”
According to a scientific climate assessment report released by the Canadian government in early September, Canada has warmed twice as fast as the global average since 1970. Under current global climate policies, the country is expected to experience an average temperature increase of 5 degrees Celsius toward the end of the century.
Climatic changes already occurring today—extreme heat, catastrophic fire seasons, melting glaciers, thawing permafrost, more severe droughts, flash floods—will continue to intensify.

The future of agentic commerce hinges on the ability to know whether itâs a human or an AI agent thatâs making a purchase, and the tools to do that are arriving fast.
Proof-of-human technology, which can let a person vouch for the AI agents acting on their behalf, could keep bad bots off of websites without forcing platforms to block all of them. But it also opens up new possibilities for how business gets done online.
World, the startup co-founded by Sam Altman that scans peopleâs irises to verify theyâre human, this week announced new tools that let people link their proof of humanity to an AI agent.
The companyâs product chief Tiago Sada told me that could eventually lead to online sellers offering perks to verified agents, such as discounts and free trials. âIf you know that an agent is coming from a human, you can actually be much more generous,â Sada said.
E-commerce may get comfortable with agent transactions before other industries. Several large US banks are restricting interaction with third-party agents, in part because they canât tell which ones a customer actually authorized, Axios reported.

Reedâs view
The world finally suffered the kind of catastrophic security disaster that experts have been warning about.
OpenAI models helped discover a set of bugs that make the majority of the internet vulnerable to a powerful exploit. Then, a botched disclosure process gave hackers a head start on taking advantage of it before the world had a chance to react.
AI didnât create this problem. Human complacency did.
The bugs have existed for more than a decade, and PHP, the programming language that contained them, is 30 years old. A security researcher named Stefan Esser discovered the class of bug that roiled the internet this week back in 2004. And during a 2024 security audit by the PHP Foundation, this weekâs discovery was theorized, but the group didnât do anything about it; it deemed other issues more pressing, according to the foundation, the organization that maintains the software.
There are so many flaws in the aging, crumbling infrastructure of the internet. Only the ones deemed most critical have been fixed, but AI makes it possible to see all cracks more clearly and connect them together to catastrophic effect. But AI canât force people to devote resources to fixing whatâs wrong.
With some luck, the PHP bugs will create more inconvenience than economic and human damage. Thereâs still time for bold efforts to proactively overhaul the foundation of our software-dominated world. But it could also go very badly.
The same can be said for other effects of AI: In parts of society or in businesses, AI could exacerbate existing weaknesses, like extreme income inequality and the loneliness epidemic. But if policymakers work on solving those vulnerabilities, the technologyâs negative impacts might not be felt.
Technology always gets better and no policy or regulation will change that. What we can do is face the things weâve long neglected and make them stronger.
Notable
- âWeâre going to have a couple years where every single week itâs going to feel like the sky is falling,â Matthew Prince, CEO of cybersecurity firm Cloudflare, told Reuters as AI uncovers new software vulnerabilities.

When PFAS concentrations in drinking water fall below laboratory reporting limits, they are sometimes treated as “zero” in statistical analyses. But a new study published in Cell Reports Sustainability, which reanalyzed federal monitoring data, found that estimated PFAS concentrations in U.S. drinking water could be more than twice as high as calculations that treat results below laboratory reporting limits as zero suggest.
PFAS are a group of thousands of synthetic chemicals used for decades in products ranging from nonstick cookware to waterproof clothing. Often called “forever chemicals,” they break down very slowly in the environment and have contaminated drinking water supplies across the United States.
“About 98 percent of the roughly 1.86 million individual PFAS test results in EPA’s January 2026 dataset were below reporting limits,” said the study’s author, Gehendra Kharel, an associate professor of environmental and sustainability sciences at Texas Christian University.
But even without an exact concentration, he said, “those records still tell us something”—that PFAS contamination of drinking water is far more prevalent than generally acknowledged.
For PFOA and PFOS, two of the most widely studied forever chemicals, the EPA sets a maximum allowable concentration of 4 parts per trillion.
By using statistical models to estimate concentrations below laboratory reporting limits, the researchers found that more sampling locations could reach or exceed the study’s comparison threshold of 4.05 parts per trillion, just above the EPA’s drinking water limit of 4 parts per trillion. Depending on the model, an additional 16 to 33 locations crossed that threshold for PFOA, and 4 to 25 for PFOS, said Kharel.
None of the newly identified sampling locations crossed the threshold for both chemicals simultaneously.
For Laurel Schaider, an environmental chemistry and engineering scientist at the Silent Spring Institute, who was not involved in the study, the findings highlight a broader problem with how scientists interpret measurements that fall below detection or reporting limits. “I think the paper raises an important point about how we think about results when we find that a chemical is not detected,” she said.
Schaider offered an analogy: Imagine you’re moving and packing all your belongings into boxes. Before shipping them, you might want to weigh each box to figure out how heavy the entire shipment will be. Some boxes might be heavy, while others might be pretty light. But assuming the lighter ones weigh nothing would underestimate the total weight of your belongings. “You don’t want to call those all zero,” she said.
Under the EPA’s Fifth Unregulated Contaminant Monitoring Rule (UCMR 5), public water systems across the U.S. are required to test their drinking water for 29 PFAS chemicals. Water suppliers collect samples and send them to EPA-approved laboratories, which use specialized equipment to measure the concentrations of these chemicals.
The EPA then receives the results, which help it assess how widespread PFAS contamination is in the nation’s drinking water. But the tests have limits. When a concentration falls below the reporting limit, the result is reported as below that threshold rather than a precise number. That does not necessarily mean the chemical is absent from the water. “Simply substituting zero is not the best way to handle a non-detect,” said Schaider.
How low a concentration a laboratory can measure reliably depends in part on its equipment and methods. “There are differences in the type of instruments. The instruments that can measure lower concentrations probably cost more,” said Schaider.
But as chemistry techniques improve, “we can be more sensitive across the board, and then we don’t have to make so many guesses anymore,” said Shelly Liu, associate professor of population health at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, who was not involved in the study.
Still, finding higher concentrations in drinking water samples does not necessarily mean people are exposed to more PFAS than previously thought. While the researchers’ statistical models produced a higher estimate of combined low, under-the-limit PFAS concentrations, it did not measure individual exposure.
“That’s not the same as demonstrating underestimated exposure,” said Kharel. “We studied water entering distribution systems, not the water people actually drank,” he said.
The findings also raise questions about whether current reporting practices provide enough information about low levels of PFAS contamination, and whether more sensitive testing, where labs can reliably achieve it, could help close those gaps.
Agencies could clearly report the limits used and how often results fell below them, show estimates that account for below-limit results alongside zero-substitution averages, and explain the uncertainty of those estimates, said Kharel.
The EPA acknowledged the request for comment but did not provide a statement in time for publication.
Understanding how much PFAS is present in drinking water matters because exposure to these chemicals is already widespread. “Over 99 percent of people have PFAS in their blood,” said Schaider.

Other research has linked PFAS exposure to thyroid disease, reproductive problems and an increased risk of certain cancers, particularly kidney and testicular cancer, Schaider said.

An oil spill from a tanker attacked near the Strait of Hormuz is spreading along the United Arab Emirates (UAE) coastline, forcing the closure of some beaches and coastal areas.
Satellite images from Monday show the beginnings of the oil spill from a ship matching the location and dimensions of Gem No.2, which was damaged between 9 and 10 October during a record surge of vessel strikes by Iran.
The slick of oil had spread more than 35km (22 miles) from the tanker by Wednesday, the satellite imagery showed.
UAE authorities said on Thursday that the incident is affecting beaches near the northern city of Umm Al Quwain and verified video from Friday shows the oil washing ashore, colouring the water black.
The UAE's Ministry of Climate Change and Environment said on Thursday that it "immediately began containment" in order to "limit environmental impacts".
Prof Steve Widdicombe, director of Sharjah Marine Science Research Centre in the UAE, told BBC Verify it was "inevitable that there will be an impact", but researchers caution it is too soon to assess extent of the damage.
Initially a much smaller oil leak could be seen emerging from the ship on 19 October.
But the slick appears to have rapidly spread over two days, according to radar satellite imagery reviewed by BBC Verify and intelligence firm MAIAR.
Oil spills can cause immediate deaths of marine animals and other organisms, for example by physically trapping turtles, smothering the feathers of seabirds or damaging the gills of fish.
They can also cause longer-lasting damage, Prof Widdicombe said, if species remain exposed to toxic compounds from the oil which could impact their ability to reproduce.
Researchers have cautioned the environmental impact at this stage is very uncertain, as it depends on factors including the volume and type of oil spilled, how quickly it evaporates or breaks down and the effectiveness of the clean-up operation.
But the spill does extend towards Siniyah and Khor Al Beidah islands, a globally recognised Key Biodiversity Area containing habitats like corals, seagrasses and saltmarshes, as well as species including green turtles and the critically endangered Halavi guitarfish.
The proximity of the spill to this area is the "most concerning environmental angle", according to Eoghan Darbyshire, a scientist at the Conflict and Environment Observatory.
Tanker hit 14 days ago
BBC Verify analysis of the dimensions and location of the ship indicate they match a crude oil tanker called Gem No.2.
Maritime intelligence firm Vanguard reported the Panama-flagged tanker was "struck by an unknown projectile" on 9 October, just north of the town of Al Jazeera Al Hamra, causing a fire on board that was later extinguished.
Verified footage first posted on social media on 10 October showed the crew running across the deck and putting on lifejackets as a large cloud of black smoke rose over the ship.
Iranian state media shared footage of a ship matching Gem No.2 which appeared to show the vessel on fire with burning oil spilling into the sea.
The ship had been attempting to exit the Strait of Hormuz via an "unauthorized and dangerous route", according to state media.
All 22 Indian crew members were rescued, the Indian consulate in Dubai said on 11 October.
Gem No.2 is one of a record number of ships that reported being attacked in and around the Strait of Hormuz at the start of October.
Security experts told BBC Verify this was part of an Iranian effort to assert greater control over the strait, in response to the US military successfully escorting more vessels through the vital shipping lane.
Tankers and other commercial vessels have come under attack from both Iranian and US forces in and around the Strait of Hormuz amid the conflict between the two countries.
Another major oil slick washed up on the shores of Iran's Qeshm Island in August, which experts said threatened wildlife, protected ecosystems and fishing communities.
Additional reporting by Charlotte Green

While a spoonful of sugar might help us gulp down a bitter-tasting antibiotic, it also may increase the damage that these drugs cause to the gut microbes.
In patients being treated for blood cancers, eating sugary items during antibiotic treatment was linked to a greater reduction in gut bacteria diversity than taking the antibiotics alone. The combination was also tied to the growth of gut bacteria associated with hard-to-treat infections, researchers report September 30 in Nature.
Cancer patients have lots of variation in their diets and take medications that can damage their microbiome. So, these patients provide a unique opportunity to study dramatic gut changes “that we believe are also relevant in the healthy context,” says Jonas Schluter, a microbiologist at NYU Langone Health.
Previous evidence separately suggested that antibiotics and sugars can disrupt the gut microbiome. But their combined effects, particularly in people at greater risk of infection, was unclear.
Researchers closely tracked more than 9,000 meals eaten by 173 people hospitalized in a treatment center to undergo blood-forming stem cell transplants. “Diet records are one of the biggest black boxes in a lot of diet microbiome studies,” since meals are often self-reported, says Tiffany Weir, a microbiologist at Colorado State University in Fort Collins, who was not involved in the research.
Standardized hospital meals allowed researchers to measure multiple days’ worth of food intake down to the gram, then compare the amounts of various nutrients eaten with bacterial diversity data obtained from stool samples.
For every additional 100 grams of sugar (the equivalent of 2.5 cans of Coke) that patients on antibiotics ate in the two days before sampling, the team found a 24 percent decrease in bacterial diversity. Consuming sweets and sugary beverages during antibiotic treatment was also associated with blooms of Enterococcus bacteria, which can be drug-resistant and are linked to difficult-to-treat infections associated with longer hospital stays and higher mortality.
“Some bacteria, sometimes, survive antibiotics, or perhaps more dangerously, they are resistant to [them],” Schluter says. By giving these bacteria the “universal resource for life, which is simple sugars, we are exacerbating their dominance. It’s almost like burning down the rainforest with a lot of fire, and then trying to extinguish the flames by putting in more petrol.”
The researchers also exposed mice on standard or sucrose-rich diets to a single dose of antibiotics. They found that the sugar exacerbated the enterococcal abundance after antibiotic exposure.
“Reducing sugar intake could be another way for patients to support their gut microbiome during antibiotic treatment,” says Sarah Berry, a nutrition scientist at King’s College London who was not involved in the study. Still, more research is needed to determine whether the findings apply to anyone on these drugs.
Schluter hopes that further studies and clinical trials can help uncover more about the exact relationship between sugar, antibiotics and the gut microbiome.
“You need to take antibiotics to fight infections, but you should also be aware that they have side effects to the microbiome,” Schluter says. “Now, we need to find strategies to mitigate this damage.”

Wyoming mechanic and amateur moonshiner Geno Stecks proudly details the modifications he's made at his two-bedroom residence to facilitate his hobby of distilling liquor in his own home.
"I turned my dining room into my shining room," boasted the bearded 66-year-old, who uses a power drill fixed to a bowl to mix some of his recipe.
Two years ago, he began tinkering with recipes for home-producing spirits. The pastime has taught him new skills and given him a signature product to share with friends and neighbors - "coffee-flavoured shine". It also happens to be illegal under US law.
"You know, keep quiet - don't make commercials or nothing," Stecks said.
But some home distillers hope they won't have to keep their hobby a secret for longer. The Supreme Court announced this week that it would reconsider the 1868 legislation forbidding the practice, and hobby distillers hope that their spirits will soon be treated like beer and wine, which are both legal to brew at home across the country.
Plaintiffs who brought the cases say Congress overstepped its powers in restricting distilling for tax purposes during the Reconstruction era. They want the highest judges in the country to agree.
But lawyers for the government argue that Congress's measure was lawful, and necessary to stop producers from avoiding taxes.
One lower court found the almost 160-year-old ban unconstitutional, but in a separate and similar case, another lower court came to the opposite conclusion. The Supreme Court will hear the case early next year and could make a ruling in the summer of 2027.
Currently, distilling alcohol in a private home carries a penalty of up to five years in prison, a $10,000 (Â£7,460) fine or both.
"The particular law in question here is both absurd and unconstitutional," said lawyer Robert Alt, representing the plaintiffs. "It's interesting to note that this is a hobby which is as American as apple pie - and certainly a lot older."
Alt, Stecks and many proponents of the change point out that George Washington himself distilled spirits at home. Historian Daniel Pierce told the BBC that home distilling was first criminalised for revenue purposes, requiring anyone making spirits to pay a tax.
When federal agents began enforcing the law, small farmers who were distilling on the side as a way to make some extra money or to barter were left with few options.
"If you're a large distiller or something, you could afford to [pay the tax], but for most people, it was out of the question," Pierce said.
When the US implemented Prohibition - the nationwide ban on the production and sale of alcohol between 1930 and 1933 - it created a whole new market for illegal distillers, particularly moonshiners, Pierce said.
NASCAR, the racing sport, was born out of the high-speed, modified cars that bootleggers once used to transport illicit liquor and outrun the law.
Many continued their illegal distilling after Prohibition's end, often passing on family recipes in secret (or, at least, in tightly-knit circles) for generations.
Then moonshine and home distilling enjoyed a new renaissance in the early 2000s, he said, thanks to reality TV shows like Moonshiners, the internet and popular culture.
"You start to get this pretty dramatic revivalâ¦. in terms of home distilling," Pierce said.
Rick Morris, the founder and president of the Hobby Distillers Association, was one of the challengers who sued in Texas to change the law. He first entered the drinks industry working with soda machines and bottled water, then became a hobbyist home brewer of beer and wine with his wife.
They made a frustrating discovery when they tried to take the "next step" into distilling.
"It didn't make sense," he said. "I could make beer, I could make wine, both perfectly legally â¦ and it was frustrating that I couldn't take what I had already legally made and do one more step to it, to start to try to make a bourbon or a brandy."
The allure for Morris and many other hobbyists, they say, is the mechanics and innovation behind the process.
"There is a lot of science and details to get straightened out, but there is still a big vein of creativity in the art that goes into it - blending flavours and aromas and all that," said Ohio challenger John Bream, an aerospace engineer by trade.
He first took up the hobby when his wife gave him a home-brewing kit around 17 years ago. He set up his operations in their kitchen but "made too many messes and got kicked out into the garage".
"Through homebrewing, I became aware that going to the next level of distilling was illegal â¦ so I stayed away from it," he said.
But he realised he could be "part of the force for good" by joining legal challenges to the archaic law.
Not everyone is on board with the move, Courtney Armour, chief legal officer at The Distilled Spirits Council of the US, told the BBC. She worries about the challenges and dangers that come with home producing.
"The distillation process can be quite dangerous, including risk of explosion, burns, fires, and more," Armour said. "The spirits industry has a clear focus on safety and process management to mitigate these risks, but even in that careful environment there are still accidents, injuries and even fatalities."
And then there are health concerns that can arise when alcohol has not been produced properly.
"In a home-distilling setting, these dangers would not just be limited to the individuals engaging in the production but also their neighbors in the surrounding area," Armour said.
While home distilling remains federally banned, states like Missouri and New Hampshire have passed legislation allowing the production of certain amounts at home for personal consumption.
Attorney Alt pointed out that "alcohol, traditionally, has been an area of state regulation â¦ so this question of state versus federal authority is really at the very heart of this case".

Tomorrow Together, an AI-focused Democratic PAC, is moving into Senate races with $2.5 million in ads against Republican Sens. Jon Husted in Ohio and Roger Marshall in Kansas, according to an announcement shared first with Semafor.
The group, founded by Biden White House alum Rob Flaherty and former Bernie Sanders spokesman Karthik Ganapathy, is âfocused on building political support for AI regulation and ensuring voters trust Democrats on AI issues,â Ganapathy told Semafor.
The Ohio and Kansas ads paint Husted and Marshall as beholden to data center projects and âtech guysâ who want to âtake our land â¦ our water â¦ our quietâ and jobs. A second ad running in both Ohio and Kansas focuses on former Trump AI czar and venture capitalist David Sacks and his influence with the Republican incumbents.
âRepublicans gave Sacks a government job pushing AI data centers and blocking AI regulation. Sacks gets rich. His friends get rich. The only person who losesâ¦ is you,â the ad states.

Ashleyâs view
Concerns about AI and technology have simmered under the surface of American campaign politics for years, but have never been a fully salient everyday issue for voters until lately.

b5d30be46f8f.text: By — Eric Tucker, Associated Press Eric Tucker, Associated Press By — Alanna Durkin Richer, Associated Press Alanna Durkin Richer, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/2-ex-fbi-officials-charged-with-making-false-statements-about-hunter-bidens-laptop Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter 2 ex-FBI officials charged with making false statements about Hunter Biden's laptop Politics Updated on Oct 23, 2026 2:45 PM EDT — Published on Oct 23, 2026 11:19 AM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — Two former FBI officials were charged Friday with lying to Congress about their involvement in investigating Hunter Biden's laptop in the run-up to the 2020 presidential election, the latest in a series of splashy and politically charged actions the Justice Department has undertaken ahead of next month's midterm contests. Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides, former leaders of a since-disbanded task force set up to counter foreign election interference, appeared in federal court in Washington, where their lawyers pressed for a speedy hearing at which they could contest allegations that they lied to lawmakers by saying that they did not participate in FBI investigations of Biden. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. The prosecution, a rare Department of Justice criminal case against a former employee, revisits a tangled and peculiar saga that roiled the final weeks of the 2020 race. It also comes amid a broader, backward-looking effort by FBI Director Kash Patel, who before taking over the nation's premier law enforcement agency was a harsh critic of it, to scrutinize high-profile episodes from the bureau's recent past that for years have animated President Donald Trump's conservative base. Floris' attorneys called her "a patriot" and said she has "served our nation as a dedicated FBI intelligence officer for nearly 20 years." "Yet today, the DOJ has accused her falsely of a crime on the say-so of politicians, not on the facts," her attorneys said in a statement. "It's no coincidence the government is filing these nonsense charges now, years later, on the eve of an election." Attorneys for Benavides accused the government of bringing "baseless criminal charges against him in a transparently political complaint." "This is another sad day for the Department of Justice," his lawyers said in an emailed statement. "But now we are in court, and the truth will come out: Brad Benavides is a true patriot who devoted his career to protecting this country and its people. These charges are a disgrace." A criminal complaint comes just before the midterms The case was filed 10 days before the Nov. 3 elections via criminal complaint, which means prosecutors have not yet presented the allegations to a grand jury for an indictment. The Justice Department has repeatedly struggled in high-profile cases to convince grand juries in the nation's capital to return indictments. READ MORE: Takeaways from Hunter Biden's deposition with Republican lawmakers During the former FBI employees' court appearance, both defense attorneys and the judge noted the unusual move to charge the case through a criminal complaint, which is more often used by prosecutors when they have an urgent need to take people into custody because, for example, they present a danger or a risk of flight. U.S. Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui remarked that it is "rare that we have charges this old coming in this nature." Faruqui set a preliminary hearing for next Tuesday over the objections of prosecutors, who pushed for more time given what the judge described as the "sword of Damocles" hanging over the defendants' head. The laptop discovery created turmoil in 2020 election The revelation of the laptop's existence in October 2020 injected a thorny storyline in the race between Trump, the Republican incumbent, and Biden's father, Joe Biden, Trump's Democratic challenger, who went on to win the race. The laptop were publicized by the New York Post, which said it had obtained from Trump ally Rudy Giuliani a hard drive of a computer dropped off by Hunter Biden at a Wilmington, Delaware, repair shop about a year earlier. The criminal complaint aims to build on longstanding congressional Republican complaints about the FBI's handling of the laptop, including allegations that the bureau was not forthcoming to the public that the materials on it — including emails that showed discussions of the younger Biden's foreign business dealings — were authentic and not the product of Russian disinformation. The curious circumstances of the laptop's discovery raised concerns among Democrats and former intelligence officials about the possibility of Russian involvement, particularly at a time when the Trump administration's own intelligence community was Moscow that Russia was attempting to interfere on Trump's behalf in the election and as Giuliani had traveled abroad looking for dirt on the Bidens. Dozens of former U.S. intelligence officials signed a letter saying that the laptop bore the "classic earmarks of an Russian information operation." But Trump's then-director of national intelligence, John Ratcliffe, said in a letter to Congress that there was no proof foreign actors had anything to do with Hunter Biden's laptop. The FBI under then-Director Chris Wray subsequently backed up that assessment. Hunter Biden was charged with, and convicted of, gun and tax offenses during his father's administration. Joe Biden pardoned him in his final weeks in office. The case shines a light on an FBI task force on foreign intelligence The complaint alleges that in their capacity as leaders of the Foreign Influence Task Force, Floris and Benavides were deeply engaged in the investigations into Hunter Biden, and that Biden was a recurring subject

Dan Sullivan loses, kicking off what many fear could become a lengthy battle between the government and states over certifying an election where the president's party is struggling. The lawsuit centers on one of the president's longstanding complaints in the Senate race — the presence of a second candidate named Dan Sullivan who Republicans fear could siphon away votes from the incumbent in what's likely to be a photo-finish contest with Democrat Mary Peltola, the state's former congresswoman. The second Dan Sullivan, who is Daniel J. Sullivan from the tiny fishing community of Petersburg, has said he decided to run on his own, but Republicans have contended he is a Democratic plant to siphon votes away from their candidate. The lawsuit Thursday by the Republican president's Department of Justice in federal court in Alaska demands that the state be blocked from certifying a Peltola win if Daniel J. Sullivan remains on the ballot. "The United States accordingly brings this lawsuit to protect the integrity of the 2026 Senate election in Alaska," the lawsuit says, contending that federal law requires states to protect the integrity of federal elections. The legal challenge came 11 days before the Nov. 3 election and months after the final ballot was set. The Alaska Supreme Court rejected a previous Republican effort to remove Daniel J. Sullivan from the ballot, and the state's Republican officials made the decisions about how to list him on the ballot. He will appear without a party designation next to his name, while the senator will be listed as the Republican incumbent. Alaska's ranked choice voting system also will allow voters to select both of the men if confused. Peltola and Sen. Sullivan were top vote-getters in nonpartisan primary The senator received more than 68,000 votes in the August primary, while the challenging Sullivan got 4,107, about 2% of the total vote. Peltola, who had previously served one term in the House, was the top vote-getter in the nonpartisan primary. Both parties expect that whoever wins in November will do so by a tight margin in a state of 738,000 people. The campaign for Sen. Dan Sullivan did not address whether the senator supports the Department of Justice's intervention. "We'll let the DOJ complaint run its course," campaign spokesman Nate Adams said in a text message. "Alaskans can tell the difference between a Democrat sideshow and Senator Sullivan's strong record of delivering for Alaska." Daniel J. Sullivan, whose presence on the ballot is at issue in the lawsuit, did not immediately respond to a request for comment. "Donald Trump knows that Dan Sullivan is going to lose the election, so now his Department of Justice is filing a sham lawsuit to overturn the will of Alaska voters and steal an election when he loses," said Devan Barber, executive director of the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee. Watch the segment in the player above. In a statement on Friday, the Department of Justice noted that Alaska's election officials, who are Republicans, determined the other Sullivan's campaign was an attempt to "mislead:" voters and wanted him removed from the ballot. Both a state court and Alaska's Supreme Court disagreed and kept the second Sullivan on the ballot. "The Justice Department, consistent with the National Voter Registration Act enacted by Congress, is taking the necessary steps to ensure that this frivolous candidacy does not undermine the integrity of Alaska's election or the will of its voters," the DoJ statement said. The Department of Justice has increasingly been used to bolster the president's political operation, targeting his enemies and suing Democratic-controlled states before the election. Democrats and many voting rights advocates have long feared that the administration will try to block certification of elections that Trump's party loses, much as he unsuccessfully tried to do when he lost the White House race to Democrat Joe Biden. U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche said that was unlikely outside of extreme circumstances. "It is not DOJ's intention to, and it's never our intention to, improperly interfere with elections or the state certification process," he told reporters Thursday in Virginia before the lawsuit was filed. The lawsuit was signed by Associate U.S. Attorney General Stanley Woodward, who represented Trump allies and Jan. 6 defendants before becoming one of the top appointees at the department. Constitution gives states the power to run elections Derek Muller, a law professor at the University of Notre Dame, said the lawsuit would likely only kick in if Republicans narrowly lost the Alaska Senate race and that it probably would not survive long. "The statute simply doesn't let the Department of Justice enjoin certification," Muller said. "The lawsuit could well be mooted by a wide Democratic victory or a narrow Republican one, and if not, the court will likely dismiss it next month."
