Climate pollutant concentrations in the Beijing region of northern China have plateaued or begun to decline—except for the world’s most potent greenhouse gas, new research concludes.
The findings, published in the journal Environmental Science & Technology, suggest a decades-long effort to clean Beijing’s air is beginning to pay off. But while it cites progress, the research also highlights a growing climate challenge, driven by the region’s surging electricity demand and the explosive growth of semiconductor manufacturing amid the AI boom.
Sulfur hexafluoride—known as SF6—is 24,300 times more effective at warming Earth’s atmosphere, pound for pound, than carbon dioxide, the leading driver of climate change. The synthetic gas is widely used as an electrical insulator in high-voltage equipment, making the power sector a key source of concern as electricity infrastructure expands. While SF6 emissions are declining in other parts of the world, they are rapidly rising in China, which accounts for more than half of global releases.
The country’s state-owned electric power companies recycle only about 30 percent of the gas they discard each year, with the remainder likely released into the atmosphere, a recent Inside Climate News analysis concluded.
The study, by researchers at the Chinese Academy of Sciences’ Institute of Atmospheric Physics in Beijing, examined greenhouse gas concentrations in the region between 1993 and 2024 to assess the effectiveness of the city’s energy transition.
The researchers found that semiconductor manufacturing, where the gas is used for etching and cleaning, is another fast-growing source of SF6 emissions in the Beijing region.
The scientists, who did not respond to interview requests or declined to comment, found that carbon dioxide concentrations have begun to decrease in China’s capital. The study attributed the shift to local policies introduced around 2008, when Beijing hosted the Summer Olympics, that promoted natural gas and electricity while discouraging or banning coal use.
Growth in atmospheric concentrations of methane and nitrous oxide, the second and third leading drivers of climate change, has slowed. The study attributes the change in methane levels to capturing landfill emissions and reusing the gas for power generation or incinerating waste before it can decompose. Increased electric-vehicle use and stricter pollution controls for gas-powered automobiles hit the brakes on growth in nitrous oxide concentrations, the researchers found.
However, SF6 concentrations are accelerating.
“These findings underscore the power and semiconductor sectors as critical domains for targeted SF6 emission control,” the study concluded.
The electric power sector is China’s leading national source of the climate pollutant, accounting for about 70 percent of all SF6 emissions, according to the study. However, emissions from semiconductor manufacturing in Beijing have grown rapidly for more than a decade and are now the pollutant’s primary local source, the study found.
Martin Vojta, an atmospheric scientist at the University of Vienna, noted that Beijing’s increase in semiconductor manufacturing correlated with rising SF6 emissions. However, other factors, such as changes in production practices, could affect the industry’s emissions, Vojta said.
Atmospheric modeling that traces SF6 emissions back to their sources would more definitively link the increase in emissions to the semiconductor industry, Vojta said.
The research results were compiled into a policy report, “Beware of Sulfur Hexafluoride Emissions Behind AI Industry Development,” which was quickly adopted by the Beijing Municipal Committee of the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference, according to an Aug. 19 press release from the Institute of Atmospheric Physics.

Artificial Intelligence, or AI, could fuel rising SF6 emissions by increasing semiconductor chip manufacturing and continuing the region’s power-grid buildout. The Beijing Municipal Committee is a government advisory body overseen by the Chinese Communist Party. The institute’s press release announcing the policy report’s adoption came less than a week after the study was published.
Members of the committee visited the institute shortly before publication for briefings. Tang Guiqian, one of the study’s co-authors, was among those speaking to the group, according to the institute.
Tang declined to comment, citing institute policies. The Beijing Municipal Committee did not respond to a request for additional information.
SF6 supplies fluorine for the semiconductor industry, where it is used to carve channels into silicon or other materials to help build circuitry in computer chips, liquid crystal display panels—better known as LCD—and other electronic devices. The gas can also clean deposition chambers where chips and other electronics are fabricated. In both processes, some sulfur hexafluoride passes through without reacting and, unless properly abated, is released into the atmosphere.
The semiconductor industry can rein that in. Among the options: optimizing production, using alternative fluorine sources and destroying waste gas.
From 1996 to 2010, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency partnered with manufacturers in a voluntary effort to reduce emissions of SF6 and other fluorinated greenhouse gases.
Scott Bartos, a former EPA official and program manager on the partnership, said any effort to reduce climate pollution as a result of the current study and subsequent policy report would be good news as China ramps up semiconductor manufacturing and electrifies its economy.

Six Flags has announced it will be adding seat belts to some of its rollercoasters after a man fell to his death on the Goliath ride in the US state of Georgia earlier this month.
The company's CEO John Reilly said in a letter to customers late on Friday that the company is reinforcing safety measure across its parks, including adding seat belts to Goliath and similar rides, which already feature lap bar restraints.
The chain of amusement parks has 34 locations across North America, with over 220 rollercoasters in total.
Georgia's Goliath ride will remain closed pending safety reviews and out of an abundance of caution, so will eight other rides at five other parks, Reilly added.
The CEO also said the company has hired independent engineers and ride inspection specialists to review safety procedures across all its amusement parks. The company is committed to taking action based on the experts' findings and will share progress updates, he said.
On 12 October, a 42-year-old man named Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem was killed at Six Flags Over Georgia after being ejected from the Goliath, police have said. Four other passengers were injured as he fell.
An investigation into the incident is ongoing.
"Our hearts remain with the family and loved ones of Hassan Kariem, those injured, and everyone impacted by the tragic incident," Reilly said in his letter.
"What happened has deeply affected all of us at Six Flags," he added.
The Goliath ride opened in 2006, and it has an elevation of 200ft (60m), a 170ft plunge, a 540-degree spiral, and a speed of up to 70mph (112km/h), according to the park website. On its "thrill scale", Six Flags ranks Goliath at level four out of five
Over 28 million guests visit Six Flags locations every year, according to the company's website.
October's fatal incident was not the first time a passenger has been hurt at one of the parks.
An Iraq War veteran died in 2011 after being ejected from a ride in New York. In 2013, a woman died after slipping from her restraints and falling 75 feet from a coaster in Texas.
In 2022, a 22-year-old man died from a brain injury after riding the X2 coaster at Six Flags Magic Mountain in California. His family settled a wrongful death suit with the theme park in August.
The following month, the California park announced it was closing its X2 rollercoaster after more 100 people alleged that they had suffered brain injuries from the ride.

80dfa1b69af0.text: By — Susie Blann, Associated Press Susie Blann, Associated Press By — Elise Morton, Associated Press Elise Morton, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/ukraines-starlink-satellite-speeds-restored-after-a-week-of-front-line-disruption Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Ukraine's Starlink satellite speeds restored after a week of front-line disruption World Oct 24, 2026 12:05 PM EDT KYIV, Ukraine (AP) — Ukraine's access to Starlink and Starshield satellite links has been restored to the speeds it had before restrictions that disrupted front-line operations for more than a week, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Saturday. "The speeds are now where they need to be," Zelenskyy wrote on X, adding that restoration began overnight and were sufficient by Saturday morning, improving front-line logistics and defense against Russian jet-powered Shahed drones. WATCH: How Starlink disruptions affected Ukraine's battlefield operations The restoration follows a new U.S. diplomatic push to end the war. Russia agreed Wednesday to resume three-way negotiations with Washington and Kyiv next month. On Friday, Kyiv and Moscow also agreed to a localized ceasefire brokered by first lady Melania Trump around Oleshky, a war-ravaged, Russian-occupied town in Ukraine's southern Kherson region. Restrictions imposed last week on Starshield — SpaceX's military-grade version of the Starlink satellite internet service and the backbone of Ukraine's drone operations and communication — alarmed the country's military and government officials, with commanders reporting lost drones and disrupted missions. The episode added to tensions between Kyiv and Washington, a relationship already strained by President Donald Trump's reported deal with Moscow on Russian diesel imports, which Ukraine viewed as a betrayal. Ukraine's Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara credited "direct dialogue" and Zelenskyy's diplomacy with Washington, adding that the outcome mattered most "for our front, for the military, the work of drones, logistics and communications." Zelenskyy on Friday said Ukraine was still experiencing Starlink and Starshield speed limits. Questions have persisted since last week about who ordered the interruptions to the Elon Musk-made satellite internet system that Ukraine has relied on for years to counter Moscow's attacks. Trump has maintained that he didn't make the call, while also saying Musk should not be blamed. Vice President JD Vance has hinted at White House coordination with Musk, while Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth have denied any administration involvement. Meanwhile, a man was killed and two others wounded in a missile attack on the city of Lozova in Ukraine's Kharkiv region, local officials said Saturday. Moscow-installed authorities in cities across Russia-occupied Crimea reported power blackouts Saturday following overnight Ukrainian attacks. Ukraine's General Staff said Saturday that its forces hit a chemical plant in the Russian city of Tolyatti, which produces materials used in rocket fuel. Tolyatti Mayor Ilya Sukhikh said the overnight attack damaged industrial facilities in the city. Ukrainian forces also hit an electronics plant in the city of Oryol, Ukraine's General Staff confirmed Saturday. Local officials in Oryol said Saturday that three people were killed in Friday's attack. The General Staff said the plant makes components for the cruise and ballistic missiles Russia fires at Ukrainian cities. Morton reported from London. Watch as fire engulfs Hitler's mountaintop Eagle's Nest retreat
Adolf Hitler's Alpine mountain retreat, known as the Eagle's Nest, was engulfed in flames on Friday night while police arrested a 33-year-old male suspect.
The residence, called the Kehlsteinhaus, is above the town of Berchtesgaden. It was one of several buildings in the area used by the Nazi dictator and his entourage during World War Two.
Hitler also used the area as a backdrop for propaganda films portraying him as a lover of animals and nature.
Local media reported that site had been "largely destroyed", with the public urged to avoid the area.

In a memo sent Friday to Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said his teams "have received intelligence that Iran has substantially increased efforts to target U.S. personnel." "The lethal plotting efforts by the Iranians against U.S. citizens have reached advanced stages in both the Middle East and certain other countries," Clayton wrote. The memo was obtained by The Associated Press and reported earlier by Axios. Three U.S. officials, speaking on condition of anonymity due to the sensitivity of the matter, confirmed that the memo was sent to Rubio in his capacity as secretary of state and national security adviser. The memo emerged shortly after the State Department announced it is reducing staff at the U.S. embassies in Jordan, Lebanon, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates. The three officials said the threats from Iran and Yemen's Iranian-backed Houthi rebels are related to the staffing changes. WATCH: Trump at GOP rally in Florida revives idea of military intervention in Cuba after Iran The embassies involved are all under what is known as "restricted operations" status that has already reduced the size of their personnel footprints. The embassies will remain open. However, unlike in Saudi Arabia, where nonessential U.S. personnel and their families were ordered Wednesday to leave the country, staff in the other four countries are not compelled to depart. In announcing the staffing drawdowns this week, the State Department pointed specifically to increased threats from Yemen's Houthi rebels and did not mention threats to U.S. personnel directly from Iran. There has been a resurgence of fighting between a Saudi-led coalition and the Houthis, with the militant group launching missile and drone strikes against Saudi Arabia. U.S. officials have adamantly denied the drawdowns are tied to any potential new U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran. The unpopular war has spiked energy costs for Americans and posed political problems for President Donald Trump and Republicans, who are trying to keep control of Congress in the Nov. 3 midterm elections. Trump, speaking at a rally Friday in Florida, touted the U.S. military operations in Iran, which were dubbed "Operation Epic Fury," and said that "we may do another little Epic Fury, or they'll agree. If they're smart, they'll just say, 'Let's get down to business.'" Mediators have been trying to bring Washington and Tehran back to formal talks as the war has reached a stalemate. According to Iranian state television, the Revolutionary Guard navy this week again threatened to strike U.S. military bases in the region if the United States keeps helping guide commercial ships through the Strait of Hormuz, a critical waterway for the global energy trade. "Any further escalation around the Strait of Hormuz or elsewhere in the region will put civilian lives and the well-being of all regional states and the global economy at great risk," Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi wrote in an opinion column in the Financial Times this week. d40de761d73b.text: By — Safiyah Riddle, Associated Press Safiyah Riddle, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/doj-orders-some-california-counties-to-set-aside-ballots-from-suspected-noncitizens Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter DOJ orders some California counties to set aside ballots from suspected noncitizens Politics Oct 24, 2026 10:49 AM EDT LOS ANGELES (AP) — Federal prosecutors sent letters to county registrars across California on Friday demanding that local officials set aside and verify ballots that the Department of Justice said may belong to noncitizens, according to the Los Angeles County registrar and a letter obtained by The Associated Press. The letters are the latest escalation in a legal battle between California and President Donald Trump's Department of Justice, which has recently focused on the state in its efforts to root out noncitizen voting ahead of the midterm elections. Data shows illegal voting by people who aren't U.S. citizens is incredibly rare, difficult to prove and has not been shown to change the outcome of races. READ MORE: DOJ has monitored elections for decades. Here's why some state officials are concerned this year Earlier this month, the federal government targeted Los Angeles County and the California Secretary of State's office in a lawsuit that aimed to block them from counting the votes of roughly 20,000 people who are "likely" noncitizen voters. A hearing on the case is scheduled for Tuesday. The Trump administration asked the 9th Circuit court of appeals to rule on the lawsuit barring a decision from the district judge assigned to the case. They set a deadline for Saturday. Now, according to the LA County registrar's office, at least 18 counties across the state have received similar letters. They have been given a 48 hour deadline to provide identifying information corresponding with ballots that the federal government believes were sent to noncitizens illegally registered to vote. The letter requests that county officials also sequester any ballots where citizenship cannot be verified. "Any election official who knowingly processes the ballot of a noncitizen is opening themselves to legal jeopardy," said First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli. The Justice Department is asking counties to send information about the voters it suspects are noncitizens including social security numbers, ID information, a copy of their registration and more. WATCH: Examining the DOJ's effort to prosecute non-citizens accused of voting That information can help the government and state quickly assess each person suspected of illegally registering to vote, said the letter sent to San Bernardino County voting officials. The letter says the government's list of suspected noncitizen voters includes 1,133 people from the inland Southern California county. California's secretary of state and the Los Angeles County registrar have opposed the federal government's demands. In legal filings, lawyers for California say the request threatens to delay the certification of the vote and undermine the legitimacy of the November midterms. They have also argued that the federal government's data is unreliable and that their demands risk disenfranchisement of citizens. Voting is underway in California, with the state's more than 23 million registered voters receiving ballots in the mail earlier this month. The state said in legal filings that over 330,000 mail-in ballots have already been counted. The letters on Friday came on the heels of statewide sweep by federal authorities earlier in the week, where 28 people from the list of 20,000 were charged with illegally registering to vote. Some were also charged with illegally voting and lying on naturalization paperwork. Those charges could lead to years in prison. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Vanessa Trump, the former wife of Donald Trump Jr, has announced that she is cancer-free following her breast cancer diagnosis earlier this year.
Trump, 48, who has five children with President Donald Trump's eldest son, shared in a short video on her 19-year-old daughter Kai's Instagram account that her recent tests results "came back clear, so I'm finally cancer-free".
The video, posted on Friday, teases the release of a longer YouTube video to come on Saturday, in which Vanessa and Kai Trump will discuss breast cancer awareness and prevention, Kai wrote in the caption.
Vanessa Trump separated from Trump Jr in 2018 and announced last year that she had begun dating US pro golfer Tiger Woods.
"October is Breast Cancer Awareness Month, a time to raise awareness about early detection, education, and support for those affected by breast cancer," Kai Trump wrote on Instagram.
"I sat down with my mom and Dr. Nicole Saphier to talk about my mom's journey with breast cancer and learn more about prevention and early detection," she continued.
Kai's post received over 20,000 likes and hundreds of comments from people offering support and well wishes, including from American singer and media personality Mary Millben.
In Friday's video, Trump said she was first diagnosed with breast cancer in April. She publicly announced the diagnosis in May, saying in a social media post that she had undergone surgery and was working on a treatment plan with her medical team.
According to the American Cancer Society, the average risk of a woman in the US developing breast cancer is about 1 in 8, or 13%. The disease also accounts for 30% of all new female cancers every year, according to the group.
Surgery cures most breast cancers, but if some disease remains, chemotherapy, radiotherapy and endocrine therapy can reduce the long-term risk.
Treatments have been advancing, including more targeted therapies for early breast cancer, new types of hormonal therapies, and more precise and effective radiotherapy.

READ MORE: North Korea threatens to restart propaganda loudspeaker broadcasts and deploy more weapons at South Korea border Kim's visit to China is his latest move in an increasingly assertive foreign policy as he seeks to align Pyongyang with Beijing and Moscow in a united front against the United States under what he portrays as a "new Cold War." It's his first visit in a year. Kim arrived in the Chinese border city of Dandong Saturday after crossing the newly opened bridge, according to South Korea's Unification Ministry, which handles affairs related to North Korea, and China's official Xinhua News Agency. Both sides promised to strengthen cooperation He met with Wang Huning, a member of the Standing Committee of China's Communist Party. The two toured a car factory, and promised to strengthen the bilateral relationship. Kim said his country "stands ready to work with China to carry forward their historical friendship and expand practical cooperation, thereby delivering tangible benefits to the peoples of both countries," Xinhua said. Wang then accompanied Kim to the bridge to send him off, according to Xinhua. North Korean state media did not immediately report on Kim's visit. New bridge was built to help expand trade between the countries Experts said the opening of the New Yalu River Bridge this month was a key symbol of strengthening ties between North Korea and China and reflected their intent to expand trade, as it is expected to accommodate two-way traffic around the clock, including container shipments and heavy cargo trucks. Kim has recently sought to strengthen ties with China, the North's traditional main ally and economic lifeline, after years of prioritizing ties with Russia. He sent thousands of troops and conventional weapons to support President Vladimir Putin's war in Ukraine, possibly in exchange for military and economic assistance. Kim's visit timed to key battle anniversary in Korean War with China Kim's latest visit to China is his sixth since taking power in late 2011 following the death of his father. The visit appears to be timed to underscore the strength of his ties with Beijing ahead of the Oct. 25 anniversary of China's first major victory in the Korean War, which was days after Chinese troops crossed the Yalu River into North Korea in October 1950. The war began with North Korea's surprise attack on the South in June 1950, prompting a U.N.-led coalition headed by the United States to intervene and push back the offensive. North Korea was backed primarily by Chinese forces, with assistance from the then-Soviet Union's air force, before fighting ended with a 1953 armistice that left the peninsula technically at war. Kim said his visit on Saturday was also to memorialize those killed in the war, according to Xinhua. Chinese President Xi Jinping traveled to Pyongyang in June for a meeting with Kim. During their summit, Xi expressed Beijing's willingness to expand bilateral cooperation in trade, agriculture, construction and technology, while Kim described ties with China as a top strategic priority. READ MORE: In a relatively mild speech, North Korea uses UN platform to lament 'mutual distrust' and tension Kim last visited Beijing in September 2025, when he met with Xi and watched a military parade alongside Putin and other foreign leaders. Kim has maintained a hard line toward Seoul and has so far rebuffed a proposal from U.S. President Donald Trump to revive their diplomacy, which broke down in 2019 during Trump's first term. Kim's government has called for Washington to abandon its "hostile policy" and drop demands for the North's denuclearization as a precondition for renewed talks. South Korea's liberal government, which favors engagement with the North, hopes renewed talks between Washington and Pyongyang will thaw inter-Korean relations, and has also urged China to play a "constructive" role in resolving the standoff. Seoul's spy agency told lawmakers last month that it saw a 50% possibility of a meeting between Trump and Kim on the sidelines of next month's Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation, or APEC, summit in Shenzhen, China. "From Seoul's perspective, if North Korea focuses more on economic development than military buildup and threats, that would be positive for diplomacy and security," said Leif-Eric Easley, a professor at Ewha University in Seoul. "But if Kim can extract ever more benefits from China and Russia, it is unclear what Seoul could offer that would be worth the political risks Pyongyang attaches to exchanges with a more prosperous, globalized, and free Korea." Wu reported from Bangkok. AP video journalist Mayuko Ono in Tokyo contributed to this report. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. 4852e8a86e6c.text: President Trump has endorsed Benjamin Netanyahu in Tuesday's Israeli election, but some of his advisers see opportunity for his Middle East agenda in a government led by someone else, U.S. officials tell Axios. Why it matters: Trump has never worked with an Israeli prime minister other than Netanyahu, and doesn't personally know any of the other candidates. The two have forged a close but often turbulent relationship. "He's the devil he knows," one Trump adviser said, describing the president's view of Netanyahu. Driving the news: After weeks of hesitation, Trump endorsed Netanyahu on Sunday — and even suggested his defeat would have consequences for U.S.-Israel relations. One U.S. official described the endorsement as a win-win for Trump, regardless of the outcome. If Netanyahu wins — or remains in power as caretaker prime minister — Trump could claim credit for rescuing him politically and use that leverage to press for concessions. If Netanyahu loses and his opponents form a government, Israel's new leaders would still have every incentive to cultivate good relations with Trump. His endorsement of their rival would quickly become a footnote. Behind the scenes: Many of Trump's closest advisers opposed his decision to endorse Netanyahu, believing the president should stay out of the Israeli election, according to sources familiar with the discussions. Vice President Vance notably declined to follow Trump's lead when asked about the election this week, amid growing hostility toward Netanyahu in parts of the MAGA movement. "I'm not attacking Bibi Netanyahu. I'm not endorsing Bibi Netanyahu. I think the president's endorsement is ultimately what matters," Vance told reporters. Zoom in: Vance, who endorsed former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán days before his election defeat in April , said he would no longer get involved in foreign elections. The vice president is among the senior Trump officials who became disillusioned with Netanyahu during the war with Iran, according to sources familiar with their thinking. Vance and other top aides believe Netanyahu's pre-war assessments to the White House were mistaken, deepening questions about whether he remains the best partner for achieving Trump's regional ambitions. The big picture: Once the Israeli election and U.S. midterms are over, Trump will face a defining choice for his Middle East agenda: whether to join Netanyahu in another major military operation against Iran. Netanyahu is eager to move forward. But the election results could influence Trump's decision, or at least the timing of any renewed large-scale fighting. Trump also wants to move beyond the Iran war and pursue an ambitious diplomatic agenda that includes implementing his Gaza peace plan , brokering deals between Israel and Lebanon and Syria , and ultimately securing a historic Israeli-Saudi peace agreement . Whether Trump can make progress on those goals will depend in part on who governs Israel — and what kind of coalition emerges from Tuesday's vote. The intrigue: Behind the scenes over the last six months, several of Trump's top advisers have grown dissatisfied with Netanyahu on key regional priorities. Gaza: Trump's envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner have expressed frustration with Netanyahu's reluctance to advance implementation of the president's peace plan. Syria: Trump's envoy Tom Barrack has similar concerns about the Netanyahu government's approach to Damascus and continued Israeli military operations in Syria. Lebanon and the West Bank: Secretary of State Marco Rubio and his team have a better relationship with Netanyahu, but believe Israel could do more to strengthen Lebanon's government. They are also frustrated by Netanyahu's failure to do more to curb settler attacks on Palestinians in the West Bank. Between the lines: Some U.S. officials say a new Israeli government without Netanyahu's far-right coalition partners could be easier to work with. White House deputy press secretary Anna Kelly declined to comment, referring Axios to Trump's endorsement of Netanyahu on Truth Social . State of play: Three major Israeli television networks released their final pre-election polls Friday, all showing Netanyahu's coalition falling well short of a parliamentary majority. All three projected just 50 seats for Netanyahu's bloc in the 120-member Knesset — 17 fewer than his current coalition holds. His Likud party, which currently holds 32 seats, was projected to win just 20. The polls gave former military chief Gadi Eisenkot's opposition bloc between 52 and 56 seats, with another 14 to 16 going to two Arab Israeli parties. Channel 11 also projected four seats for a reservists party unaffiliated with either bloc. Pro-Netanyahu Channel 14 was the major outlier, projecting 60 seats for his bloc and 30 for Likud in a poll earlier this week. What to watch: The polls point to a potential political deadlock: Neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot appears to have a clear path to the 61 seats needed to form a government. Eisenkot would need to bring Arab Israeli parties into his coalition, which he has ruled out, or form a minority government with their outside support — an arrangement some of his potential partners oppose. A unity government between Netanyahu and his rivals is considered highly unlikely. If neither side can assemble a governing majority, Israel could face another election, with Netanyahu remaining in power as caretaker prime minister. The bottom line: Rather than ushering in a new government more receptive to Trump's agenda, Tuesday's election could leave the president dealing with a weakened Netanyahu and an Israeli political system consumed by another prolonged crisis.

Iran has "substantially increased efforts to target US personnel" in the Middle East and other areas, the US national intelligence director has warned in a memo seen by the BBC.
Jay Clayton's assessment come as the US State Department makes adjustments to staffing at diplomatic posts in the region, including the ordered departure earlier this week of non-emergency US embassy staff from Saudi Arabia.
The order came in response to escalating attacks by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis against Saudi Arabia in the past month.
Clayton's memo was marked unclassified and sent to US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Friday.
It said: "The lethal plotting efforts by the Iranians against US citizens have reached advanced stages in both the Middle East and certain other countries."
Clayton said he was making every effort to downgrade as much intelligence as possible so Rubio could share it with US State Department personnel.
A US official told the BBC: "When it comes to our staffing at embassies, we constantly evaluate new information about the security environment.
"The threat of Houthi attacks and of Iranian terror plots targeting US officials are informing our decisions on staffing adjustments for embassies on [Restricted Operations] Status in the region."
At least 21 people have now been killed in Houthi attacks on Saudi airports since the start of October, according to Saudi authorities.
One missile strike on Riyadh's international airport on 10 October killed 13 people and injured 308 others â the deadliest attack in Saudi Arabia in more than a decade.
The Houthis say the attacks on Saudi Arabia are in retaliation to what they call a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport they blame on the kingdom.
Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.
A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks. Some 155 civilians have been killed in Yemen since, according to the Houthi-run health ministry.
This particular conflict has re-emerged on the backdrop of a wider conflict in the Middle East.
The US and Israel launched an air campaign against Iran in February, killing its leader and prompting the regime in Tehran to retaliate with strikes on US allies across the region and the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, through which around a fifth of the world's oil and gas usually travels.
In June, the US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait, but it collapsed within weeks after the Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade.
The situation in the Strait of Hormuz has seen oil prices surge, exacerbated by the Houthis' "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia.

a98bb2af1667.text: By — Bill Barrow, Associated Press Bill Barrow, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/republican-billionaire-rick-jackson-is-walking-a-trump-tightrope-in-his-quest-to-lead-georgia Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Republican billionaire Rick Jackson is walking a Trump tightrope in his quest to lead Georgia Politics Oct 24, 2026 3:04 PM EDT ATLANTA (AP) — He's hardly the first billionaire to promise working-class voters he'll fight for them in public office. Rick Jackson, the Republican candidate for Georgia governor, has even compared himself to the real estate mogul who reached the Oval Office. But Jackson's path differs from Donald Trump's, and the 72-year-old healthcare magnate and investor brings a vastly different persona to his first campaign. Unlike Trump, who was born to wealth, Jackson spent his early years bouncing through foster homes before launching his first company as a young man. Now, he wants to leverage both his similarities and contrasts with the president, a challenge he's tackling with buckets of his own campaign cash and a personal story that anchors his appeal to voters. Please check your inbox to confirm. "I have lived in poverty," Jackson says. "When you have not eaten, you never forget that, and you don't forget the people that are struggling." Democratic nominee Keisha Lance Bottoms, a former Atlanta mayor, disputes Jackson's altruistic pitch, setting up the Nov. 3 election as a test of whether an alternate, softer version of conservative billionaire politics can complement or even counter Trump's pugilistic populism in a key swing state. Jackson planned to join Trump at a rally Saturday in Perry, in what would be his second appearance with the president in the closing stretch of the campaign. 'From foster care to billionaire' "My father left me at nine months old. My mother was a sixth-grade educated waitress with a severe alcohol problem," Jackson said in the only debate of their general election campaign. "I had seven stepfathers before I was 12. I lived in the projects, went to 13 different schools, and lived in five different foster homes." He left college to start a business at 21. That led to Jackson Healthcare, a behemoth company that provides contract nurses and other workers to hospitals and health systems, including public entities that have helped fuel Jackson's fortunes with taxpayer money. At events with supporters, Jackson gets more personal. "I have, because of my background, severe abandonment issues," he told hundreds of voters in Cleveland, a conservative enclave in the north Georgia mountains. He turns that acknowledgment into a promise: "Let me tell you one thing: I will never abandon you." READ MORE: Trump will rally Georgia Republicans despite party divisions in battleground state Rags-to-riches themes are not uncommon in politics, and it's yielded Jackson's campaign motto: "From foster care to billionaire." But the scale is eye-popping, illuminated by the nearly $200 million Jackson has spent personally on the campaign. That puts him among the largest self-funding candidates in the history of American elections. But on that score, too, Jackson tries to soften the caricature of the billionaire executive. "It's not my money," he said in a northern suburb of Atlanta. Jackson calls his fortune "God's money" and says that "my job is to have kingdom impact" with it. "The reason I have spent so much money to do this," he said, is to "help 11 million Georgians, to keep them from struggling." A range of images over a long campaign Jackson launched his bid as a relative unknown, though Capitol insiders knew him because of Jackson Healthcare, its lucrative state contracts and his lobbying interest in healthcare, business and tax policy. The Republican primary field featured a trio of statewide elected officials, including Lt. Gov. Burt Jones, who won Trump's endorsement in August 2025, before Jackson got in. During the primary, Jackson embraced the president even though he wasn't Trump's choice. Jackson sometimes promised to "be like Trump, but with Southern tone." He pledged to "deliver for Georgia the same type of business solutions that President Trump is bringing to our country." Largely aligning himself with Trump on immigration, Jackson promised to make Georgia a national leader in deportations. "I don't care if you're Muslim or Mongolian, you don't have the right to force your culture on our country," he said in one ad. "Criminal illegals" who "commit sick, violent crimes" would "end up deported or departed," he promised. Soon after defeating Jones in a runoff, Jackson shelved the immigration ad, but not before using it as part of a spot featuring his grandchildren. "Granddad, why do you look so mean in these ads?" one asks after watching the "deported or departed" clip on her phone. The children and teenagers then tell their grandfather how he can "look cool" with a pickup truck, a dog and a hipper wardrobe. "Let's make Georgia better together," the redressed Jackson concludes. He has since circulated an ad with several young adults who benefited from the millions he spent helping foster children who age out of the Georgia system when they turn 18. "I am so proud of you," he tells them as he chokes up. On policy, Republican fare and centrist appeals As he softens his image, Jackson maintains traditional Republican positions, pledging to cut taxes, regulation and what he describes as waste. If he cannot halve the state income tax in four years, he promises not to seek a second term. 6edf0296fbfb.text: By — Philip Marcelo, Associated Press Philip Marcelo, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/new-york-state-woman-charged-with-voting-illegally-says-she-recently-learned-she-wasnt-a-citizen Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter New York state woman charged with voting illegally says she recently learned she wasn't a citizen Politics Oct 24, 2026 2:07 PM EDT An upstate New York woman who says she only recently learned she wasn't born in the U.S. has been charged with voting illegally, one of the latest arrests touted by the Trump administration as it hunts for noncitizen voters ahead of the midterm elections. Marva Cook was adopted as a toddler and had always assumed she was a U.S. citizen, she told Homeland Security investigators earlier this month, according to the criminal complaint. READ MORE: DOJ orders some California counties to set aside ballots from suspected noncitizens But in searching for her biological mother, the 66-year-old Syracuse resident, who starred on Syracuse University's women's basketball team decades ago, said she discovered she had a German birth certificate. Federal prosecutors say Cook has had a green card for several years now, but she still cast ballots in recent elections despite not having citizenship. She faces a single federal charge of voting by an alien stemming from her vote in the 2022 midterms. The misdemeanor offense carries a maximum sentence of one year in prison and a fine up to $100,000, if convicted. Cook can also face deportation, under federal law. Cook says she has faith in God and support from community Reached by phone Friday, Cook declined to discuss the criminal case, her voting record or her past efforts at becoming a citizen. But she said she was "not thrilled" by her court appearance Wednesday as she was placed in shackles despite having voluntarily turned herself in just hours earlier. "It was a difficult time," Cook said. "I'm about kindness and service and doing for others as I want to be treated." WATCH: Examining the DOJ's effort to prosecute non-citizens accused of voting She also said she appreciated the outpouring of support of community members, a number of whom accompanied her to court Wednesday. "The prayers and the support is a big part of how I will get through this," Cook said. "I have a deep faith that God will get me through it." Cook's lawyer, Paul Tuck, also declined to discuss details of the criminal case Friday other than to say there are no upcoming hearings or filing deadlines. There are no pending immigration proceedings, he added, but Cook has an immigration lawyer in the event that changes. Spokespersons for the U.S. Department of Homeland Security and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement didn't immediately respond to emails seeking comment. Cook is latest arrest in Trump's nationwide crackdown on noncitizen voting First Assistant U.S. Attorney John A. Sarcone III, whose upstate New York office is prosecuting the case, said Cook's arrest showed "voter fraud is rampant" in the state. Other federal agencies amplified the statement on social media, even as the administration's own investigations have demonstrated that such instances are incredibly rare and been shown not to change the outcome of elections. "We cannot and will not allow the votes of American citizens to be canceled out by noncitizens illegally voting in our elections," the Homeland Security wrote in a post on X that included Sarcone's statement. In California, federal authorities on Monday charged more than two dozen legal permanent residents with illegally casting ballots or registering to vote. Weeks earlier, 10 people were charged in Minnesota with illegally voting over the last three elections. Supporters say Cook is a valuable member of the community Cook's supporters, meanwhile, described her as a vital part of the local community where she had lived nearly all of her life and had starred in college basketball. The Syracuse University athletics department confirmed Cook was the team's leading scorer in the 1979-80 season, averaging 15 points per game. She also holds the school record for most steals in a single season. READ MORE: DOJ has monitored elections for decades. Here's why some state officials are concerned this year Fred Daley, pastor at All Saints Church, said Cook is an active member of the parish who for years has been the church's go-to Easter Bunny, decked out in full costume during the spring holiday season. "If the government wanted to make a case, they chose the wrong person," he said. "She's a poster child of an amazing person. She's highly respected throughout the community." Dale Avers, a parishioner who has known Cook for almost 20 years, described her as a "person of service" who "never sought limelight." She said Cook supports low-income families and youth as the YMCA's community school program director. "I'm in total shock that they're putting this much effort into this," Avers said. "They understood the story. There was no intent. There's no malice. There was no deception involved." A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. 9b0bd02376f3.text: By — Russ Bynum, Associated Press Russ Bynum, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/six-flags-says-it-will-install-seat-belts-on-georgia-roller-coaster-after-riders-death Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Six Flags says it will install seat belts on Georgia roller coaster after rider's death Nation Oct 24, 2026 1:32 PM EDT The chief executive of Six Flags says the company will install seat belts on the Georgia roller coaster from which a rider fell to his death earlier this month. The company's rides with similar restraints will also get the safety upgrade. The theme park operator announced the extra safeguard less than two weeks after 42-year-old Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem of Atlanta died after being ejected from his seat on the Goliath coaster at Six Flags Over Georgia. READ MORE: More roller coasters shut down as authorities investigate fatal fall at Georgia amusement park "We are reinforcing safety precautions at our parks and taking additional measures, including adding seat belts on Goliath and other coasters with a similar restraint," John Reilly, president and CEO of Six Flags Entertainment Corporation, said in a statement Friday. Goliath remains shut down while state and local officials investigate the Oct. 12 death. Reilly didn't specify which other Six Flags coasters will get seat belts. But it has temporarily closed eight additional roller coasters at five other parks in the U.S. and Canada. Those rides all share the same manufacturer and a similar restraint system. Six Flags hasn't said when those coasters are expected to reopen. Reilly's statement said Six Flags has enlisted independent engineers and inspectors to review safety procedures for all rides at its theme parks. Investigators haven't said what went wrong on the Georgia coaster. Witnesses said they saw Kariem rise up out of his seat and fall headfirst back into the cart before being ejected. Some people who rode Goliath before him that day said they had concerns about its restraints. All nine of the Six Flags coasters taken offline were manufactured by the Swiss company Bolliger & Mabillard. They also feature similar clamshell restraints that sit at the top of a vertical bar between each rider's knees. The bar locks a padded restraint into place over the rider's lap and upper legs. The U.S. patent granted to Bolliger & Mabillard for the restraint system in 2001 says it's designed to make each rider feel "that he is seated on a flying carpet or that he is at the controls of a kind of flying scooter, while still guaranteeing optimum security." Following the death in Georgia, non-Six Flags theme parks SeaWorld Orlando in Florida and La Ronde in Montreal, Canada, also temporarily closed one roller coaster apiece that use clamshell restraints. SeaWorld reopened its Mako coaster Tuesday after it had been offline for a week. The Associated Press emailed the company Saturday asking if seat belts or other safety upgrades were planned for the coaster. The AP also emailed a spokesperson for La Ronde seeking an update on its shuttered coaster. In addition to Goliath in Georgia, eight coasters remain closed at Six Flags parks in Gurnee, Illinois; Jackson Township, New Jersey; Charlotte, North Carolina; Mason, Ohio; and Vaughan, Ontario. Bynum reported from Savannah, Georgia. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. The Israeli military has launched a sweeping crackdown in the occupied West Bank, demolishing homes and businesses in the city of Hebron and displacing hundreds of families, according to local officials.
Footage shared online showed destruction caused by Israeli bulldozers, with at least one whole street appearing to have been flattened. The military has also cordoned off the city, heavily restricting the movement of its 200,000 residents.
The operation was announced by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Friday, in response to the killing of two Israeli soldiers by two Palestinian gunmen in an attack on a checkpoint. Three other Israeli soldiers were injured, and the gunmen were also killed.
Netanyahu said on Friday that buildings around the site of the attack and the neighbourhoods that the two gunmen were from would be "destroyed".
Hebron's Mayor Youssef al-Jaabari said more than 1,000 people had been displaced by the operation, which centred on the Ein Deir Baha and Farsh al-Hawa neighbourhoods, and targeted homes, businesses, industrial sites and infrastructure.
He said dozens of families had been forced to spend the night outside, with some told to leave without taking their vehicles, while homes were marked for demolition with spray paint.
He added that he believed the military planned to displace a total of 2,500 people from about 0.35 sq km of urban land. The city's governor and deputy mayor meanwhile said at least 200 families had been displaced.
The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) did not respond immediately to the BBC's request for comment. It said in a statement on social media that it had dozens of targets across the West Bank and that its operations would last for several days.
1 of 3
It is common practice for Israeli forces to demolish the homes of Palestinians who are suspected of carrying out attacks on Israelis in the West Bank - a practice Israeli rights groups have criticised as collective punishment.
Netanyahu likened the operation to previous operations in Palestinian refugee camps in the north of the territory, when the Israeli military demolished hundreds of homes and displaced tens of thousands in 2025.
Friday's shooting came during a tense time for the region, with Israel's general election taking place in four days' time.
Netanyahu - who has built his campaign on the promise of security - cancelled his party's campaign events for Friday morning and headed to Hebron, wearing protective armour and posting a video on social media from the scene.
"We will evacuate the residents, go house to house, remove the weapons we find there, and deal with and destroy all terrorist infrastructure," he said.
He also announced he had reviewed plans for the largest military operation in the West Bank since 1967 - though did not say when it could be carried out. It is not clear whether the ongoing Hebron operation forms part of that.
In an interview with Israel's i24 television channel released on Saturday, he threatened "a very big surprise" for the Palestinian Authority (PA), which governs parts of the territory.
In a statement, the PA called for "urgent international action that went beyond condemnation" to prevent further forced displacement.
Meanwhile, his far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich called for Israel to launch a campaign in the West Bank "exactly like in Gaza or Lebanon," while far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir called for Israel to dismantle the PA.
Speaking to journalists, Hebron's mayor said the operation was "driven by the elections," and that Netanyahu and his ministers were attempting to secure the votes of the far-right and the settlers.

b9d4dd1dedd8.text: By — Thomas Adamson, Associated Press Thomas Adamson, Associated Press By — John Leicester, Associated Press John Leicester, Associated Press By — Tom Nouvian, Associated Press Tom Nouvian, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/more-than-400000-protest-across-france-challenging-macron-as-paris-clashes-erupt Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter More than 400,000 protest across France, challenging Macron as Paris clashes erupt World Updated on Oct 24, 2026 2:48 PM EDT — Published on Oct 24, 2026 12:51 PM EDT PARIS (AP) — Clashes erupted in Paris as a mass march drew to a close Saturday, with more than 400,000 people rallying across France over school funding and soaring living costs in a fresh challenge to President Emmanuel Macron. Police made nearly 1,000 arrests, the government said. The Paris march began peacefully, a week after widespread rioting and looting during protests across the country. But near the demonstration's endpoint in eastern Paris, masked protesters hurled objects and fireworks at police, who answered with clouds of tear gas, deafening sound grenades and jets of water cannons. READ MORE: From France to Albania, how social unrest is fueling protests across Europe Officers with megaphones urged protesters to disperse. Some demonstrators panicked as tear-gas canisters landed in their midst, scattering with screams. Veteran protesters shouted after them: "Don't run!" The Interior Ministry put nationwide turnout at 410,000 — fewer than the 550,000 it said protested last weekend — while the CGT union that helped organize some of Saturday's protests estimated nearly 800,000. The ministry's estimate included 110,000 in Paris, where authorities confined the march to the city's southeastern edge, away from the center. The CGT put the number of protesters in Paris at 250,000. Unrest is challenging Macron's final months in power More than a month of unrest that started with protests in high schools for more funding and teachers is testing Macron's authority in the final months of his presidency before voters choose his successor in May. The stakes are high: The far-right National Rally party has accused his government of failing to protect the public and urged people to channel their anger into votes for its candidate Marine Le Pen. On the far left, presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon has backed demonstrators and criticized policing that has left some teenage protesters with life-changing injuries. As dusk fell Saturday, violence erupted at the end of some of the 289 protests counted by the Interior Ministry nationwide. Street fires burned in the cities of Marseille and Lyon. Police used tear gas in Lyon, Clermont-Ferrand, Strasbourg and Bordeaux and water cannons in Nice and Nantes, French media reported. In Nice, far-right extremists fought with demonstrators downtown and 11 people were arrested, regional authorities said. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said police made nearly 1,000 arrests but added that the number is expected to increase significantly as more are counted. Nuñez said beefed-up policing, with 70,000 officers backed by helicopters, armored vehicles and other support, helped prevent a repeat of widespread looting and damage to shops the previous weekend. A small protest became a national movement Protesters attend an authorised demonstration organised by labour unions in Paris as part of nationwide protests called by the "Yellow Vests" movement joined by French high school and university students against the cost of living and rising fuel prices, in France, on Oct. 24, 2026. Photo by Abdul Saboor/Reuters What began last month as a protest over staff shortages at one high school southeast of Paris spread nationwide, drawing students demanding more funding for education and workers seeking help with soaring costs for fuel and other necessities. In Paris, Bénédicte Pittion, a 46-year-old teacher, marched with her 16-year-old daughter, Garance, a high school student — in their first protest together. "The young people who have been demonstrating have not been heard, and as a parent and as a teacher, I stand with them," Pittion said. Garance said she'd been "really scared" after seeing the previous weekend's violence, but felt that staying away would hand the government a victory. Macron met high school representatives Friday. They said he had promised to overhaul university admissions, but they called for protests to continue until concrete measures are announced. Some protests have been banned Soumaya Abed, a 58-year-old nurse wearing a red CGT union vest, complained that authorities in Paris wanted to stifle protesters by making them march on the capital's outskirts, keeping them away from the center where the Louvre and other major museums closed exceptionally. "But it won't stop the movement. It won't stop students from demanding better conditions in schools," she said. aa9d77c86d24.text: By — Nicholas Riccardi, Associated Press Nicholas Riccardi, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/whats-going-on-with-dan-sullivan-and-dan-sullivan-the-alaska-senate-litigation-explained Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter What's going on with Dan Sullivan and Dan Sullivan? The Alaska Senate litigation, explained Politics Oct 24, 2026 12:36 PM EDT President Donald Trump's administration has taken its first step to block the results of a midterm election, and it's all about the fact that there are two Dan Sullivans on the Alaska Senate ballot. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. One of them is a Republican senator and ally of the president. The other is a retired schoolteacher whom Republicans accuse of being a Democratic plant to siphon away votes. Trump said Friday that he directed the Justice Department to file its lawsuit. What is going on? Here's an explanation: Why is there a lawsuit over this? The campaign is likely to be decided by only a few thousand votes, and it could determine which party controls the Senate. So the stakes are high, and Republicans worry that voters will get confused and accidentally vote for the wrong Sullivan. That's why Republicans have been trying to get the second Dan Sullivan — hereafter known as Daniel J. Sullivan — thrown off the ballot for months. The lawsuit went all the way to the Alaska Supreme Court, but Republicans lost. Republicans think the presence of Daniel J. Sullivan is a Democratic dirty trick. But Daniel J. Sullivan, who lives in the tiny fishing community of Petersburg, says he is running of his own accord. WATCH: Trump says he ordered suit to block Alaska Senate results if GOP loses Alaskan voters will see "Dan S. Sullivan" identified as a "registered Republican" and "incumbent" on their ballots, while "Daniel J. Sullivan Jr." will not have a party affiliation. Former Rep. Mary Peltola is the Democratic candidate. So the Trump administration is filing in federal court to try to block certification of the election if its Dan Sullivan — the senator — loses. "Should Alaska certify any electoral results tainted by the inclusion on the ballot of Daniel J. Sullivan," the lawsuit said, "the State and its officers will fail in its obligation to protect the integrity of its election." Trump said of the lawsuit: "I'm the one who said do it." Will this work? Dan Sullivan, who has filed to run for U.S. Senate in Alaska, poses for a photo on June 26, 2026, in Petersburg, Alaska. Photo by Katie Holmlund/AP The lawsuit is essentially a placeholder and only becomes an issue after Election Day if the incumbent loses. Even if that happens, legal experts say it has no chance of success. The suit cites a clause in the preamble to the National Voter Registration Act that says states must "protect the integrity" of elections. It says that gives federal courts grounds to overturn elections which, under the U.S. Constitution, are entirely state affairs. But that vague turn of phrase probably isn't enough for any judge to try to overrule the will of the voters, experts say. Technically, the lawsuit only asks the court to block certification until an investigation determines whether enough voters were fooled by the two Sullivans to have swung the election. It doesn't explain how that would happen, which seems like a big issue given that votes are supposed to be confidential. Why does this matter? Dirty tricks and voter confusion are nothing new in American politics. In Ohio's Senate race, Republicans have been tied to an effort to boost a socialist on the ballot who would pull votes from the Democratic candidate challenging Sen. Jon Husted. What is new is that the Justice Department is trying to block an election result. Trump wanted the department to help him try to overturn his loss to Democratic President Joe Biden in 2020, but career attorneys stopped it. Now most of those career attorneys have been forced out and replaced by Trump loyalists. WATCH: How Alaska became a key battleground in the fight for the Senate The top Justice Department official who signed onto the lawsuit, Stanley Woodward, had previously served as a defense attorney for those prosecuted for the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the U.S. Capitol. There's been widespread concern that Trump will try to nullify the voters' will in November, which Attorney General Todd Blanche was asked about in Virginia on Thursday. He said he didn't want to rule out intervening in some sort of "doomsday" scenario but that "it is not DOJ's intention to, and it's never our intention to, improperly interfere with elections or the state certification process." Hours later the department filed its lawsuit over Alaska's certification process. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. Former President Barack Obama attacked the Trump administration over the Iran war and high consumer prices as he hit the campaign trail for Democrats ahead the US midterm elections.
On Saturday, the Democrat held a campaign rally in Ohio to stump for candidates Amy Acton and Sherrod Brown. Later, he will appear in Michigan to push for Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed.
Meanwhile, Donald Trump cast his early ballot in Florida, and later on Saturday will head to Georgia to hold a rally for Republican candidates.
Earlier voting has begun ahead of the 3 November elections, which will decide which party controls Congress for the rest of Trump's presidency.
Speaking on Saturday in Cleveland, Ohio, Obama targeted Trump and his cabinet members, and attacked the president for not lowering costs for American consumers while waging war against Iran.
"This election is our last best chance to at least rein in some of the foolishness of this administration," Obama said.
"This is a circuit breaker in the system. We need to flip that circuit breaker. We need to start bringing some accountability to this administration," the former president said.
He said he sympathised with voters who rejected Democrats in 2024 over economic and inflation concerns following the Covid pandemic.
But he said Trump has only himself to blame for the current state of the economy.
"If you thought everyone was too expensive before 'you know who'," he said, referring to Trump, "everything is more expensive now".
He also said that the war has given Iran "veto power" over the Strait of Hormuz, which was open to marine traffic before hostilities began in February.
When asked about the Iran war on Saturday afternoon, Trump said: "I've done it very effectively and I may have to finish it off, or maybe they'll make a deal, but I'm not sure. Either way, we win."
He and and First Lady Melania Trump were casting advance votes in Florida before leaving to Georgia.
Trump also told reporters "we will see" when asked if Melania Trump would visit Ukraine, after the White House said that she "successfully secured" a ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky.
The Republican president has faced significant pressure to lower oil prices, which have jumped due to the wars in Iran and Ukraine.
He recently struck a deal with Russia to export the country's diesel to the US, despite pushback from both Republican and Democratic lawmakers.
At his afternoon rally, Obama also took a swipe at Trump's efforts to renovate the White House.
"What's with all the gold? He's got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened up a Cheesecake Factory," Obama joked.
Obama's trip to Ohio was to show support for ex-Senator Sherrod Brown, who is running to unseat incumbent Republican Senator John Husted, and Amy Acton, who is running for state governor against Republican Vivek Ramaswamy.
In his remarks, Obama criticised Ramaswamy for a campaign ad released this week in which Acton's estranged mother was featured calling her a liar. The ad didn't mention that the woman's husband was charged with raping Acton when she was a child.
"In recent days, we've seen there is no line he will not cross. No low he will not sink to to try to get in the limelight," Obama said. "I mean, think about this latest ad he ran."
Acton also spoke at the campaign rally before Obama to argue that Ramaswamy "has chosen to exploit my childhood" to "save his struggling campaign".

Nearly 1,000 arrests were made as hundreds of thousands of people took part in another day of protests across France which were followed by some clashes late on Saturday, officials have said.
After a day of largely peaceful demonstrations, police fired tear gas and water cannon to disperse protesters in a number of cities including Paris, while barricades were set alight in Marseille and people ripped boards from a shop in Bordeaux.
But officials have so far managed to avoid rioting and looting on the scale seen last weekend, which resulted in some of the worst scenes of disorder in France's modern history.
The interior ministry said an estimated 410,000 people protested on Saturday, while the unions put the number at about 800,000.
Some 70,000 police officers were deployed and restrictions imposed in several cities to prevent the latest protests over the cost of living and poor school conditions from descending into the kind of chaos which saw officers outnumbered, hundreds of businesses looted and buildings torched.
President Emmanuel Macron had decreed earlier this week that only demonstrations organised by a recognised trade unions would be permitted. Hundreds of people have been jailed for vandalism, arson and looting after fast-track court hearings in recent days.
Clashes between protesters and riot police in Paris erupted at the end of a peaceful march from the city's Porte d'Italie towards Porte de Vincennes on Saturday, where the police operation included an elite unit that usually deals with organised crime and counter-terrorism.
Some protesters were seen erecting makeshift barricades and pelting officers with projectiles, while police baton-charged groups of masked youths who were smashing the windows of a car dealership.
French Interior Minister Laurent NuÃ±ez said that "several thousand radical activists gathered at the rear of the march, including around 500 individuals identified as rioters", the AFP news agency reported.
In the southern port of Marseille, rubbish bins were set ablaze and metal sheets used to block streets. A law enforcement vehicle was seen driving through a burning barricade in France's second-largest city.
Meanwhile, some protesters in dark clothing and face coverings were seen taking boards off a building to build a street barricade in the southern city of Bordeaux.
In Lyon, police used tear gas grenades to disperse a crowd which had reportedly gathered in an area deemed off-limits by the local prefecture.
"There were around 150 of us, mostly secondary school and university students. Then the tear gas came almost immediately. You could barely see anything in the street," said one protester in France's third-largest city.
NuÃ±ez said late in the day that nearly 1,000 people had been arrested, a number he said would increase.
The minister also said two people had been "seriously injured": one in the south-western city of Toulouse, and another one in Clermont-Ferrand, central France.
Earlier, a peaceful protester in Paris who gave her name as Zelie told the BBC people had taken to the streets because they were "really frustrated" and had been "suffering a lot" since Macron came to office.
"They keep us quiet. They take our money, they tax us a lot and we can't say anything. Today we are in the streets because it's been too long, it's been too much," the 26-year-old said.
Two masked teenage protesters, who did not want to give their names, also said their generation was in despair and felt abandoned by the government.
"I think looting is really not good," one of the demonstrators said of last Saturday's disorder. "But it's because of poverty and the violence of the police."
He added that the protests would end "when we have a response to our demands. We really want a change in France".
Meanwhile, some 13,000 people joined a rally against the hard-right National Rally party in the north-central city of OrlÃ©ans which proceeded peacefully.
Mass protests triggered by similar issues as in France also rocked several other European cities on Saturday.
In Albania's capital Tirana, riot police fired tear gas to disperse thousands of anti-government demonstrators, while clashes were also reported in Belgium's capital Brussels.
In Milan, northern Italy, a major security operation including hundreds of soldiers alongside police prevented protesters gathering in the city. Many had feared a repeat of violent scenes last week when some started fires, smashed windows and looted shops.
Around 550,000 people took part in last weekend's demonstrations against rising fuel prices and the cost of living, with frustrations escalating after weeks of student protests. The chaos which followed resulted in more than 2,500 arrests.
Marches were initially largely peaceful but became marred by scenes of violence, looting and destruction, with more than 2,000 shops and other businesses across France said to have been directly impacted. The damage was estimated "at hundreds of millions euros", France's Chambers of Commerce and Industry (CCI) said.
One demonstrator's hand was blown off by a police crowd-control grenade, according to the AFP news agency, while about 1,000 police officers were injured.
The French authorities later said they were forced to impose overnight curfews in Paris and other cities.
The continuing protests come ahead of France's presidential elections in six months' time, and leading contenders have levelled the blame at Macron and his ministers.

0e631ec3f992.text: By — Colleen Barry, Associated Press Colleen Barry, Associated Press By — Demetris Nellas, Associated Press Demetris Nellas, Associated Press By — Sylvia Hui, Associated Press Sylvia Hui, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/soldiers-guard-center-of-milan-as-thousands-of-protesters-march-in-cities-across-europe Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Soldiers guard center of Milan as thousands of protesters march in cities across Europe World Oct 24, 2026 3:50 PM EDT MILAN (AP) — Thousands of young people marched Saturday through the streets of several Italian cities, including Milan, Rome and Turin as authorities deployed large numbers of police and soldiers in a largely successful bid to stave off a repeat of the violent clashes and looting that marred similar protests last week. The demonstration in Milan remained peaceful, but there were brief clashes with police in both Rome and Turin. In Milan, thousands of young people marched the streets as soldiers were deployed and luxury boutiques were boarded up, but by late afternoon, most shops had opened, Italian media reported. READ MORE: More than 400,000 protest across France, challenging Macron as Paris clashes erupt Premier Giorgia Meloni announced a raft of measures, including sending an additional 500 soldiers to Milan and tougher penalties for minors, who police said made up a large part of the violent protesters last week. In Milan, police detained several minors as a preventive measure, media reported. While protests in France have claimed most international attention, large demonstrations also rocked many European cities Saturday from Milan to Rome to Madrid, Lisbon and Tirana. The protests encompass a broad range of issues from education and corruption to anti-war movements, pensions and housing. Army vehicles and boarded-up luxury stores in Milan In Milan, huge crowds of mostly young people gathered as night fell, chanting insults to Meloni and holding aloft banners such as "No to lies of the state." A group of protesters dumped manure outside Italy's energy regulator and burned a symbolic, oversized electricity bill, images broadcast on local television showed. The 500 soldiers deployed to Milan came in addition to hundreds already stationed there, supporting about 5,000 police and other security personnel. Authorities used drone surveillance, checks at railway stations, rapid-response units and online monitoring for potential calls to violence. A mayoral hopeful, Pierfrancesco Majorino, who announced his candidacy Thursday, joined the marchers and remarked how peaceful the day was, according to Italian media. He will contest a center-left primary in early 2027. Milan's center-left Mayor Giuseppe Sala, who has held the role since 2016, is not running again. Many stores, particularly luxury boutiques within Milan's fashion district including Omega, Tiffany and Gucci, boarded up their front windows. The Apple store also shut down and remained shut even as others reopened. Security measures extended beyond the city center over concerns protesters could move into other neighborhoods. The protesters ended their march peacefully Saturday evening outside the Milan Polytechnic, more than 3 kilometers (2 miles) from the city center. Officials said Saturday they were investigating a 30-year-old freelance journalist said to be the "mastermind" of the newly formed Oct. 17 movement, which has been the main driver of the recent protests in Italy. Milan police say last week's violence and looting involved about 2,000 very young protesters, many of them "naturalized, second-generation Italians," alongside foreign nationals. Over two days, police arrested 45 people, including 34 minors. A group of about 30 far-right activists, described as hooligans linked to Inter Milan soccer club, made a brief appearance chanting anti-immigrant and anti-Muslim slogans but were isolated by police. Defense Minister Guido Crosetto said the soldiers deployed Saturday were only recently allowed to use plastic restraint ties and only in areas around train stations, not throughout the city. They are not authorized to carry pepper spray or tasers, he said. Protesters try to force entry into Colosseum in Rome People attend a spontaneous demonstration against the rising cost of living, a week after protests ended in clashes and looting in northern cities, in Milan, Italy, on Oct. 24, 2026. Photo by Yara Nardi/Reuters Security was also heightened in Rome, where authorities locked down luxury shopping streets and stepped up controls around the Circus Maximus and Piazza del Popolo. A small number of protesters tried to force their way into the Colosseum, but were ushered out by guards. Elsewhere, several hundred students demonstrated peacefully to stress they were not rioters. "I think the images from last week were truly something terrible, especially for the young people, for the students, for the vast majority of the younger generations who want to study ... and do not accept being represented by those who use issues and needs to devastate entire cities," said Riccardo Ponzio, national president of an Italian far-right student association.
